stories.Headline: Expedia Says Travelers Plan With AI Agents but Book Direct
stories.Summary:
Travelers are increasingly using AI assistants to plan trips, but they still tend to complete their bookings with brands they trust, according to Expedia Group. CEO Ariane Gorin made the point on the company's third-quarter earnings call, held around November 4, 2026. She said the real strength of agentic AI is in discovery, and that people want to book with a brand that will take care of them if something goes wrong. Traffic from agents is high intent, she said, and third-party data shows Expedia leading in citation share in the U.S. She told CNBC the company has not yet seen AI agents change customers' booking habits, and that travel's complexities would make it hard for AI to fully replace travel services.

On the numbers, Expedia grew gross bookings 11% and revenue 12% in the quarter, while B2B bookings rose 19%. Advertising growth slowed to 7% from 13% the prior quarter, and CFO Derek Andersen said product changes are coming to give advertisers better campaign tools. Expedia has partnered with Google in AI Mode, announced a Meta Muse integration expected to go live in the U.S., and is testing OpenAI's new ad products. Qantas is the first partner on Expedia's new agentic template, and Reserve Now, Pay Later has been rolled out across all its brands. Inside the company, an agentic voice experience on Vrbo resolved more than 15% of inbound contacts in its first two months, and travelers who used the new activity agent were twice as likely to book an activity within seven days.

Gorin said agent traffic does not appear to cut into direct traffic, and is either incremental or taken from other paid channels. She added that the volume is too small to draw conclusions, and the company said the economics of its agent partnerships are still being worked out. She also said a small team built an autonomous hotel onboarding agent in less than a quarter, work that once took multiple quarters and many more people. In the booking flow, a compare agent and a property expert agent help travelers weigh hotels, which she said pushes people deeper into the funnel and leads to larger purchases. CNBC reported that Expedia's fourth-quarter guidance came in below analysts' expectations.

Rival Booking Holdings reported a similar picture on its own earnings call on November 3, 2026. CFO Ewout Steenbergen said users of its AI assistants at Priceline and Agoda converted at about twice the rate of non-users, and Agoda assistant users had average booking values about 20% higher. Referrals from large language models still account for significantly less than 1% of Booking.com's room nights, he said, though they have accelerated in recent weeks. Booking Holdings expects a slowdown in the fourth quarter, forecasting a 1% to 3% increase in room nights and a 2% to 4% rise in gross bookings. CEO Glenn Fogel suggested regulation could slow adoption of horizontal personal AI agents in parts of the world, particularly Europe.

stories.Headline: Ricursive AI Releases Ripple-65B Preview: A 65B Dense Open-Weight Model Scoring 80.5 on Terminal-Bench 2.1
stories.Summary:
Ricursive AI released Ripple-65B Preview on November 4, 2026. It is a 65B dense open-weight model pretrained from scratch for agentic coding, and it is a general-purpose variant of the proprietary model behind Ricursive's AI chip design platform. Ricursive reports a score of 80.52 on Terminal-Bench 2.1, which it calls the top self-reported score among US open-weight models. The release includes three checkpoints under Apache 2.0: an instruction-tuned BF16 model, an NVFP4 version, and a BF16 base model.

The model was pretrained on 12 trillion tokens with support for up to 1M context. Ricursive says the full R&D cost was $32M, which it estimates at one-tenth the cost of the prior open-weight agentic coding leader. The model runs in BF16 on datacenter GPUs at 250 tokens per second on 2x B200, and an experimental NVFP4 build targets NVIDIA DGX Spark. Ricursive chose a dense Transformer over Mixture-of-Experts to reduce infrastructure complexity, and training held 40% MFU with simple sharding, no custom kernels and no quantization.

The architecture is thin and deep, with a d_model of 5120 across 80 layers. Ricursive says it built its post-training recipe without buying any post-training data, using its own synthetic pipelines. Its mixed RL recipe uses truncated importance sampling, score centering and a linear length penalty, and it reached 80.5 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 with 1.4M rollouts, which Ricursive puts at roughly 70x fewer than Beam. On other benchmarks it scored 79.1 on SWE-bench Pro v2.0 Hard, 76.5 on SWE-bench Verified, 98.3 on AIME 2025 and 90.5 on HMMT Feb 2026.

Its weak spots include SciCode at 39.4, DeepSWE 1.1 at 44.3, MCP Atlas at 71.67 and GPQA Diamond at 85.2. Ricursive compares Ripple with larger MoE rivals: Reflection Beam at 501B total parameters scored 80.1, Meta Muse Spark Open at 816B scored 76.4, Thinking Machines Inkling at 975B scored 63.8 and NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra at 550B scored 56.4. In a rerun of Terminal-Bench 2.1 with the official Terminus 2 harness at 128K, most rivals dropped, with Beam falling to 70.8 and Muse Spark Open rising to 78.7, still below Ripple's 80.5. Ripple-65B Preview is available on Hugging Face, Together AI, GMI Cloud and OpenRouter, and Fireworks goes live later today.

stories.Headline: “AI will generate nearly half of network traffic by 2035”
stories.Summary:
Nokia published its Global Network Traffic Report on 4 November 2026 from its base in Espoo, Finland, forecasting that artificial intelligence will drive nearly half of global network traffic by 2035. The company says networks will increasingly have to serve connected machines as well as people, with AI pushing up demand for uplink capacity, faster response times and processing closer to users and devices. It expects total traffic to nearly quadruple from 2026 levels to almost 3,789 exabytes per month, with 44% of that driven by AI. DCD, republishing a piece from SDxCentral two days later, put overall growth at 28 percent a year and the AI-native share at roughly 1,681 exabytes per month.

The report breaks the AI figures down further. Traffic generated directly by AI applications and workflows is forecast to rise 60-fold from this year's level, at a 58 percent compound annual growth rate, reaching 987 exabytes per month or 26 percent of global traffic. Another 694 exabytes per month, or 18 percent, is expected to come from AI-influenced traffic such as extra video consumption or online shopping. Agentic AI traffic is projected to grow about 160-fold to 585 exabytes per month, a 76 percent rate, while physical AI traffic from robots and robotaxis is set to grow 105-fold to around 67 exabytes per month, a 68 percent rate. Physical AI is expected to send more than 90% of its traffic over the uplink by 2035.

Most AI traffic is expected to stay in the central cloud, but edge and metro core infrastructure is projected to carry 36% of AI-native traffic by 2035, with the edge handling nine percent and the metro core 27 percent. Nokia links this shift to more efficient models, low-latency needs and data sovereignty requirements, which it says will support a more distributed setup it calls the AI grid. Enterprise AI traffic is forecast to grow at a 59 percent rate, faster than consumer AI, with industrial IoT devices such as cameras, drones and sensors producing about 70 percent of it. Beyond AI, the report says fixed wireless access will account for more than one-third of consumer cellular traffic by 2035.

Pallavi Mahajan, Nokia's Chief Technology and AI Officer, said AI is changing what networks must provide, not only how much traffic they carry. She argued that networks built for traditional internet applications will have to support machines that need real-time responses and strain the uplink, and that network readiness should be central to AI planning rather than an afterthought. Nokia also warned that rising uplink demand will stress cellular networks, noting that latency and jitter begin to climb once a cell's uplink utilization passes 70 percent during busy hours. The report rests on a bottom-up model of consumer, enterprise and AI traffic, combining application usage, device activity and agentic workflows with third-party research, expert review and Nokia lab testing.

stories.Headline: Embodied AI's Next Frontier: Integrating Intelligence with Real-World Systems
stories.Summary:
New research published on November 4, 2026, highlights the challenge of integrating intelligence, sensing, movement, computing, energy management and connectivity into embodied AI systems that can perform reliably in demanding environments. The findings come from a white paper titled From Specialized to General-Purpose: 2026 White Paper on Embodied AI Technology Evolution and Industrial Deployment. It was jointly published by Avnet, the National and Local Co-Built Humanoid Robotics Innovation Center and GYH.AI. Embodied AI combines artificial intelligence with physical systems such as robots and autonomous machines, enabling them to perceive their surroundings, make decisions and act in the physical world.

The research identifies four factors that will influence the shift from specialized embodied AI applications toward broader industrial deployment. System integration is fundamental to performance, because AI models, computing platforms, sensors, motion control, energy management and communications must function as a coordinated system. Technology selection must reflect application requirements, balancing performance, energy efficiency, reliability, scalability and cost. The path to general-purpose embodied AI will be gradual, building on specialized systems designed for defined tasks, and industrial deployment requires lifecycle planning covering testing, software compatibility, component availability, safety, maintenance and long-term support.

Edward Tsaur, VP of Avnet Design Services, Marketing & Communications for Asia Pacific, said much of the discussion around embodied AI focuses on individual technologies, but the next stage will depend on how well they work together. He said the challenge is not just making systems smarter but ensuring they perform reliably, adapt to changing conditions and deliver consistent results over time. He added that across Asia Pacific there is growing interest in intelligent systems for manufacturing, logistics, healthcare and other operational environments. He said collaboration across the technology ecosystem will be critical to translating advances into practical solutions, looking beyond individual components to how hardware, software and engineering expertise can work together.

Separately, Envision announced on November 2, 2026, the world's first commercial deployment of an integrated 800-volt direct current power system in a large-scale AI data center. The system is powering live computing workloads at Envision's Galaxy AI data center campus in Ulanqab, China, delivering power end to end from grid input to computing loads. The 800V DC architecture simplifies AI data center power systems, bringing higher power conversion and watt-to-bit efficiency, a more compact equipment footprint, and reduced cabling and copper requirements. The system combines solid-state transformers, battery energy storage and equipment that adjusts direct-current voltage for computing hardware, coordinated in real time by Envision's Dubhe Controller, supported by its Dubhe Energy Foundation Model.

Kevin Huang, Senior Vice President of Envision Energy and President of Energy Storage and AIDC Power Systems, said AI data centers need power systems that coordinate renewable energy, energy storage and the grid to meet computing demand. He said the integrated 800V DC system is now powering live computing workloads, demonstrating an end-to-end architecture that connects renewable energy supply with computing demand. The Galaxy campus began operations in August 2026 and has a planned capacity of 3GW, designed to support up to one million AI accelerators operating in parallel at full build-out, with more than 80% of its power planned to come from direct renewable electricity connections. Envision aims to scale the approach through its Mission Gobi initiative, which targets 5GW of green AI data center capacity in desert regions worldwide by 2030.

stories.Headline: AMD forecasts Q4 revenue above estimates on data-center growth
stories.Summary:
AMD reported third-quarter results on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, and forecast fourth-quarter revenue above Wall Street estimates. Revenue for the quarter rose 45% from a year earlier to $13.38 billion, ahead of the $13.09 billion analysts expected. Adjusted earnings came to $2.09 per share against a forecast of $1.95, and net income reached $3.47 billion, up 77% from $1.96 billion a year before. Shares rose more than 5% in late trading after the report.

The data-center business was the standout, with revenue up 97% to a record $8.55 billion and making up 64% of total sales, compared with 47% a year earlier. For the fourth quarter, AMD expects revenue of about $17 billion, plus or minus 3%, versus an analyst average of about $16.23 billion. It expects an adjusted gross margin of about 55%, down from 56% in the third quarter and just under the 55.3% the Street had forecast. Outside the data center, the segment that includes PC and game console chips saw revenue fall 8% to $3.7 billion, with gaming revenue down 40%. AMD also expects its server revenue to double year over year in fiscal 2027.

Chief Executive Lisa Su said adoption of agentic AI is only beginning and that she expects demand to grow sharply as AI agents are deployed more widely and handle more complex work. She said AMD has lined up the wafers, substrates, advanced packaging, memory and other components needed to support much higher growth next year, after a trip to Taiwan last month where she met Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. and other supply chain partners. Su also said Anthropic, OpenAI, Microsoft, Oracle and Meta are all using AMD's Helios rack-scale systems in their data centers. Analyst Jacob Bourne of eMarketer said the results should encourage investors after the recent semiconductor selloff and that demand for AI computing is not about to collapse.

The results come as AMD takes market share from Intel, which last week forecast quarterly revenue well below estimates and saw its stock fall more than 30% on Friday. AMD's Helios rack, which pairs the MI455X accelerator with new "Venice" server chips, is in production and set for a larger ramp-up in the fourth quarter, with initial systems being tested at Meta. In February, AMD agreed to sell up to $60 billion of AI chips to Meta over five years, and it has committed $5 billion to Anthropic, which has filed a prospectus for an initial public offering. In September, AMD agreed to buy Fei-Fei Li's World Labs in an $8.2 billion all-stock deal, and it also acquired Taalas, a maker of model-specific chips. Separately, Arm Holdings beat second-quarter revenue estimates, reporting $1.44 billion against the $1.38 billion expected and forecasting third-quarter revenue of $1.54 billion.

stories.Headline: US midterm blue tsunami jolts Asian markets as tighter AI, fiscal scrutiny looms
stories.Summary:
Voters in the US midterm elections on Tuesday delivered a strong rebuke to the artificial intelligence industry, according to The New York Times. They backed governors and legislators who have promised to protect individuals from threats posed by AI, and they pushed back hard on data center construction. Tech executives had given record donations to candidates friendly to the industry, but those efforts did not carry the day. Democratic leaders who won are now eager to investigate the close ties between AI companies and the administration.

The clearest numbers came from local ballot measures on data centers. Of 41 local initiatives across the country, citizens voted to limit or prevent data center development in 40, and more than half of those 41 were in Ohio. Governors and congressional candidates who ran on anti-tech platforms also prevailed in Texas, Ohio, Georgia and other states. Senior Democrats promised to move quickly against the industry once they take up their new authority. The article's full details were cut off before it could list specific rules or legislation.

Darrell West, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, a think tank, said to expect a tsunami of new rules and oversight. Democrats' stated aim is to scrutinize the relationship between AI firms and the administration, though the available text does not name which senior Democrats made the promises. President Trump has taken the position that the industry should be mostly free of regulations that could slow the country's race against China for AI leadership. The Republican-led Congress and White House have done little to regulate the industry over the past two years.

That hands-off approach stirred broad anger, the article said. Communities across the country protested the building of giant, energy-hungry data centers near their homes, and many objected to Republican leaders' reluctance to impose AI safety rules. Fears have grown about the safety of advanced models, the threat to jobs and even the possibility that AI could end humanity. What comes next appears to be a period of closer scrutiny of the industry, though the articles provided do not lay out a timeline or specific measures.

stories.Headline: Nigeria: Voter Audit - Ai and Electoral Integrity
stories.Summary:
Nigeria's Independent National Electoral Commission, known as INEC, announced that it has built AI-driven Automated Biometric Identification Systems and facial recognition tools into an audit of the national voter register, which now stands at more than 103 million citizens. The tools are meant to use machine learning to remove double registrations, ghost entries and underage voters. The announcement was reported on 4 November 2026, and the Leadership newspaper's editorial board called it a significant technological shift. It said the step looks laudable on paper but warned that technology must support transparency and cannot replace human accountability or public trust. The paper also noted that the register is the main pillar on which the credibility of the 2027 general elections rests.

The editorial listed the changes and safeguards it wants to see attached to the audit. INEC should publish an operational framework explaining the parameters its biometric and facial recognition tools use to flag discrepancies, and it should open its AI systems to independent technical audits. Cybersecurity experts, political party representatives and civil society groups should be given access to examine the system's logic. No voter, it said, should be removed solely because of an automated alert, and flagged people should receive clear notice, a chance at physical verification at local government electoral offices, and a simple appeal process. It also asked INEC to guard against AI-generated deepfakes, manipulated media and cyber intrusion into voter databases.

The paper expressed particular concern for Northern Nigeria, which accounts for a large share of the electorate and where digital infrastructure is uneven and internet connections are often unreliable. It argued that rural women, displaced people without updated identification and manual labourers may have faces or fingerprints altered by environmental exposure. If low-resolution hardware or rigid algorithms read those changes as fraud, it warned, hundreds of thousands of legitimate voters could be quietly dropped from the roll. Because regional representation and electoral leverage are tied to registered voter numbers, it said such deletions could cause serious political friction and deepen distrust.

Separately, the former INEC chairman Attahiru Jega spoke at a national summit in Abuja on AI, foreign information manipulation and electoral information integrity. He called for strong safeguards for information integrity before the 2027 elections and urged electoral bodies in Africa to consider chatbots built on officially verified data so citizens can check what they read. The current INEC chairman, Joash Amupitan, said public awareness alone is no longer enough against well-funded, coordinated manipulation and called for a trusted, rights-respecting system linking authorities, security bodies, fact-checkers, media and platforms. Information Minister Mohammed Idris, represented by Nigerian Press Council head Dili Ezughah, noted that President Bola Tinubu signed the amended Electoral Act 2026 on 18 February, providing for mandatory electronic transmission of polling unit results, and urged summit participants to produce practical commitments such as stronger verification and rapid correction of false information.

stories.Headline: Tovi Announces AI-Powered Music Creation for Its Interactive Toy in Early 2027
stories.Summary:
Tovi, a screen-free, voice-interactive plush toy for children ages 3 to 10, announced on November 5, 2026 that it plans to add AI-powered music creation in early 2027. The feature will let children turn their own ideas into original music through conversation and play. It will sit alongside the toy's existing personalized stories, games, riddles, and knowledge-building activities. The company also plans to offer access to popular songs through a third-party streaming service, but the original music creation is the main addition.

The toy is sold through HeyTovi.com and is designed to work without a screen during normal use. Tovi says the new feature gives children a chance to take part in making musical content instead of only listening to existing songs. The company describes the update as a new creative activity inside the toy's current voice-based experience. The announcement was distributed as a press release through Newsfile, and the articles note that Postmedia did not review that content.

Tovi says its existing system has been tested across thousands of conversation scenarios and interaction flows to check how it handles requests, declines unsuitable content, and redirects personal concerns to parents or trusted adults. The companion parent app lets caregivers set the child's age and interests, review text conversation transcripts, and delete conversation history. The company states that its platform complies with the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act and that raw voice recordings are not permanently stored during normal operation. Tovi also says it offers unlimited stories, games, riddles, and questions without a monthly subscription.

Separately, Tovi was named Best Interactive Toy in the United States for 2026 by Best of Best Review, a recognition the company cites as support for its approach. The articles report that the toy has no camera. The company's business contact is listed as Nicole, at the email address given in the press release. The articles do not say how the music feature will be priced or how it will be built, and they give no details beyond the early 2027 timeline.

stories.Headline: “AI Sandbox” workshop allows faculty and staff to put AI through its paces in low-stakes environment
stories.Summary:
A University of Pittsburgh workshop called the "AI Sandbox," run through the Faculty and Staff Development Program, gave faculty and staff a low-stakes chance to test how AI handles basic writing tasks and whether it is worth using. The session was led by J. D. Wright, an English faculty member who also consults for the University Center for Teaching and Learning. Participants practiced writing prompts, refining them to get different versions of a document, and judging whether the results helped them. The article was published on November 6, 2026.

Wright told attendees that longer and more detailed prompts generally produce more complete and accurate output, and he urged people not to accept the first answer. He described AI as more like a conversation with a colleague than a source of single correct answers, and as a tool for generating options rather than final truths. In one exercise, students asked an AI to draft a social media invitation to a department event, and reactions varied: some were pleased with the layout, tone, and extra details, while others found it made assumptions they had not requested. Wright noted that asking for 100 paper titles takes little more effort than asking for five, and that a few of them may be strong. He also suggested asking the AI to point out what a user might be overlooking, predict how an output could be misread, and recommend a workflow for future tasks.

Wright was candid that his own use is limited, saying he rarely uses AI to create full documents, though he recommends it for first drafts that can be revised. One participant said she likes the tool but does not fully trust it, since she still has to check its work and is unsure it saves her time. Wright's central test for any use was whether it saved time or produced a better result than the user would have on their own. The article reports these views without describing any broader institutional policy.

Separately, a Nebraska Public Media report dated November 5, 2026, describes a different approach at the University of Nebraska, where President Jeffrey Gold announced university-wide expectations for AI use in a Thursday message. The executive memorandum bars using institutional and research data in personal AI subscriptions, prohibits tools that claim ownership of user data or use it to train other models, and makes users responsible for checking outputs, facts, and citations. The university is providing an enterprise ChatGPT license that faculty and staff must complete training to access, with Gold asking everyone to move to it by the end of 2026, and faculty can request enterprise access for students. Copilot is already available system-wide, and a new NU AI Governance Group with faculty, staff, and units such as the NU AI Institute, legal, and finance will help implement the memorandum. Gold said faculty and staff still decide whether AI is used in their courses or research, and that the rules are meant to keep pace with fast-changing technology.

stories.Headline: European Parliament President Metsola warns against using AI to draft laws
stories.Summary:
On November 5, 2026, the European Commission said in its annual simplification report that it has begun using artificial intelligence to draft new laws and to simplify existing ones. The report, presented that Wednesday, described new digital tools that help staff spot overlaps, inconsistencies and duplicates across legal acts. The Commission is also strengthening legal training and staffing so that new rules are not overly complicated. The changes form part of a wider plan to cut red tape and administrative costs for businesses across areas such as tech, agriculture, migration, environmental protection and taxation.

The Commission reports that it has produced 12 so-called omnibus packages to revise and simplify existing legislation, which it estimates will save the EU economy €22.3 billion in costs. It also launched 874 infringement procedures between August 2025 and July 2026, which the report describes as the highest number in the last 10 years. The Commission is pressing member states to stop "gold-plating," the practice of adding extra requirements when turning EU law into national law, and it expects to sign a pact against gold-plating with governments by the end of the year. Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis, who oversees simplification, called for a joint effort with member countries. He warned that some omnibus proposals may end the legislative process with much less simplification than the Commission proposed, because governments keep weakening them during negotiations.

Responsibility for the simplification drive rests with the Commission, which is led by Ursula von der Leyen, who has made simplification a central part of her second term. Dombrovskis said the agenda is already changing daily life for small business owners, who now spend less time on forms. Separately, European Parliament President Roberta Metsola has urged lawmakers to be careful about adopting AI in decision-making. Speaking to MEPs, she said AI can help draft amendments but cannot replace debate or the critical thinking that complex legal decisions require, and that elected representatives must remain personally responsible for their decisions. She wants Parliament to be open about its AI use so citizens can hold their representatives to account.

The articles show that the institutions are moving in parallel, with the Commission leaning into AI for drafting and review while Parliament works on guidelines. Parliament's administration is preparing rules based on transparency, keeping confidential documents off public platforms and checking all AI output carefully. Staff have been required to disclose AI use since 2024, but MEPs are not yet bound by that rule for speeches or amendments, and binding it would likely require a change to Parliament's Rules of Procedure considered by the Committee on Constitutional Affairs. Parliament is also building an internal platform called EPGenAI Hub for sensitive data. The articles do not say when the rules for MEPs will be adopted.

stories.Headline: Figma banks on AI credits, in-house model to lift margins
stories.Summary:
Figma is using its AI features, sold through a credit system and powered by its own in-house model, to improve its profit margins, according to finance chief Praveer Melwani, who spoke to Reuters on Wednesday. The company raised its annual revenue and operating margin forecast, citing demand for its AI tools, including a design assistant called Figma Agent. Its shares, however, fell 8 per cent in extended trading after third-quarter gross margin came in slightly below estimates. Melwani said the company is increasingly running its product on its first-party model, which brings lower latency, higher quality and a more efficient price point.

Through October, more than 80 per cent of Figma's large paid customers were using AI credits every week, which Melwani said has boosted monetization. The company changed its pricing to give customers more AI credits than they had originally paid for, and this also drove higher credit usage and retention. Melwani added that the utilization rate of those add-ons rose by 40 per cent after the repricing. Figma has more than doubled the share of work handled by its proprietary post-trained design model. The company now expects 2026 revenue of between $1.497 billion and $1.499 billion, up from an earlier forecast of $1.463 billion to $1.467 billion.

The revised outlook also calls for adjusted operating income of $158 million to $163 million and an operating margin of 11 per cent, compared with earlier projections of $125 million to $135 million and 9 per cent. Melwani, speaking for the company, framed these gains as the result of its shift to the in-house model and its credit-based AI pricing. Third-quarter revenue jumped 43 per cent to $391.4 million, beating estimates, while gross margin of 80 per cent was just below the expected 81 per cent. The report was published by TechGig on November 6, 2026, drawing on Reuters reporting from the same day. The articles do not say how the share price moved after the initial extended-trading drop.

stories.Headline: Democrats line up AI testing, liability and power-bill measures for the new Congress
stories.Summary:
Democrats plan to introduce a wave of bills on artificial intelligence and data centers when they take control of Congress in January, Reuters reported on November 6, citing lawmakers, aides and advocates. The outgoing Republican-led Congress mostly promoted AI development and passed no restrictions on it. Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, expected to become majority leader, said protecting consumers from rising electricity bills linked to data centers would be a priority. Representative Lori Trahan of Massachusetts plans legislation requiring independent experts to test leading AI models against safety standards. Trahan's office says she also plans a bill clarifying when AI companies are liable for harm their systems cause.

Committee control would give Democrats subpoenas and hearings before any bill passes. Representative Greg Casar of Texas, chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, wants AI executives to testify under oath. In October, House Democratic committee leaders asked OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Google and SpaceX to detail their security practices. Representative Zoe Lofgren of California, who is seeking to chair the House Science Committee, said Democrats would pursue responsible regulation of AI while also fostering innovation.

President Trump has rejected mandatory AI rules, and overriding a veto requires two-thirds of both chambers. Ed Mills of Raymond James said the probability of legislation is much higher than people expect, pointing to must-pass annual bills as a possible vehicle. The plans follow a CNBC voter poll finding that 56% of voters called AI and data centers a crucial or major factor in their vote. Tech shares sold off on Thursday over concern that a new Congress would slow AI development, Reuters said.

stories.Headline: AI Productivity to Add $28 Billion to $84 Billion to India's GDP: Cognizant Study
stories.Summary:
A Cognizant study released in early November 2026 estimates that AI-enabled productivity could add between $28 billion and $84 billion a year to India's nominal GDP under realistic adoption scenarios. The same study found that most business leaders have not yet seen financial returns from the technology. The size of the gain depends on how widely AI is adopted and how much of the productivity improvement turns into economic output. Cognizant's model also sets a theoretical ceiling of $830 billion a year, which assumes AI is used across the entire workforce and that all gains become output. The company says that ceiling is not a forecast and that all the figures are modelled estimates based on self-reported survey responses.

The research surveyed 700 enterprise employees and 75 C-suite and business executives at companies with revenues from $100 million to more than $10 billion across 10 major industries. About 97 percent of the employees said AI had improved their productivity, with an average reported uplift of 15 percent. Indian employees were more prepared than their global peers, with 74 percent having completed AI training against 56 percent globally. Gains differed by sector, with 38 percent of healthcare employees reporting improvements above 20 percent, while manufacturing had the lowest share reporting any gain at 82 percent.

Business leaders said only 36 percent of employees, on average, have access to AI tools, and 84 percent had not yet seen AI lower their costs. Cognizant's India chief, Rajesh Varrier, said India has a strong foundation to capture more value from AI, but that this will require wider adoption of AI tools across enterprises, continued investment in skilling and an environment that supports responsible AI at scale. The company says organisations need to broaden access to AI tools, keep workforce skills current, extend AI into more complex and higher-value work and improve how they measure business outcomes. Its stated aim is to turn gains at the level of individual workers into broader enterprise and economic value.

A separate report from the Ayre Think Tank, published the same day, puts the potential boost at $79.1 billion to India's GDP over ten years under a moderate scenario, with a range of about $39.6 billion to $118.7 billion. That report notes that India is home to about 382 million people aged 15 to 29, and that nearly 89 percent of young Indians want to use AI for education or work within the next year. It also flags that only about two-thirds of young people own a mobile phone and that around 30 percent are outside employment, education or training. Calvin Ayre of the think tank pointed to a national plan announced in August 2026 to train ten million young people in AI skills within a year.

stories.Headline: Where US Courts Stand on AI Training
stories.Summary:
Courts in the United States have not yet settled whether AI developers may train their systems on copyrighted works without permission, and the rulings so far point in different directions. On 29 September 2026 the US Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit held that training an AI legal research tool on case summaries was not fair use, the copying exception in US copyright law. Two California judges had ruled for AI developers on training in June 2025, but on different grounds, so neither decision binds other courts. The judges weigh four factors when deciding fair use, including the purpose of the copying and its effect on the market for the original work. In AI cases the dispute centres on whether training is transformative, meaning it serves a new purpose, and whether it harms the market for the source material.

A summary judgment ruling, issued before trial when the key facts are not disputed, can settle the question for the parties in one case. The US Copyright Office's report of 9 May 2025 said some AI training may qualify as fair use and some may not, leaving the matter to courts and possibly to Congress. The question is also being argued across the Atlantic. Advocate General Maciej Szpunar gave a non-binding opinion on 3 November 2026 in case C-250/25, a Hungarian news publisher's claim against Google's Gemini chatbot. He told the EU's top court it should find the training questions inadmissible, but offered provisional views anyway.

In those views, training on copyrighted material is generally lawful in the EU if the developer avoids pirate sources, respects paywalls, bot blocks and machine-readable opt-outs, and shows it took steps to stop the model reproducing specific works. OpenAI asked a New York court on 4 September 2026 to rule that training its models is fair use, and that request remains pending. Meanwhile the Rio Times reports that Brazilian and Norwegian media groups won court orders suspending new terms from Meta, the owner of Facebook and Instagram. Because no court has settled the core question, developers and rights holders on both sides of the Atlantic are still waiting for a binding answer.

stories.Headline: SEALSQ, WISeQey, SEALCOIN and Eco Wave Power Sign Three-Year MoU and Demonstrate Trusted Energy Transactions for AI Data Centers
stories.Summary:
On November 5, 2026, SEALSQ, its parent WISeQey, sister company SEALCOIN AG and Eco Wave Power U.S. Inc. announced a three-year Memorandum of Understanding to explore how renewable wave energy can securely connect with digital services and energy buyers. The partners have demonstrated the technology at Eco Wave Power's wave-energy installation in Jaffa Port, Israel. The demonstration linked physical energy production to an authenticated digital twin, so the origin and integrity of production data could be verified, and used that trusted data to start a secure, auditable transaction between known counterparties under predefined commercial terms. The articles say the proof of concept is shown in a video linked in the release.

The MoU sets out a framework for further development and evaluation of these capabilities, with the main aim of connecting renewable energy producers to AI data centers, industrial facilities, energy aggregators and utilities. The companies argue that as electricity demand from AI infrastructure grows, trusted digital systems could let producers share authenticated production information with qualified buyers and automate transactions. The collaboration also intends to explore integrating SEALSQ's QS7001 post-quantum secure element and quantum-resistant cryptography to support the long-term security needs of critical infrastructure. The releases state plainly that the initial demonstration is not a physical electricity supply agreement or a completed financial settlement, and that future deployments depend on technical validation, regulation and separate commercial contracts.

Carlos Moreira, Founder and CEO of SEALSQ, said the collaboration extends the WISeQey ecosystem into renewable energy, where secure connectivity and trusted transactions could support new digital services. Inna Braverman, Founder and CEO of Eco Wave Power, said wave energy aims to become part of the energy infrastructure for AI and that the demonstration suggests wave producers could eventually transact directly with data centers and other buyers. Jonathan Llamas, Chief Product & Strategy Officer of SEALCOIN, said the work moves machines from exchanging information to acting on trusted physical-world data. Eco Wave Power U.S., its AI and data center arm, will lead its side of the collaboration and has begun talks with data center developers and infrastructure partners about possible future supply.

The collaboration will be presented at Quantum Days 2026 on November 19 at Hôtel Barrière Le Majestic in Cannes, France, where a live demonstration and fireside chat with Braverman, Llamas and WISeQey representatives is scheduled for 13:45 CET. Eco Wave Power, listed on Nasdaq as WAVE, describes its onshore technology as generating power from waves at breakwaters, jetties and piers, and says it operates Israel's first grid-connected wave energy station and launched a pilot at the Port of Los Angeles with Shell Marine Renewable Energy. It also reports a project pipeline of 404.7 MW across Portugal, Taiwan and India. The articles do not say what the financial terms of the MoU are or when a commercial deployment might begin.

stories.Headline: Conflicting With Employees' Sincerely Held Religious Beliefs- AI
stories.Summary:
Two Utah? No, let me give the paragraphs as requested. In June 2026, Erin Maus, a Unitarian Universalist software engineer in North Carolina, asked her employer, an entertainment technology company, for an exemption from AI use. She said the ethical and environmental effects of AI conflicted with her beliefs, and the company granted the request, allowing her to write code by hand instead. Later, David Durman, a Humanist research administrator at the University of Kentucky, received a similar religious accommodation exempting him from AI at work.

He argued that generative AI runs contrary to human wellbeing, pointing to its environmental impact, job losses, and what he called theft of human creativity. The university's Office of Equal Opportunity approved his request after finding that it posed no undue burden on his department. The article, written by Laura Lawless of Squire Patton Boggs and published November 5, 2026, says employers should expect more such requests as religious and ethical leaders raise concerns about AI. It draws a comparison to the COVID-19 period, when accommodation requests over masking and vaccination rose sharply.

Under Title VII, little is required to show that a belief is sincere, and employers should avoid demanding proof such as anti-AI religious texts or statements from spiritual advisors. The article also notes that Title VII does not protect social, political, or economic philosophies or personal preferences, so employers should consider whether an objection is rooted in a moral belief system or reflects a secular policy view. Under the Supreme Court's 2023 decision in Groff v. DeJoy, an employer must show substantial increased costs to deny an accommodation, and speculative hardships do not suffice.

The article advises employers to ask whether an employee objects to some AI tools or all of them, and to craft individualized accommodations where possible. It also suggests checking whether AI use is truly necessary for a role or only preferred for efficiency. Employers should update accommodation policies and train HR staff and managers to recognize requests without requiring magic words like religion or spiritual objection. The article notes that objections to AI are a new and morally complex area, and it does not describe any court decisions yet on the issue.

stories.Headline: AI Shopping Agents on Black Friday: Who Pays for Mistakes
stories.Summary:
Visa predicted in December 2025 that millions of shoppers would use AI agents to buy things by the 2026 holiday season, but on 27 October its chief executive Ryan McInerney said such volumes were very small. Meta launched its Muse agent on 8 September, and it asks US users to approve every purchase total and pays through Stripe's Link wallet or a single-use virtual card. Amazon blocked Muse from Amazon.com in September, saying Meta never asked permission and the agent did not identify itself as AI. Black Friday falls on 27 November this year, and it is the deadline Visa set for itself.

Muse pays with a saved method at more than one million businesses that accept Link, and elsewhere Link issues a single-use virtual card limited to the approved purchase. Meta says Link's protections for lost or damaged items, price drops and returns cover eligible Muse orders, but that is a product promise and not a legal right. Mark Zuckerberg said on 21 October that Meta plans to charge businesses a fee when Muse helps close a sale, and computing costs are one reason the agent is limited to the US and Canada. Google's agentic checkout in Search has been able to buy a tracked item at a shopper's target price since November 2025, and in May Google announced Universal Cart, a cross-retailer cart that pays with Google Pay. OpenAI stepped back from Instant Checkout in March, saying the first version lacked flexibility, and its dots agent launched on 29 September with rules that require approval for chosen actions.

Regulation E caps a consumer's loss at $50 when a lost or stolen debit card is reported within two business days, but it excludes transfers by someone the consumer gave access to, and the law does not say whether an AI agent counts. Credit cards fall under the Truth in Lending Act and Regulation Z, where unauthorised use turns on whether someone had actual, implied or apparent authority over the account. Carla Sanchez-Adams of the National Consumer Law Center told Bloomberg Law in June that federal lending and transfer laws, along with network chargeback and return standards, still apply when an agent uses a person's credit card. Eric Goldberg of Davis Wright Tremaine said in the same report that debit cards give somewhat less protection and that stablecoins allow no refunds or chargebacks.

Mastercard added trust and intelligence services to its Agent Pay programme on 30 September, including a probability score now in US testing that estimates whether an agent started a transaction. Its Verifiable Intent framework records the shopper's identity, the limits given to the agent, the shopper's consent and the actions taken. Mastercard chief executive Michael Miebach said on the 29 October results call that he expects the trend to build through the holidays, though he conceded merchants vary widely in readiness. Visa's finance chief Chris Suh told Fortune in June that he was hesitant to lean into the stablecoin and agentic commerce narratives too much, noting that most of Visa's business has nothing to do with either.

stories.Headline: Supermicro taps SambaNova to power AI inference racks alongside Nvidia
stories.Summary:
SambaNova and Supermicro have announced a partnership to build and sell AI inference systems that combine SambaNova's SN50 chips with Nvidia GPUs, and Supermicro initially plans to work with 10,000 SN50 chips. The systems split inference work between the two kinds of processor. Nvidia GPUs handle prefill, which means processing incoming prompts, while SambaNova's fifth-generation reconfigurable dataflow units handle decode, which means generating responses. SambaNova says this pairing can improve performance and efficiency while extending the useful life of GPUs customers already own.

Supermicro will integrate, test, deliver and support the systems for customers, including on-site service. SambaNova engineers will get models running and tuned on the SN50 chips and help Supermicro with deployments. The companies plan to start with NeoClouds and sovereign clouds, then expand to enterprises that run AI in their own data centers. Rodrigo Liang, co-founder and CEO of SambaNova, said that agentic AI is the next wave of inference and needs to run everywhere. He said customers can now order SN50 units alongside GPUs from a partner they trust.

A separate announcement from Supermicro, dated the same day, describes a KV-cache storage solution built with IBM and Nvidia to speed up AI inference. The solution combines Supermicro Petascale storage servers, IBM Storage Scale software, Nvidia Dynamo inference software and Nvidia Spectrum-X Ethernet switches. Keeping key-value cache data outside local GPU memory is meant to raise GPU utilization and throughput, which matters more as businesses run agentic and long-context AI workflows. Charles Liang, president and CEO of Supermicro, said the approach removes bottlenecks that limit GPU efficiency for these inference workloads.

In tests run by Supermicro and Nvidia with a 120-billion-parameter model, a persistent KV cache cut time-to-first-token by up to 56 times on prompts of 130,000 tokens. When input length grew from 30,000 to 130,000 tokens, time-to-first-token rose by only 0.377 seconds with the cache, compared with 29.55 seconds without it. The companies also say the rack-level integration and on-site deployment services can shorten rollout time from weeks to days. Sam Werner, general manager of IBM Storage, and Shruti Koparkar, AI Inference Product Lead at Nvidia, both described the work as a step toward more scalable and cost-efficient enterprise inference.

stories.Headline: Sysdig AI Defense Targets Compromised Agents at the Moment They Act
stories.Summary:
Sysdig launched AI Defense on November 4, a product that applies automated runtime security and governance to AI agents, aiming to stop unauthorized actions before they finish. The launch responds to a shift in which AI systems move from answering questions to performing actions such as shipping code, changing infrastructure, and accessing production systems. Sysdig argues that the operating system kernel is the only reliable record of what actually ran, since an agent deployed in the morning may behave differently by the afternoon. Its central claim is that an agent's own explanation needs an independent check against what really happened. The timing matters because many enterprises have approved AI tools without equivalent controls over their actions.

The product monitors every action an agent takes, from its origin to completion, including underlying kernel processes that might quietly change how the agent functions. It maintains a live inventory of agents, harnesses, models, MCP servers, skills, and plugins built from runtime telemetry, and it can trace each agent to an accountable human. Risky actions can be detected, held for human review, or blocked before they complete, using policy templates whose rules are mapped to the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications. Sysdig's founder and CTO, Loris Degioanni, said blocking must happen in real time, in line with the action, and before it finishes.

Actions are recorded as they occur, creating audit-quality immutable records. The company cites IBM Institute for Business Value findings that enterprises expect to deploy an average of 1,661 AI agents by 2027, a 38 per cent increase from current deployments. Sysdig presents this as a product that changes the placement of organizational authority, so that approval is checked at execution rather than left inside an agent's instructions. Degioanni frames the problem as agents gaining the speed to act faster than human teams can review.

Responsibility for setting the rules and deciding which actions are legitimate remains with the organization, since a security product can enforce a rule but cannot independently decide whether a given export belongs in an approved workflow. The company also says policies start in alert mode, reporting activity without stopping it. The vendor's own claims about product behavior have not been independently verified. The launch sits within a competitive field where NVIDIA's OpenShell emphasizes isolated execution and credentials kept outside the agent workload, while CrowdStrike has announced an integration with NVIDIA OpenShell and a planned NVIDIA Sentry integration.

These approaches place security decisions outside the model's judgment, but they differ in where they check authority. The articles do not establish which approach performs better across equivalent tasks. Buyers are advised to verify supported platforms, integrations, and enforcement points, and to test whether a blocked action is stopped before it begins or only interrupted after it starts. Whether these controls hold up in practice will depend on that testing.

stories.Summary:
On November 5, 2026, Clark University published a podcast episode in which Arthur C. Evans Jr., CEO of the American Psychological Association, spoke with Jonathan Rodriguez, a graduate student studying psychology. The conversation was recorded earlier that month during Evans's visit to the Clark University campus. The episode, part of the series called Challenge. Change., focuses on how artificial intelligence may affect the mental health of young people. The discussion was produced by Melissa Hanson for the university.

The article draws a comparison between artificial intelligence and social media, which researchers studied as it spread among teenagers. Researchers at that time noted that heavy engagement with the technology disturbed young people's sleep, among other effects. Evans and Rodriguez discuss the challenges and opportunities that artificial intelligence presents for youth mental health. The article does not describe any new rule, requirement, or policy that would change because of this discussion. Evans is quoted describing artificial intelligence as the biggest experiment on the human brain and behavior in the history of humanity.

He says the long-term effects of many of its features are not known, particularly for young people. The article presents these as his views during the conversation and does not attribute to him any specific plan or recommendation. The article is a university feature rather than a news report of an event, and it includes no data on how many young people are affected. It does not say whether further episodes, studies, or APA actions are planned. Listeners can find the episode on Spotify, Apple Podcasts, and other podcast platforms.

stories.Headline: Bengaluru Skill Summit 2026 Concludes with Focus on AI, Future-Ready Skills and Global Opportunities
stories.Summary:
The second edition of the Bengaluru Skill Summit 2026 wrapped up in Bengaluru, Karnataka, on November 6 after three days of discussions, industry and academic engagements, and knowledge-sharing sessions. Organised by the Department of Skill Development, Entrepreneurship and Livelihood with the Karnataka Skill Development Corporation and the Karnataka Skill Development Authority, the event drew a total footfall of 9,500 people, including government leaders, policymakers, industry representatives, academics, international stakeholders and young people. Japan was the Country Partner for this edition. Under the theme "Workforce 2030: Scale, Systems, Synergy," the summit focused on building a future-ready workforce and strengthening Karnataka's skills ecosystem. The programme was organised around four tracks: Emerging Skills, covering green jobs, AI, Industry 4.0 and the digital economy; Skills for All, covering women, youth, informal workers and the gig economy; Innovation, showcasing best practices in skilling; and Global Skills, aimed at workforce employability and mobility abroad.

On the second day, November 4, the state launched Yuva Udyoga Sethu, a digital employment platform meant to connect young jobseekers from Karnataka with employers. The day also saw the Expo Zone opened and a Skillathon held, a national ideas competition on labour market intelligence, which was won by InUnity from Mangaluru. Another ceremony recognised 138 medal winners from the Karnataka Skill Olympics 2025-26, comprising 59 gold, 45 silver and 34 bronze medalists, across more than 50 skill categories. The summit's sessions were led by senior officials and experts, including Chief Minister D. K. Shivakumar, who launched the employment platform, and Minister Dr. Sharanprakash R. Patil, who inaugurated the Expo Zone. On the final day, Debashree Mukherjee, Secretary of the Union Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship, argued that children need to be shown clear pathways into work, saying the system is failing them if it does not do so.

Sanjeev Kumar Gupta, CEO of the Karnataka Digital Economy Mission, said the most valuable worker is one who works alongside AI rather than competing with it. Discussions on the final day also covered hands-on careers, the care economy and how AI can augment rather than replace workers. The summit closed with a clear message that Karnataka's workforce planning should rest on skills matched to industry demand, inclusion of underrepresented groups, and preparation for global mobility. The organisers have pointed to the forthcoming Karnataka Skills Intelligence System, which the Skillathon ideas are meant to help shape, as one way those priorities will be carried forward.

stories.Headline: Looking Past the Chips: Tuttle Capital Launches the AI Bottleneck ETF (DLAY)
stories.Summary:
Tuttle Capital Management, a Riverside, Connecticut firm that issues thematic and rules-based ETFs, announced on November 5, 2026 the launch of the Tuttle Capital AI Bottleneck ETF, which trades on Cboe BZX under the ticker DLAY. The fund is actively managed and invests across nine sleeves of companies that the adviser believes are the industrial chokepoints behind the buildout of artificial intelligence. Those sleeves include advanced chip packaging, memory, photonics, power and grid equipment, nuclear fuel, chip-making equipment, industrial materials, cooling systems, and data center siting. Unlike many AI-themed funds, DLAY excludes companies whose main business is designing or making AI chips for sale, operating large cloud infrastructure, or building large language models. The fund's rules set several limits and weightings.

Holdings are weighted using a proprietary AI Bottleneck Score built on supply concentration, order backlogs, and demand inelasticity, and the fund is rebalanced quarterly. At least 80% of net assets must be invested in companies scored this way. A company must meet at least two of three tests to be eligible, and single names are capped at 4% while each sleeve is capped at 18%. Non-U.S. holdings may reach 35% of assets, with emerging-market holdings capped at 25% combined. The total annual operating expense ratio is 0.75%, and the fund is excluded from issuers under U.S. sanctions or on the Commerce Department's Entity List.

Matthew Tuttle, founder and CEO of Tuttle Capital Management, said that many investors are focused on the same handful of AI stocks and that the fund was built to target parts of the buildout that receive less attention. He argued that the industry needs these inputs no matter which chip or chatbot ultimately succeeds. The fund's disclosures stress that its thesis depends on bottlenecks persisting, and that they may be resolved through added capacity, substitution, falling demand, or policy changes. The prospectus also flags concentration in Taiwan and China, currency and emerging-market risk, and the fact that the fund is new and has no operating history.

Investors are directed to the prospectus at tuttlecap.com or by calling 1-800-773-3863 before investing. The launch places DLAY among a growing set of AI-related funds that look beyond the most widely held chip and software stocks. The articles do not describe any investor reaction, early trading, or assets gathered, so the fund's performance and future size remain unknown. Distribution is handled by Paralel Distributors LLC, which the release says is not affiliated with Tuttle Capital Management.

stories.Headline: 3 charged in scheme to use AI to impersonate CEOs and attorneys to steal $129 million
stories.Summary:
Three people have been indicted in New York on charges of wire fraud and aggravated identity theft for allegedly using artificial intelligence to impersonate corporate executives and attorneys in a scheme that prosecutors say stole about $129 million. The indictment, filed in a U.S. District Court in New York, names Jacob Soall, 41, Sharon Hazan, 54, and Guy Sheetrit, 42. Prosecutors announced the charges on a Thursday, and the three were arrested between June and September. The defendants, who come from Spain, the United Kingdom, Israel and the United Arab Emirates, were also charged with money laundering.

According to court documents, the group targeted thousands of companies worldwide over more than a year and a half. Their victims included hospital systems in Missouri and California, a bank in Rhode Island, a financial technology company in the United Kingdom, a mutual fund company in Massachusetts and a pet food company in Florida. The scheme usually began with an email that appeared to come from a chief executive, asking an accounting employee for help with a confidential financial transaction. A phone or video call followed, in which the defendants used AI to mimic the executive's voice and sometimes his or her image. The defendants then directed the employee to contact an attorney at a major law firm, whom the group also impersonated.

The impersonated attorney would instruct the employee to wire large payments to bank accounts around the world. The money was then converted into cryptocurrency to conceal its origin before being distributed to the three defendants and others involved. Soall mainly posed as attorneys from the United Kingdom and used a handwritten script titled "Lawyer Call," according to the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York. An FBI official said the case shows how advanced technology can be used for large-scale fraud and that the bureau is adapting its capabilities to pursue such criminals. Lawyers for Soall and Sheetrit did not immediately respond to requests for comment, and it was not clear whether Hazan had an attorney.

The charges carry significant penalties if the defendants are convicted. Each charge other than aggravated identity theft carries a maximum sentence of 20 years, while aggravated identity theft carries a maximum of two years. Hazan was previously convicted in 2008 in a New York court of conspiracy to commit bank fraud. The group members reportedly go by nicknames including "Rocky Balboa," "Superman Cash" and "Fat Boy." Court documents describe the case as a warning about how readily AI tools can be used to deceive businesses.

stories.Headline: Pathways World School Gurgaon Sets New Direction for Responsible AI in Education
stories.Summary:
Pathways World School in Gurgaon held a two-day workshop on 25 and 26 September to set up a framework for responsible use of AI in its classrooms. The workshop included students, faculty, school leaders, its AI Advisory Group, IT teams and parents, and it was led by Rita Bateson, co-founder and Director of Education at Eblana Learning and a former IB curriculum leader. The school aimed to use AI to support teaching and learning while protecting independent thinking, creativity and academic integrity. Rather than banning the technology or ignoring it, the school chose to build a structured approach with the people who will use it daily. The initiative was reported in a press release distributed by VMPL and carried by ANI in early November 2026.

The first day of the workshop covered governance, risk management and guidelines on academic integrity, data privacy and student wellbeing. The second day moved to implementation, with AI literacy for administrators, resource creation, safe data handling and planning for initial classroom pilots. Under the proposed framework, students will be expected to question AI-generated responses and recognise possible bias and inaccuracies. They will also need to protect personal information and be open about how AI contributed to their work. Teachers will keep full professional judgement over teaching and assessment, and they will model the responsible technology use they expect from students.

Pranay Jain, Director of Pathways World School, said the initiative continues the school's long record of educational innovation. He pointed out that in 2003 Pathways Gurgaon became the first school in India to offer campus-wide wireless connectivity, and said the school now applies the same pioneering approach to AI. Malcolm Nicolson, School Director of Pathways Gurgaon, said schools have a duty to help students handle a technology already part of their daily lives. He said the school is setting clear principles and building practices and literacy so students use AI to think more deeply rather than less.

The school is now finalising its AI policy and writing age-appropriate guidance for students at different stages of learning. Initial classroom pilots will come first, so the school can assess the effect on learning before any wider rollout. Students, teachers and parents will also receive orientation on the technology's potential, its limits and responsible use. The article says the goal is to help students use AI with curiosity, discernment and confidence while building the intellectual independence to reason for themselves. The school's stated view is that technology should expand what students can learn without diminishing the thinking that makes learning meaningful.

stories.Headline: Ohio receiving $8 million in GM settlement over data privacy
stories.Summary:
Ohio is set to receive about $8 million from a settlement that General Motors reached with a coalition of states over allegations that it collected and sold driver data without permission. Ohio joined 34 other states and Washington, D.C. in the lawsuit, which centered on the Smart Driver program, a service that was marketed as a way for drivers to track their own driving habits. The program was run by GM subsidiary OnStar and let drivers view their data through a smartphone app. In late October, attorneys general announced that GM would pay $220 million to resolve the case. Ohio's share of that total is the roughly $8 million now flowing to the state.

The settlement also requires GM to limit and protect the driving data it gathers, and it mandates third-party data protection assessments. Those changes build on a federal requirement imposed earlier this year, when the Federal Trade Commission placed a five-year ban on GM disclosing driver location and behavior data to consumer reporting agencies. The FTC also required GM to get affirmative express consent from consumers before collecting or using their data. Consumers must also be given an easier way to opt out of data collection and to delete data already gathered. GM had discontinued the Smart Driver product in 2024.

Ohio Attorney General Andy Wilson is the state official who led the state's involvement, and he said GM broke consumers' trust by selling their data without their knowledge or consent. Wilson said Ohioans should not have to fear that information collected by their own vehicles could be used against them. He added that companies must be held accountable when they put profits ahead of consumer privacy. According to the state, the OnStar app told 380,000 drivers they were not enrolled in data collection, even though they were.

The case grew out of a 2024 report by the New York Times, which revealed that GM had been sending driver behavior data to LexisNexis without consumers' permission. LexisNexis then produced reports for insurance companies, which could adjust premiums or deny coverage based on that information. The settlement and the federal restrictions together set new limits on how the automaker handles this kind of data. The articles do not say when Ohio's payment will arrive or how the third-party assessments will be carried out.

stories.Headline: AmeriLife and Palantir Announce Enterprise Partnership to Bring AI-Driven Transformation to Insurance and Retirement Distribution
stories.Summary:
AmeriLife Group, a national insurance and retirement distributor based in Clearwater and Miami, Florida, announced on November 5, 2026 a partnership with Palantir Technologies, the data analytics and artificial intelligence company. The enterprise-wide agreement brings Palantir's Foundry and Artificial Intelligence Platform into AmeriLife's Health and Wealth distribution organizations. The work begins with Crump Life Insurance Services, where Palantir-powered tools are already running in production. Rather than adding AI on top of current processes, AmeriLife says it is building an AI-driven operating model on one unified data foundation.

The company describes the change as a fundamental shift in how it runs its business. The goal is a faster and more connected experience for the agents, advisors, financial professionals and carrier partners it serves. AmeriLife also says it hopes to set a new standard for independent insurance and retirement product distribution. Over the coming months, the two companies plan to deploy AI capabilities across many workflows to speed up how business moves and to give agents and advisors better visibility. The release does not give dollar figures for the deal.

AmeriLife chairman and CEO Scott R. Perry said that much of the industry's AI discussion has centered on productivity tools and digital assistants. He argued that working with Palantir lets AmeriLife rebuild how its business operates, from the first client conversation to the placed policy. Ryan Taylor, Palantir's Chief Revenue and Legal Officer, said AmeriLife is putting AI at the center of how it works and serves professionals. He said the deployment is building a lasting operating advantage in a complex, highly regulated industry. Taylor added that the work already in production at Crump is only the beginning.

The release places AmeriLife as a long-established distributor, saying it has partnered with top carriers for more than 50 years. It says the company's network includes over 325,000 insurance agents, advisors and financial professionals, along with 160 marketing organizations and agency locations across the United States. The Crump deployment is part of the next generation of its ACE platform, which supports case management and back-office operations. The release also includes standard forward-looking statement warnings about risks, including the failure of the platforms to perform as desired and the customer's ability to modify or terminate the contract. Media and partnership contacts were listed for both companies.

stories.Headline: CoreWeave's 15% Bond Yield Is a Warning for AI Debt. Here Are the Stocks Most Exposed.
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave, a "neocloud" provider of AI infrastructure services, has grown rapidly, but its heavy borrowing has pushed its senior unsecured bond yields to between 14.1% and 15.6%, a level the article describes as a warning sign for AI-related debt. The company operates 51 data centers with more than a quarter-million Nvidia GPUs, and its revenue rose from $16 million in 2022 to $5.13 billion in 2025. Its net loss widened over the same period, from $31 million to $1.17 billion, as it leased data centers and bought more chips. The article's analysis, published on November 3, 2026, examines how this debt load could affect the company and its peers.

To fund its expansion, CoreWeave has increased its share count by 19% since its March 2025 IPO and ended the second quarter of 2026 with $72 billion in total liabilities and a debt-to-equity ratio of 14.3. Interest payments consumed roughly a quarter of its revenue, at $1.23 billion in 2025 and $1.18 billion in the first half of 2026. To reduce reliance on bonds, the company has issued $10.8 billion in convertible debt carrying lower cash coupons of 1.75% to 2.875%, though those notes could dilute existing shareholders if converted. Most of its senior notes trade at about $0.80 on the dollar, which the article reads as market confidence that the company can stay solvent into the early 2030s, when those bonds begin to mature.

The article, written by Leo Sun of The Motley Fool, argues that rising interest rates would push CoreWeave to issue even higher-yielding bonds if the Federal Reserve keeps raising its benchmark rate. It also notes that analysts expect revenue to climb from $5.13 billion in 2025 to $43.55 billion in 2028, while net losses would only shrink from $1.20 billion to $1.09 billion over that span, meaning more borrowing may be needed. Sun cautions that competitors face similar pressure if rates keep rising, though they are less leveraged. Nebius and IREN had debt-to-equity ratios of 1.7 and 2.8 and average coupons of roughly 1.7% to 2.2% and 1% to 3.5%, respectively, which the article presents as evidence that CoreWeave sits much closer to the edge.

The article concludes that CoreWeave's large backlog, reported at $104 billion in the second quarter of 2026, could still support growth if it converts into revenue. It warns, however, that continued rate increases could make it harder for CoreWeave to meet its debt obligations in the early 2030s and could make financing more expensive for smaller players like Nebius and IREN. The piece advises investors in neocloud stocks to weigh these long-term risks. It also carries a promotional note for a Motley Fool stock-picking service, which says CoreWeave was not among its recommended top 10 stocks.

stories.Headline: Longbridge Group and Cyberport announce strategic partnership to advance responsible agentic AI innovation in Hong Kong
stories.Summary:
Longbridge Group, an AI-native financial technology company, announced on November 5, 2026 that its AI arm, Longbridge AI Technologies Limited, has signed a three-year strategic partnership with Hong Kong Cyberport Management Company Limited to advance the responsible development and adoption of agentic artificial intelligence in Hong Kong. The partnership will support the establishment of a Hong Kong AI Lab that brings together fintech expertise, research talent and technology innovation. It sets out a framework for collaboration across AI research, industry engagement, talent development and innovation. The AI Lab is meant to gather financial institutions, technology companies, academic institutions and start-ups to explore practical uses of AI. Longbridge says closer ties between the fintech and research communities should foster growth and mutual trust in AI-enabled financial solutions.

Under the arrangement, Longbridge AI will contribute its fintech expertise, AI capabilities and industry experience, while Cyberport will connect the partners to its technology and innovation ecosystem. The organisations plan to explore work in four areas: responsible AI research and innovation, the Hong Kong AI Lab as a platform for research and experimentation, industry engagement through roundtables, seminars and publications, and talent development through hackathons, workshops and mentorship programmes. The partnership also aims to turn research into proof-of-concept initiatives. The partners describe these steps as a way to support Hong Kong's development as an international financial centre and AI innovation hub.

The companies have not stated in these articles a budget or any figures beyond the three-year term. Nowa Zhu, Co-founder and CEO of Longbridge, said that agentic AI could change how people interact with financial information but that realising this requires trust, accountability and close collaboration across the financial ecosystem. Ir Eric Chan, Chief Public Mission Officer of Cyberport, said that agentic AI offers significant potential for financial services and that the AI Lab should help test, validate and deploy solutions in the real world. Zhu added that Longbridge sees Hong Kong as an important market for shaping how AI is adopted responsibly.

Longbridge describes itself as a group that operates licensed financial businesses across several jurisdictions and holds 22 financial regulatory licences or qualifications, and it was founded in 2019. The announcement comes as AI systems move beyond providing insights toward supporting complex financial decisions, which raises questions about transparency and accountability, according to the release. The articles do not describe any specific next steps or timelines beyond the planned establishment of the AI Lab and the partnership's stated areas of work. A separate CIO commentary in the same period, not tied to the partnership, notes that autonomous agents require governance built in from the outset and that human oversight matters most in high-stakes areas such as financial transactions and regulatory compliance.

stories.Headline: Financial policymakers to monitor U.S. AI, trade policies following election
stories.Summary:
South Korea's top financial policymakers vowed on Thursday, November 5, 2026, to watch closely for shifts in U.S. policy on artificial intelligence and trade and what those shifts could mean for the South Korean economy. Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il met with Bank of Korea Governor Shin Hyun-song, Financial Services Commission Chairman Lee Eog-weon and Financial Supervisory Service Governor Lee Chan-jin after the U.S. Democratic Party won a strong result in the midterm elections earlier that week. Although major stock markets in the United States and Europe had gained, worries about tighter regulation of the AI industry had pushed semiconductor shares lower. The officials said the meeting addressed the likely effects of the election on U.S. fiscal, trade and industrial policy, and the participants agreed to follow the regulatory environment closely.

The officials also said they would keep track of U.S. tariffs and developments in the Middle East war, which could affect the economy. According to the finance ministry, they agreed to step up efforts to support stable growth by coordinating closely with relevant organizations to respond to changes in the external environment. They also agreed to prepare thoroughly for a possible rise in financial market volatility. The ministry's statement described these steps as a joint response to outside pressures rather than a set of new measures. The meeting was held in Seoul, and the ministry released a photo of the four officials posing before their talks.

Responsibility for these monitoring efforts rests with the finance minister and the heads of the central bank, the financial regulator and the financial services commission, who met to coordinate the response. The finance ministry said the officials had agreed to coordinate closely and prepare for possible market swings. The articles do not give details on specific policy actions or timelines beyond this pledge to keep watching and preparing. Context from the same reporting shows semiconductor shares had already fallen on AI regulation concerns, which made the officials' focus on the sector clear. The articles do not say what the officials would do if U.S. policy changes actually materialized.
