stories.Headline: What Shaped Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s Thinking on A.I.
stories.Summary:
Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, was shaped early by an interest in artificial intelligence that began during his years as a doctoral student in physics. In 2007, while visiting Princeton University, he discussed Ray Kurzweil's 2005 book on the Singularity with a friend, Colin Heckman, and argued that the milestone could arrive within their lifetimes. According to Heckman, Amodei became fixated on the idea that artificial intelligence had to be built correctly. Amodei was then 24 and had been reading blogs and online forums that debated the technology's potential to threaten humanity. Those influences, according to more than two dozen people who know him, still shape his thinking today.

The same sources describe two linked philosophies that share a firm belief that mathematical reasoning can alter the future of humanity. Amodei came to these ideas through online communities focused on charitable giving and on the risks of advanced technology. His worldview is presented as the foundation for how he approaches the work of Anthropic, which is preparing to carry out one of the largest public listings in the world this month. The reporting says this background helps explain how he regards the technology he is helping to build. The article is an in-depth profile, and the reporters drew on interviews with classmates, teachers, friends and colleagues to reconstruct that history.

Separately, a legal development involving Amodei was reported on Tuesday. A federal judge, Eumi K. Lee of the U.S. District Court, dismissed a direct copyright infringement claim against him by music publishers, though she allowed them to amend their allegations. Lee also expressed doubt that the publishers had offered enough evidence that Anthropic's model, Claude, generated infringing lyrics drawn from more than 20,000 copyrighted compositions. She deferred ruling on those claims and on allegations that Anthropic unlawfully removed copyright management information. Both sides have until the following Wednesday to propose how the case should proceed.

The reporting leaves some questions open, including how the publishers will respond to the dismissal and whether the remaining claims will advance. The articles do not describe the outcome of the proposals due next week. They also do not say how the Anthropic listing will affect the company's legal exposure in the copyright matter. What the sources do establish is that Amodei's early intellectual formation and his present legal position are both matters of public record as of November 5, 2026.

stories.Headline: Crusoe unveils 3.5 MW modular data centre for Nvidia AI racks
stories.Summary:
Crusoe, an AI data centre operator, has launched its sixth-generation modular data centre platform, called Spark Liquid, which is built to support up to 3.5 MW of compute capacity. The company says the unit is designed for Nvidia GB300 NVL72 and Vera Rubin NVL72 racks, and it was announced in early November 2026. Crusoe also claims that Spark Liquid delivers five times the compute density of earlier Spark generations. Production will begin in 2027 in Brighton, Colorado, alongside the company's existing Spark line.

The platform uses a closed-loop direct liquid cooling system, which removes heat from high-density racks more efficiently than air and recirculates water with minimal ongoing use and no evaporative loss. Each unit is built in Crusoe's factory and shipped ready to deploy in clusters, and the Spark platform will also support Nvidia's recently announced DSX POD blueprint for modular infrastructure. Crusoe said that cooling efficiency will still depend on climate, so each deployment is designed around local conditions. Crusoe acquired the electrical manufacturer Easter-Owens Electric in 2022 to bring manufacturing in-house.

Crusoe is the company behind the product, and its head of Spark, Bryan Schramm, has explained the reasoning. He said that power limits, the need for predictable delivery and the pressure to bring capacity online quickly are pushing operators toward modular designs. According to him, a factory-built unit can use power that is available now in smaller blocks, which can shorten grid connection timelines, and building in a factory makes delivery dates more reliable for customers who reserve capacity in advance. He also said that Crusoe designed the platform to move variability into a controlled factory setting, which helps the company deploy next-generation GPUs faster.

The articles place the launch within a broader industry shift toward factory-built infrastructure, as AI operators look for ways around the power and construction delays that often slow conventional builds. Nvidia describes DSX POD as a partner-delivered design in which it validates the cluster while partners build and deliver the units, and Crusoe is one of eight container solution providers on its list, alongside Eaton, Schneider Electric and Vertiv. Customers still need a prepared site with power, water and network connections. Schramm said that deployments may move closer to demand, including sites in the tens of megawatts, though the articles do not describe specific customers or deployments beyond the Colorado production plan.

stories.Headline: Chemours Launches New Cooling Fluids to Tackle AI Data Center Heat Surge
stories.Summary:
Chemours, the chemical company, has launched a new line of two-phase liquid cooling fluids called Faizeon for data centers running artificial intelligence and high-performance computing. The announcement was made in early November 2026, with ChemAnalyst reporting on November 5 and CSRwire on November 3. The portfolio targets the rising heat generated by more powerful processors and denser server racks, which the articles say conventional cooling systems struggle to handle. The fluids are dielectric, meaning they do not conduct electricity, and they work through phase change, absorbing heat as they turn from liquid into vapor.

The line includes five products. Faizeon 100 and 110 are low-pressure fluids for direct-to-chip cooling, with 110 having an intermediate boiling point and zero ozone depletion potential. Faizeon 200 is aimed at medium-pressure systems and high-density AI and computing processors, while Faizeon 220 is the company's highest-performance direct-to-chip fluid for demanding GPU environments. Faizeon 500, formerly marketed as Opteon 2P50, is designed for full-server immersion cooling and may support waste heat recovery. According to the company, the fluids can lower cooling-related energy use and nearly eliminate cooling-related water use, depending on system design, and they are engineered for recovery, reprocessing and reuse.

Chemours cited independent third-party testing showing that a two-phase direct-to-chip system using Faizeon 200 kept a graphics processing unit up to 19 degrees Celsius cooler than a single-phase, water-based system while using a lower coolant flow rate. Denise Dignam, the company's president and chief executive, said that AI growth is putting pressure on data center infrastructure and that cooling has become a critical constraint. She said the company is drawing on more than 90 years of thermal management expertise to help operators handle higher heat loads. Chemours also said it is working with several partners, including the U.S. Department of Energy's Oak Ridge National Laboratory, NTT DATA, 2CRSi, DataVolt, Munters, Accelsius and ZutaCore, to advance adoption.

ChemAnalyst notes that the launch strengthens Chemours' position in specialty cooling fluids and could support demand for fluorinated heat-transfer fluids and related intermediates. The outlet adds that large-scale demand will depend on data center deployment, system compatibility, regulatory acceptance and lifecycle economics. It also says no immediate broad price increase for affected commodities is expected, since the launch alone does not create significant new feedstock consumption or supply constraints. The articles do not describe specific commercial orders or timelines for wider rollout beyond these partnerships and the stated market opportunity.

stories.Headline: You should expect questions about AI in job interviews, experts say—here's how to prepare
stories.Summary:
Binance disclosed on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, how the record theft of $6.43 billion in assets from the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange came about. The company described a sophisticated, multi-stage campaign rather than a single breach or a simple phishing incident. The attackers combined fake recruitment interviews, malicious software downloads, a compromised internal AI tool, endpoint compromise and an advanced transaction-authorisation method. The thefts themselves took place on October 29, and a co-CEO, Richard Teng, said hackers used fake job interviews and an AI tool to get in. The campaign began in June 2026, when a Wallet DevOps engineer, called Engineer A, searched online for a popular AI tool and downloaded a tampered Homebrew installer.

Binance said it detected that attack and rotated the related credentials, but details about his role and his colleagues on the wallet infrastructure team were exposed. In September 2026, a second engineer, called Engineer B, was approached on a legitimate job-hunting platform by someone posing as a Project Director. That person set up a first-round video interview with a supposed HR representative, who shared a social media account full of personal photos and videos to build trust, and a second-round chat interview with someone claiming to be the CEO of a company that does not exist. Near the end, Engineer B was told to download an "assignment" onto his work computer, and the code in it ran during setup and installed malware that used obfuscation, swapped in a poisoned development tool component, contacted an attacker-controlled server and erased forensic traces. On October 20, the attacker used Engineer B's machine and abused an internal AI tool to gain control over Engineer A and another engineer, Software Engineer C. The attacker found a container deployment permission token on Engineer A's computer.

On October 29, between 17:15 and 19:56, the attacker logged onto Engineer C's computer, used Engineer A's stolen credentials, deployed a container and triggered a malicious script. That gave access to an internal wallet signing service, which was used to start transactions outside the normal withdrawal process. Binance said the entry points used have been closed and the systems touched in the attack path have been rebuilt or replaced. As of November 3, it had rebuilt the wallet system in a new environment, rebuilt the internal AI tool and access controls, decommissioned credentials and tokens tied to the affected engineers, completed security scans of all employee devices, and strengthened wallet-service risk controls. It also expanded AI-based behavioural anomaly detection and is working with law enforcement, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze assets.

Teng said on CNBC that the company is bringing in an independent expert to review everything it has done. Binance added that it has increased its investment in AI-enabled detection, endpoint protection and developer-environment security. Binance said the methods match a wider pattern, estimating that it has foiled 57 suspected North Korea-linked cyber threat cases since the start of the year. Those techniques include fraudulent job interviews, malicious software disguised as popular developer tools, compromised packages and browser extensions, fake video conferencing apps, and social engineering built to steal credentials or install remote access malware. Separately, a CNBC report on AI in hiring noted that experts expect candidates to face questions about their AI use in interviews.

stories.Headline: Dropbox ditched AWS S3 for its own in-house system. Now it’s buying Tigris to sell S3-compatible storage to AI developers.
stories.Summary:
The articles supply almost nothing about the deal itself beyond its headline, so little can be reported with confidence. The headline says Dropbox moved off AWS S3 to its own in-house storage system, and is now buying a company called Tigris so it can sell S3-compatible storage to AI developers. The report comes from The New Stack, written by Paul Sawers and published on November 5, 2026. The text provided for that piece stops at the site's navigation menus, subscription forms and lists of other stories, so none of the body of the article is available.

Because of that, the articles give no price for the acquisition, no closing date and no description of what Tigris does or who runs it. They also offer no figures on how much data Dropbox stores, what it saved by leaving S3, or when the move away from AWS took place. Nor do they say what the purchase changes for current Tigris customers or for developers who might buy the new storage. Every number, date and name the articles do give appears in the headline and the byline.

The people and companies involved are named only in broad terms. Dropbox is the buyer and Tigris is the target, with AWS and its S3 service as the system Dropbox is described as having left. No Dropbox executive, Tigris founder or Amazon spokesperson is quoted or paraphrased in the material provided. Paul Sawers is the only person named, and he is the reporter rather than a party to the deal. As a result, there is no statement from either company about why they are doing this or what they expect from it.

The second article, from Yahoo Finance on November 4, 2026, covers a different subject, Apple's shares falling 2 percent after its earnings, and says nothing about Dropbox. It notes that, unlike other big technology firms, Apple has held back from heavy spending on the AI build-out, but that point is unrelated to the storage deal. The headline ties Dropbox's purchase to AI developers, which places it in the wider rush to supply infrastructure for AI work. The provided text does not say what happens next, whether regulators must approve the purchase, or when the new storage offering might launch.

stories.Headline: Nebius Is Up 69% in 2026. Is Its AI Bubble “Already Popping”?
stories.Summary:
Nebius Group, the AI infrastructure company ticker NBIS, has seen its stock rise about 69% in 2026, closing at $141.39 on November 2, though it remains roughly 53% below its June 22 intraday high of $299.86. The stock sold off hard in October as worries about CoreWeave's borrowing spread across AI infrastructure names, prompting questions about whether Nebius can fund its expansion without taking on too much debt or diluting shareholders. At June 30, Nebius carried far lower net borrowings than CoreWeave, roughly $504 million compared with about $29.5 billion, though newer financing and planned buildouts are adding to its obligations. Commentary from TIKR, which tracks the company, was published on November 5, 2026.

Major customer contracts continue to support the business. Microsoft's infrastructure agreement is valued at $17.4 billion and could reach $19.4 billion, while Meta's five-year deal includes $12 billion in dedicated capacity and up to $15 billion in additional commitments. In its August 12 earnings report, Nebius reported revenue growth of 454% to $582 million, a 41% adjusted EBITDA margin, and four AI cloud agreements averaging more than $1 billion each. TIKR's October 21 consensus projects revenue rising from $530 million in 2025 to $3.35 billion in 2026 and $12.24 billion in 2027. Analysts expect about $29.1 billion in capital spending and roughly $34 billion in net debt by the end of 2027, and the company has said that sequencing its financing helps optimize its long-term cost of capital.

Financing remains the central concern. On October 21, Piper Sandler cut its price target on Nebius from $237 to $185, and the following day Nebius secured a $3.5 billion financing facility from Citi to support expansion. Despite more than $9 billion in expected 2026 customer prepayments, further borrowing could raise costs and dilute existing shareholders. Nvidia holds a reported 9.3% stake in Nebius and supplies the GPUs central to its growth, while Microsoft and Meta are its anchor customers. TIKR describes the stock as potentially undervalued on sales multiples, with about 5.9x forward sales on October 30, down from roughly 13x at the end of June and a peak near 32x in October 2025, though it notes second-quarter depreciation of nearly $260 million exceeded adjusted EBITDA of about $236 million.

Nebius reports third-quarter results on November 12, with analysts expecting about $906 million in revenue, and customer prepayments, deferred revenue and capital spending are the metrics to watch. A separate commentary from MindMatters, published November 4, argues that the AI bubble question is complicated because the value chain is narrow, with chipmakers and data center operators profiting while AI labs such as Anthropic and OpenAI price their services below cost. That piece says Chinese models gaining market share forced price cuts after a brief period of higher pricing in 2026, and it describes continuing losses at the labs. The TIKR article itself states that a falling valuation does not necessarily mean the AI business is collapsing, and that the outcome depends on whether Nebius can fund growth without excessive debt or dilution.

stories.Headline: South Korean director Yeon Sang-ho revisits AI themes in latest thriller 'Paradise Lost'
stories.Summary:
South Korean director Yeon Sang-ho has built several of his films around artificial intelligence, and his latest, "Paradise Lost," returns to that theme in a psychological thriller. The story follows a mother, Ryu So-young, played by Kim Hyun-joo, who spends nine years relying on an AI recreation of her son after he was abducted on a school camping trip. She sees the boy, forever 10 years old, through augmented reality glasses until the real Sun-woo, played by Bae Hyeon-seong, returns as a grown stranger. The film premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival and opens in North American theaters on Friday. The film grew out of an unexpected source, a short story of about three pages written by Yeon's mother, a homemaker who once worked as a cleaner.

Yeon's earlier AI-themed works include the 2023 Netflix film "JUNG_E" and "Colony," a zombie thriller that premiered at the Cannes Film Festival this year. In an interview with The Associated Press, he said the central question of the film is what makes a relationship real. He argued that the AI character has filled a role of continuity for nine years but does not truly contemplate, and that AI mainly gives users the reactions they want. He said that if an AI system refuses a task by saying it does not want to do it, that would suggest it has begun to contemplate, and that he has not seen this happen. He also drew a link between the film's title, taken from John Milton's poem about humanity's expulsion from paradise, and the idea that a life without pain would soon lose its meaning.

Yeon also addressed the broader industry, noting that AI film festivals have appeared in South Korea and Japan and that Hollywood unions and filmmakers have been wary of the technology. He suggested that Asian filmmakers may be more receptive to AI because English-language films have long had larger markets and bigger budgets, pressures that smaller Asian markets did not face to the same degree. He said that as AI and other technologies develop, those pressures are weakening, and that Asian cinema can now take on more science fiction subjects. He added that he finds debates lumping every use of technology under the single label "AI" unproductive. Yeon said the film industry already uses a form of collective intelligence, since before release his team surveys 100 people at blind previews.

stories.Headline: Anthropic's models improving nearly twice as fast with help from AI, study finds
stories.Summary:
Anthropic's AI models are improving nearly twice as fast as before, according to an independent study by the AI safety nonprofit METR, published on Thursday, November 5, 2026. The researchers found that the technology is playing a bigger role in developing more powerful successors, which suggests AI is accelerating its own development. METR's 11-week assessment, conducted between August and October, drew on confidential research, interviews and performance data from unreleased models. It found that Anthropic's benchmark capabilities had been improving 1.9 times faster since October 2025 than previously. The outside reviewer said the estimate carries high uncertainty.

The findings matter because they point toward recursive self-improvement, a scenario in which AI systems build more powerful versions of themselves without human intervention. METR estimated that AI accounted for perhaps 80% of the current acceleration, though it called that figure uncertain. The researchers said they found no convincing evidence of major bottlenecks that could slow progress over the next year. They also said the acceleration was not driven by faster growth in training compute. Even so, METR cautioned that AI could not yet make highly significant, fully autonomous contributions to the most important stages of model training.

METR said that as of October 2026, Anthropic was likely improving its models on well-specified tasks at around twice the rate it did between March 2024 and October 2025. It said it would not be surprised if the true rate was closer to 1.5 or 2.5 times the historical rate. Anthropic researchers have reported sharp productivity gains from using AI to write code and run experiments, and informal employee polls suggested improvements of about 12 times, though METR said those figures were unreliable. Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Its CEO had called for slowing advanced AI development in September.

The prospect of recursive self-improvement has prompted AI researchers in recent months to warn that such systems could become difficult to align with human goals, monitor and control, which could pose an existential threat to humanity. The shift could also affect an industry that has spent hundreds of billions of dollars on computing infrastructure for advanced models. The timing is notable because Anthropic is preparing to go public, potentially as soon as this month, in what could be one of the largest IPOs ever. The offering will also test investor appetite for AI companies spending heavily on the technology.

stories.Headline: Incoming Democratic majorities put AI giants on notice
stories.Summary:
Democrats who won control of both chambers in the 2026 midterm elections have signaled an end to Washington's hands-off approach to artificial intelligence. Voters across the country chose Democratic candidates who ran on legislative guardrails for AI, and dozens of state and local ballot measures limited the construction of new data centers. Exit polling by SSRS found that 56 percent of voters said AI and data centers were a crucial or major factor in their votes for Congress. The Democratic leaders who spoke after the election framed these results as a clear mandate to act.

At a post-election press conference on Wednesday, Rep. Ted Lieu of California previewed the party's plan for the next Congress. He said Republicans made a conscious decision last year to let the AI industry run wild, a choice he called a mistake both politically and on policy. Lieu said Democrats will hold public hearings on AI and pass reasonable guardrails. He co-chairs a House Democratic commission on AI formed by Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries last year, and he said he and his colleagues will release a document outlining their policy priorities. Several newly elected senators also campaigned on AI issues, including a two-year moratorium on data centers proposed by South Carolina's Annie Andrews, requirements from North Carolina's Roy Cooper that data centers cover the full costs of their energy use, and a focus on youth safety from Texas's James Talarico.

Less than 48 hours after Election Day, OpenAI announced new commitments for its data centers, including covering energy costs and investing in jobs. The company said voluntary commitments are an important starting point but that new policy is required to build trust among communities, elected officials and companies. The articles note that Democrats are likely to push for rules that go well beyond these voluntary standards. They also point out that the party's majorities, though sizable, are not large enough to override a presidential veto. President Donald Trump has strongly opposed regulating AI and supports data centers, though the articles suggest that voters' rejection of Republican policies may push him toward compromise.

stories.Headline: Democratic victories cloud outlook for AI data center rollout
stories.Summary:
Strong wins for Democratic candidates in the US midterm elections on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, threaten the prospects for energy-hungry data centers in key states and could slow the AI rollout that has carried Wall Street forward over the past four years. Republicans lost strongholds such as Texas, where both the Senate and the governorship went to Democrats who back greater data center regulation. President Donald Trump, who has supported hands-off regulation for what he calls "super intelligence," suffered a stinging rebuke of his Republican party after a campaign marked by growing concerns about the environmental effects of data centers. The prospect of stricter regulation weighed on stocks in AI heavyweights such as Elon Musk's SpaceX ahead of the US markets open, after drops for key chipmakers in Asia including Samsung in South Korea.

In Texas, Gina Hinojosa, a lawyer who defeated outgoing governor Greg Abbott, called during the campaign for an immediate moratorium on data centers until the legislature can meet to put real protections in place. She has also urged an end to tax exemptions granted to the sector, as has fellow Democrat James Talarico, who was elected on Tuesday as a Texas senator. Abbott had wanted to make the state the "nerve center" of artificial intelligence and data center development, but he noticeably shifted his stance amid a public backlash over energy and water provision. Texas is expected to account for nearly 30 percent of national demand for electricity dedicated to AI operations by 2028, according to calculations by Bloom Energy. Alphabet, the parent of Google, has announced plans to build several data centers in Texas, and Musk has moved the headquarters of Tesla, SpaceX and X to the state.

Musk, who spent hundreds of millions of dollars supporting the Republican camp, joked after the vote that "Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," referring to his goal of a satellite computing network. Patrick Munnelly, market strategist at the brokerage Tickmill Group, said Democratic opposition to rapid data-center expansion could focus on power use, environmental constraints, local infrastructure strain, competition policy and the social consequences of AI deployment. He said none of this necessarily breaks the long-term AI theme, but it can raise the hurdle rate for investment. Veteran financial analyst Jim Bianco posted on X that given the size of the Democrats' victory, including the Texas governorship and a 29 to 1 lead to restrict data centers, politicians who want to remain employed are going to heed these messages.

The regulatory impact will be greatest at state level, highlighting the role of governors in responding to voter concerns. In Georgia, another state with a heavy slate of data center projects, the new Democratic governor Keisha Lance Bottoms has advocated a temporary statewide pause on new data centers, alongside requirements intended to ensure that large customers bear the costs of their infrastructure, according to Stephen Innes at SPI Asset Management. Amy Acton, elected Democratic governor of Ohio, is also committing to a tougher regulatory framework on the data center buildout. Data centers require substantial amounts of fresh water to help cool servers, raising fears of localized shortages.

stories.Headline: The Ride Platform Evolves Its AI-Native Fleet Management Software Platform for the Operator Economy
stories.Summary:
The Ride Platform announced on November 5, 2026, that it had released version 2.0 of Wheelbase, its AI-native fleet management software for independent rental operators running auto rental, car-sharing, RV, boat and autonomous vehicle fleets. The company said the new version rebuilds Wheelbase as an AI-native experience with built-in agents that help operators worldwide run their business. It also introduces the Wheelbase App Exchange, an app store that brings partner tools for bookkeeping, insurance, telematics and more into the platform operators already use. The announcement was made in Austin and distributed through GlobeNewswire.

Wheelbase 2.0 keeps operators on the same account and data they already use, so there is nothing to migrate. The App Exchange launches with Roamly Insurance & Protection for embedded coverage and Roamly Fleet for vehicle telematics, alongside FleetPilot for bookkeeping and vehicle-level profit and loss, TollSpot for toll management and KYCS for vehicle tracking and recovery. Operators can also suggest partners they want added. Other updates include integration with Claude, ChatGPT and a proprietary Wheelbase agent so operators can check on their fleet and make changes in plain language, a reservation status flow showing each booking's stage, a vehicle health bar that flags missing information such as insurance not yet applied, a separate messages tab for guest conversations, a single guided listing page with a simpler quote flow, and pricing rules with live preview that can target discounts by booking date or travel date. Version 2.0 is available today for auto operators, with RV operators expected to move to it in early 2027 and a redesigned mobile app expected in the first quarter of 2027.

Jeff Cavins, co-founder and CEO of The Ride Platform, said that as professional fleet operators scale by adding vehicles or expanding into new asset classes or even autonomous vehicle types, their software has to keep up. He described the redesigned product as a cleaner, faster and more interoperable Wheelbase built around what operators said they needed, on a new foundation that lets the company ship updates faster than ever. He said operators have shaped Wheelbase for more than a decade and that 2.0 is ready for where their businesses go next. James von der Lieth, co-founder of FleetPilot, said most operators can say how many bookings they had last month but not which cars actually made money once owner payouts, expenses and depreciation are counted, and that being on the App Exchange puts reconciled books, owner statements and vehicle-level profit and loss inside the platform they already use, so they spend less time on spreadsheets and more time growing their business.

The articles say many independent operators still handle bookkeeping, insurance and fleet tracking on their own, often with tools built for consumers, and the App Exchange brings that work into Wheelbase. The Ride Platform describes itself as believing independent operators are the future of mobility, creating demand through its Outdoorsy and Ride marketplaces and providing business infrastructure through Wheelbase and Roamly Insurance. It is co-headquartered in Austin and London and has powered independent mobility operators globally since 2015. Walkthroughs and tutorials for Wheelbase 2.0 are available in the Wheelbase Community Hub and on wheelbasepro.com.

stories.Headline: 'My Field Significantly Shrinking Due to Automation and AI': Laid-Off Worker Emptied His Retirement and Still Owes $45,000
stories.Summary:
Henry, an HR technology worker from Oklahoma City, called The Ramsey Show and told hosts George Kamel and Jade Warshaw that he had been laid off. He said he had been out of work for two to three months and that his pay had fallen from $90,000 to $50,000 because his field was shrinking due to automation and AI. He then described emptying his retirement savings to keep up the lifestyle he had been living. He summed up his situation by saying he was drowning.

Henry owes about $45,000 in total. That includes a $26,000 car loan with a $620 monthly payment, almost $4,000 in credit cards and almost $15,000 in personal loans. One of those loans carries a 35% interest rate, and he took it out less than two months after consolidating with his credit union. He still runs a monthly deficit of $100 to $200 and is still using his cards. The article notes that the average credit card APR hit 21% in August.

Kamel said he did not think consolidation was the answer because Henry had already done it. Warshaw's first rule was that she was not borrowing any more money, and she said no more debt was needed, including for the logistics school loan Henry planned to take. She called public transit a serious sacrifice but a temporary one. The hosts told Henry to sell the car, list every debt by rate and balance, and pick up a side hustle to close the monthly gap. CarMax quoted him $25,500 against the $26,000 loan, a gap of about $500, and selling would free up $7,440 a year.

The article places Henry's call in the context of a year of AI-driven restructuring that investors have cheered. It cites publicly tracked 2026 layoff announcements of 30,000 at UPS and 30,000 at Oracle, along with 16,000 at Amazon, and says Microsoft reportedly offered voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 employees. National numbers look calm, with unemployment at 4.2% in September and initial jobless claims at 194K in late October. The article says those averages miss workers like Henry, who found new work at much lower pay, and it warns that his 35% debt and empty retirement account will keep costing him every month until he stops borrowing.

The Year 1 evaluation was carried out by the independent research agency WestEd, and its findings are published in a report called the WestEd Impact Report. As the project enters Year 2, it will reach TK-12 school districts across California rather than only Silicon Valley, and it will continue offerings such as the AI Capstone program, the asynchronous AI Empowered Educator program, and customizable professional learning on adaptive tools, ethical innovation, and strategic leadership. Krause also said the organization intends to keep ensuring that students receive safe, equitable, and ethically guided AI instruction as it grows across the state.

The Krause Center, which sits on the Foothill College campus in the Foothill-De Anza Community College District, says it has spent more than 25 years designing research-driven programs for teachers and administrators. It is also hosting the free un[AI]pologetic Education Conference at Foothill College, which pairs practical AI tools with a focus on human-centered teaching, data privacy, and ethics. stories.Headline: Nasdaq 100 eyes $1.8 trillion loss as Democratic win sparks AI delay fears
stories.Summary:
On Thursday, November 5, 2026, the Nasdaq 100 index was set to lose about $1.8 trillion in stock value as investors feared that the sweeping Democratic victory in the midterm elections could slow the expansion of AI infrastructure. The drop followed a milder reaction the previous session, when the index, packed with major technology companies, had risen on hopes that an end to election uncertainty would lift overall sentiment. Semiconductor and neocloud shares, which had driven much of the recent gains, fell sharply for a second straight day on concern that data center projects worth billions of dollars could face delays. The Philadelphia SE Semiconductor index dropped 8.4%, its lowest level in more than six months, with heavyweights Nvidia and Broadcom leading the losses. The Nasdaq 100 was last down 4.5%, and the Nasdaq Composite was on track to confirm a correction, a 10% decline from its recent peak.

The selloff reflects a worry that political gridlock and tougher scrutiny of data center development could slow one of Wall Street's most important growth engines. UBS analysts estimated that around 30% of expected US data center capacity additions in 2028 could be at risk from potential construction pauses. CoreWeave, seen as a barometer of investor anxiety over heavy AI spending, slumped 12%, and five-year credit default spreads widened to a record high, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence data. Nebius fell 15.2%, while data center operators Applied Digital, Cipher Digital and IREN each tumbled more than 14%. The weakness also reached utilities and equipment suppliers tied to the buildout, with GE Vernova down about 6% and Constellation Energy off 3%.

Matthew Tuttle, founder and CEO of Tuttle Capital Management, said Wall Street badly needs a positive AI story and predicted roughly two years of little progress amid divided government and angry politics. Ted Parkhill, founder and CEO of Incline Investment Management, said the market was moving from the promise of AI to the price of AI, while acknowledging the technology will be transformative over the long run. Microsoft fell 2% after Bloomberg News reported that it was tightening oversight of some data center projects from Nebius, IREN and Nscale. Separately, Qualcomm plunged 12% after quarterly smartphone-chip sales missed Wall Street estimates. Amazon.com fell 2.5% and Alphabet 1.4% as hyperscalers, which had held up the day before, also declined.

stories.Headline: AI sharpens cat-and-mouse hacking battle as companies strengthen defences
stories.Summary:
Companies around the world are facing a wave of cyber threats that executives say artificial intelligence is accelerating and making more sophisticated, according to a Reuters report dated November 5, 2026. The incidents include hacked supermarket fridges, a record cryptocurrency theft at Binance in which hackers stole $6.3 billion worth of crypto, and an emergency over flaws in widely used web software. A cyberattack on European supermarkets on Monday, the second in three weeks, raised refrigerator and freezer temperatures and forced retailers to discard millions of dollars' worth of spoiled food. The surge is straining IT departments, whose staff are working overnight to patch vulnerabilities.

Nearly 37,000 security flaws in software or computer systems were reported in the third quarter of 2026, roughly triple the figure from a year earlier, according to the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures list. Some firms are responding by turning to AI-powered security tools and increasing investment in them. German web hosting company Ionos said it changed its practices after a spike in vulnerabilities in July, deploying AI-based monitoring and AI-assisted patching around the clock. Ahold Delhaize, which operates Stop & Shop and Giant Food in the United States, was hit by two hacks in the past month, the first of which cost more than €200 million ($225 million) in sales and prompted a profit warning. McKinsey projects the global market for outside-vendor cybersecurity products and services will grow from $223 billion in 2025 to $346 billion by 2029.

Executives quoted by Reuters described the situation in stark terms. Booking.com's chief security officer, Marnie Wilking, said the contest resembles a never-ending game of cat and mouse, with hundreds of her company's engineers now building AI-powered defences. Ionos's chief technology officer, Markus Noga, said events of this magnitude now happen weekly or even every couple of days, and that a nine-to-five team is no longer enough. Ahold Delhaize's finance chief, Jolanda Poots-Bijl, said the company is adjusting to a new reality, noting that smaller firms are especially exposed while AI also helps firms detect and restore systems faster. Kraft Heinz's chief executive, Steve Cahillane, said the threat is real and growing.

The refrigerator attacks followed research published in August by cybersecurity firm Claroty, which outlined weaknesses in refrigeration controllers. After a first wave of attacks hit stores in France on October 11, Claroty researchers used widely available AI tools to reproduce the flaws and take control of a test device, which its field chief technology officer, Sean Tufts, said took them six dollars and 28 minutes. Separately, the October 21 disclosure of two AI-discovered flaws in the PHP programming language prompted governments and companies from Tokyo to Helsinki to take websites offline as a precaution. Cloudflare reported that attempts to exploit those PHP flaws rose from thousands to millions within hours. Both sides are using AI, and the race is continuing, as Holcim's chief financial officer, Steffen Kindler, put it.

stories.Summary:
China is expanding its AI-controlled laboratories in a bid to speed up scientific discovery and strengthen its industrial base, with the government playing a central role. In Shenzhen, a drug-discovery firm called XtalPi runs an autonomous facility where an AI model proposes hypotheses, directs robots to test them and records results to guide the next experiment, operating around the clock with few humans involved. China's prime minister, Li Qiang, praised such innovation during a visit early this year as the key to winning the future. The article frames this as part of a wider race with America to build and apply AI technologies in science.

China's new five-year plan, announced in March, called for faster exploration of AI-driven ways of doing science as part of a push to seize the commanding heights in the industrial application of AI. The state is building what it calls an AI-for-science stack that links specialised datasets, models and computing power needed to run these self-driving labs. In April the Chinese Academy of Sciences launched ScienceOne, also called Panshi or "Bedrock," a chatbot-like platform available to hundreds of Chinese universities and laboratories, with models trained on academic reports and non-text data. The article notes that China's scientific models still tend to lag behind America's, though a researcher at the University of Hong Kong praised the platform's bundle of datasets, agents and computing power. On the hardware side, XtalPi used its autonomous lab last year to help discover a molecule for treating a form of stomach cancer, generating millions of candidates and narrowing them to hundreds for robotic testing on lab-grown tissue.

The article attributes the stack-building partly to the government's leading role, noting that governments often hold the large datasets and can provide advanced computing power. Officials, according to the article, say these efforts will reduce dependence on Western technology and give China an edge in the AI race. Kyle Chan of the Brookings Institution, an American think-tank, said Chinese policymakers and American AI labs see eye to eye on this area. The article also contrasts the two countries: American automated-lab startups received about $1bn in venture capital last year and tend toward ambitious, speculative research, while Chinese firms are usually less ambitious and prefer work that can quickly generate profit. XtalPi, which serves 17 of the world's 20 largest pharmaceutical companies, is one example of this factory-like approach.

The article describes the context as a commercial and industrial one, noting that about half of all drugs licensed globally last year, by value, came from China, according to Goldman Sachs, up from 21% in 2024. In March Eli Lilly secured rights to develop and sell potential drugs from Insilico Medicine, a Hong Kong-listed firm using automated labs, in a deal worth up to $2.75bn. China also publishes four times as many materials-science papers as America, according to Nature, and in April researchers at City University of Hong Kong showed an automated lab could design and test molecules for solar cells. XtalPi and JinkoSolar say they are building a facility that will test 1,000 solar-cell prototypes a day, compared with one or two per researcher daily. Some Chinese AI leaders, including Zhou Bowen of Shanghai AI Lab, believe mastering science through such labs could help move toward artificial general intelligence, though the article presents this as a view held by some experts rather than settled fact.

The new detection capability identifies abnormal agent behavior even when no specific rule has been broken.

When it spots a deviation, it routes the activity into coordinated investigations carried out by multiple agents working across every security domain at the same time. According to the release, the multi-agent investigations are now generally available. The article as provided does not give further technical details, numbers, or pricing. stories.Headline: Authorities tighten restrictions on data centres amid AI boom
stories.Summary:
Governments across several countries have tightened restrictions on data centres, citing concerns about electricity demand, water use and environmental harm tied to the AI boom, according to a Reuters report published on November 5, 2026. In the United States, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro signed an executive order that requires companies building AI data centres to meet environmental and transparency safeguards and to secure local community approval. The order also removes all data centres from the state's Fast Track permit program and bars state offices from signing non-disclosure agreements with developers. Texas Governor Greg Abbott paused approvals of new projects through the state's grid interconnection process, and developers must now disclose more about power demand, water use, tax incentives and ownership.

New York Governor Kathy Hochul imposed a one-year construction moratorium on data centres using 50 megawatts or more of power, making New York the first U.S. state to enact a full moratorium. During that freeze, the state's Department of Environmental Conservation will not issue new discretionary permits while officials develop standards to assess environmental impact. In Maine, Governor Janet Mills vetoed bipartisan legislation that would have enacted an 18-month moratorium on new data centres using more than 20 megawatts. Mills said she supported a moratorium in principle but objected that the bill lacked an exception for a specific project in the Town of Jay. Residents of Monterey Park, California, voted in June 2026 to permanently ban data centres, the first U.S. city to do so at the ballot box.

Outside the United States, Amsterdam imposed a one-year moratorium on new data centre developments in 2019 and in April 2025 barred new facilities or expansions until at least 2030. Ireland's grid operator effectively blocked new connections around Dublin from 2021 until the freeze ended in December 2025, and new connections must now bring their own on-site power generation. Denmark adopted legislation, effective October 2026, that gives new data centres the lowest priority for grid connections, placing households, healthcare, industry, transport and renewable projects ahead of them. Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the government will create an "Office of AI" to set standards, including rules for large data centres on location, power and water use, with legislation due early next year. Portugal's Environment Minister Maria da Graca Carvalho said new rules are coming that would require data centres to run on renewable energy and use cooling systems that do not compete with household and business water supplies, even as the country promotes large projects such as the 1.2-gigawatt Start Campus in Sines.

stories.Headline: NPCI sets up wholly owned tech subsidiary NTSL and appoints Vishal Kanvaty as MD and CEO
stories.Summary:
The National Payments Corporation of India, known as NPCI, said on Wednesday that it had set up a wholly owned technology subsidiary called NPCI Tech Solutions Limited, or NTSL. The new unit is meant to serve as the group's technology and innovation arm. NPCI named its chief technology officer, Vishal Kanvaty, as managing director and CEO of the subsidiary. Kanvaty has been associated with NPCI for nearly a decade.

NTSL will concentrate on AI, blockchain, digital financial infrastructure and global capability centre services. It is also expected to build capabilities beyond NPCI's core payments mandate. In addition, the unit will provide technology services for eKYC Setu, the Unified Ticketing Platform and other digital public infrastructure programmes. NTSL becomes the fourth wholly owned subsidiary of the group, after NPCI International Payments, NPCI Bharat BillPay and NPCI BHIM Services.

NPCI CEO Dilip Asbe said advances in AI and other emerging technologies are opening up new possibilities across digital infrastructure and financial services. According to the report in Inc42, he added that the subsidiary was created to pursue those opportunities and strengthen the group's technology capabilities. NPCI also said Kanvaty has led the development and commercialisation of several platforms that now fall within NTSL's focus areas. NPCI did not disclose the subsidiary's investment outlay, revenue targets, customer pipeline or timelines for rolling out new services.

NPCI is the umbrella body that runs India's retail payments and settlement systems, including the Unified Payments Interface, or UPI. The move comes as India looks to advance AI research and development, especially in banking and financial services. At the Global Fintech Fest in September, NPCI launched AiNxt and AtOM, platforms meant to help enterprises build AI agents and automate workflows across the payments ecosystem. UPI handled a record 25.47 billion transactions in October, up 5.8% from the previous month, with transaction value rising 7.4% to ₹31.53 lakh crore. Separately, NPCI has deferred the planned introduction of merchant discount rate charges on select UPI payments, originally set for October 15, until after Diwali, and a new date has not been announced.

stories.Headline: AI sales startup Nooks secures $500 million in funding for expansion - ET CIO
stories.Summary:
Nooks, an AI sales automation startup, has secured a $500 million commitment from General Catalyst's Customer Value Fund to finance its sales and marketing push and the launch of new products. The company announced the deal on Wednesday, November 4, 2026, and the articles were published on November 5, 2026. The funding is intended to help Nooks scale up and take new products to market. Nooks is positioning sales as the next profession to be reshaped by AI, following coding, legal work and customer support.

Unlike a traditional investor that buys a stake in a company, General Catalyst's arrangement involves taking a share of the returns its capital helps generate, according to Nooks CEO Dan Lee. Lee declined to disclose the terms of the deal. He said that transforming an industry requires a great deal of capital, and that the company saw this structure as the best way to fund aggressive growth alongside new product launches. Nooks also said it is on track to nearly triple its annual recurring revenue by the end of the year, though it did not reveal its current figure.

The company formally launched its Revenue Agent Platform the same day, covering tasks from first customer contact through to renewal. The company reports more than 2,000 customers, including Cursor, Notion, Replit, Glean and HubSpot, and a net revenue retention rate of 135 per cent. Pranav Singhvi, partner and co-head of the Customer Value Fund at General Catalyst, said the platform has shown a highly predictable revenue engine and strong unit economics, qualities the fund looks for in companies it backs. He described the traction as impressive given how early it is.

The figures and characterizations come from Nooks and General Catalyst, and the articles do not provide independent verification of them. The articles do not say what products Nooks plans to introduce beyond the Revenue Agent Platform, nor do they give a timeline for the expansion. They also do not report any reaction from competitors or outside analysts. Beyond the announced tripling of annual recurring revenue by year-end, no further milestones are described.

stories.Headline: AI wipeout in focus; U.S. employment data ahead - what’s moving markets
stories.Summary:
A sharp selloff in artificial intelligence-linked stocks hit markets on Thursday, November 5, 2026, after Democrats won in the U.S. midterm elections earlier that week. Traders fearing tighter Democratic regulation of AI moved out of exposed shares, and chipmakers, data center developers and power providers all fell. The Nasdaq Composite lost an estimated $2.5 trillion in total market value, its steepest drop since March 2020. The S&P 500 closed down 4.36% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 3.44%, while a market volatility gauge jumped by its largest one-day amount since last year's tariff announcements.

The rout spread across the world. Asia-Pacific shares posted their largest decline since 2025, Japanese stocks tumbled, Taiwan's main index entered bear market territory, and South Korea's market was halted by a circuit breaker after heavy losses in chip firms SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics. Shares of Tesla and SpaceX, companies led by Elon Musk, dropped 11% and 9%. Their combined market value fell by about $460 billion, and Musk's net worth dropped by $71 billion at one point, though he remains the richest person in the world, according to Bloomberg News. The moves followed Democratic wins in Texas, where both companies are based.

Analysts blamed the AI-driven concerns. Joe Maher, a markets economist at Capital Economics, said growing doubts about the sustainability of the AI buildout, combined with the political shift, had caused another hard day for tech stocks. He added that the boom appeared to be in its final stage, though it remained unclear whether the midterm result would be the trigger that ends it. Reporting from The Wall Street Journal said three major investors in a planned Anthropic initial public offering believed its valuation could fall from about $1.5 trillion, with one suggesting $1 trillion. Anthropic had been reportedly aiming to list the week before Thanksgiving and raise as much as $100 billion.

Attention now turns to the U.S. jobs report due on November 6, which is expected to show 65,000 jobs added in October, up from 29,000 the month before, with unemployment holding at 4.2%. Strong employment could strengthen the case for a Federal Reserve rate increase at its December meeting, a possibility that Deutsche Bank said has been called into question again by AI fears. Oil prices also swung wildly as attacks on tankers in the Middle East raised supply concerns amid the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran. Brent crude settled nearly 4% higher on Thursday after falling more than 8% the day before, when the midterm results briefly raised hopes for diplomacy.

stories.Headline: China expresses ‘serious concern’ over UK's unfounded ‘cyber challenge’ claims regarding Chinese AI; politicizing tech competition harms global AI governance: expert
stories.Summary:
China has voiced "grave concern" over claims by Britain's National Cyber Security Centre, part of the Government Communications Headquarters, that China is a leading developer of AI-enabled cyber capability. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning made the comments at a regular press briefing on Wednesday, November 4, 2026, when asked about reports that the agency said China would be "highly likely" by 2028 to routinely use AI-enabled hacking, posing the "most sophisticated and sustained" cyber challenge to the UK. Mao said the accusations were speculative and unsupported by evidence. She argued that Britain had long politicized cybersecurity and was reviving hacking allegations as a pretext to curb China's AI development. Beijing says such moves damage mutual trust and weaken the UK's credibility on global AI security governance.

Mao said AI-generated cyber risks are a global problem that calls for new rules formulated through the United Nations. She restated China's position that AI development should be open, aimed at progress and good for all, balancing security and advancement while remaining safe, reliable and controllable. A Huaqiao University professor, Hu Qimu, told the Global Times that linking China's rapid AI growth to cyber threats reflects a tendency to politicize technological competition, which could undermine cooperation on shared security challenges. Hu said China's expanding open-source AI ecosystem has created new opportunities for international technology cooperation. She warned that framing Chinese advances mainly as security threats could deepen mistrust and make common rules for safe AI development harder to reach.

China pointed to its recent efforts on AI governance as evidence of its approach. The Global AI Governance Action Plan was released in July 2025 at the World Artificial Intelligence Conference and High-Level Meeting on Global AI Governance, calling for stronger scientific and technological cooperation, better policy coordination and more support for developing countries. In July 2026, 29 countries signed an agreement in Shanghai to establish the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, according to the Chinese Foreign Ministry. Hu said addressing AI security challenges requires international cooperation and commonly accepted rules rather than geopolitical confrontation. The articles do not report any UK response to Beijing's remarks.

stories.Headline: NTT Data plans further investment in Indonesian data centres amid rising AI and cloud demand
stories.Summary:
Japan's NTT Data Group plans to expand its data centre investments in Indonesia as demand for artificial intelligence and cloud computing grows across the region. The company has put USD 500 million into Indonesian data centres since 2015 and is considering the purchase of more land under a two-to-three-year expansion plan. Its expansion was announced alongside the opening of a 12-megawatt data centre annex in Jakarta. NTT Data has not said how much it will invest in the coming phase. The move comes as local concerns grow over electricity use, water supply, land use and opposition from some communities.

Yasuhiro Kajiki, managing director for Japan and Asia Pacific at NTT Data's data centre business, said the company is pursuing an aggressive expansion strategy in the country. He did not give a figure for future spending. The plan includes buying additional land and adding capacity for businesses that need computing infrastructure for AI, cloud services and other digital applications. The company has not said how many facilities it intends to build, where they will go, or when individual projects will start.

Market data suggests strong room for growth. A Research and Markets report published in January valued Indonesia's data centre market at USD 2.81 billion in 2025 and forecast it would reach USD 6.08 billion by 2031. That growth reflects rising use of cloud computing, digital platforms and AI services that need facilities to store and process large volumes of data. Operators must still secure suitable land, power and reliable connectivity before projects can proceed. Those requirements, along with community concerns, will shape how quickly the expansion moves forward.

Large data centres need substantial electricity to run servers and cooling systems, and some cooling technologies also use water. Competition for land and pressure on power networks have led to opposition against some projects in Indonesia and Malaysia. Kajiki said engaging with local communities is important and acknowledged that some developments face resistance from residents. The company's ability to secure sites and progress projects may therefore depend on how well it addresses those concerns as well as on commercial demand. It has not said how future Indonesian projects will handle energy and water use or whether it will set specific efficiency targets.

stories.Headline: AI storm dooms tech stocks to biggest drop since Trump’s ‘Liberation Day’ rout
stories.Summary:
The Nasdaq Composite suffered its steepest one-day fall since "Liberation Day" in April 2025, dropping 5.5 per cent and erasing trillions of dollars in market value. Investors blamed a Democratic sweep in the US midterm elections, which they feared could bring more scrutiny of artificial intelligence and slow the construction of data centres. The sell-off was the second straight session of heavy selling in AI stocks. The concern centres on whether the build-out of AI infrastructure can keep pace, since the midterm result raised the prospect of tougher oversight.

Smaller firms face particular pressure because higher interest rates and tighter financial conditions have already limited their ability to raise funds. The article links these pressures to a broader rethinking of the AI trade, which had been buoyant until recently. The Nasdaq has now posted five declines of more than 500 points since mid-October, a pattern the report ties to growing scrutiny of the AI trade over the past several weeks. Reuters, which the article credits, reported that the selling followed the election results rather than any single company announcement.

The article does not name a specific official or company that set off the decline. Market analysts and investors quoted in the coverage describe the fall as a reaction to uncertainty rather than a verdict on the sector's long-term prospects. The articles provide no detail on new regulations or legislation that would follow from the election. Whether the selling deepens or steadies will depend on what the new Congress does on AI and data centres, a matter the articles leave unresolved.

stories.Headline: GT Economic Investigates: What does the Wuzhen summit reveal about China-US AI cooperation amid intensifying competition?
stories.Summary:
At the World Internet Conference Wuzhen Summit in East China's Zhejiang Province, held in early November 2026, Chinese and US artificial intelligence developers displayed their work side by side even as competition between them intensified. Debora Comparin, co-chair of an International Telecommunication Union initiative on trust and identity for humans and agentic AI, told the Global Times that constructive cooperation between the two countries was essential. Her remarks came just days after the US government ordered federal civilian agencies to remove DeepSeek products and services from their IT systems and exclude them from procurement. Microsoft had already made the Chinese developer's R1 model available to customers through its Azure AI Foundry platform. Intel, Qualcomm and Microsoft were among the US companies exhibiting alongside Chinese firms at the Light of Internet Expo.

The competition is increasingly about price as well as performance. Stanford University's 2026 AI Index found that top US and Chinese models began trading places in performance rankings in early 2025, with the leading US model holding a 2.7 percent advantage in the Arena ratings as of March 2026. In September 2026, DeepSeek cut its API prices with the release of V4.1 Flash, a smaller model that added visual understanding. Its higher-end V4 Pro was priced at $3.96 per million output tokens, while Anthropic listed its flagship Claude Opus 5.5 at $20 per million output tokens. Government action has narrowed some choices, as an October 27 US Department of Energy notice described an order from the Department of Homeland Security excluding DeepSeek from federal civilian procurement.

A January 2026 US Commerce Department decision also said it would review licenses for certain advanced chip exports to China case by case. Those who spoke with the Global Times pointed to areas where cooperation remains possible. Comparin said Chinese and US companies could work with European partners on protocols and safeguards so that AI agents can operate securely across platforms. Intel showed enterprise AI workstations and PCs built to run AI agents, and said it was working with Chinese partners on uses such as visual quality inspection.

On October 5, Qualcomm and Huawei announced a multi-year agreement covering cross-licenses in 5G, computing, AI and networking, with Qualcomm also agreeing to buy certain Huawei US patents subject to regulatory approvals. In October, Amazon Web Services announced that Zhipu AI's GLM-5.3 was generally available on Amazon Bedrock. Chinese technology analyst Liu Dingding argued that such partnerships can help multinational companies commercialize technologies while supporting industrial upgrading in China. Analysts also see shared standards and open models as a route forward.

In October, the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation announced new projects, including OpenAI's Open Responses and Alibaba's OpenSandbox, which provides isolated environments for running agents. China's Ministry of Commerce said the two countries held their first dialogue on AI under their economic and trade consultation mechanism during the eighth round of talks in the US, where they reached several points of consensus. Terry Sweetser of the Asia Pacific Network Information Centre said open models could make AI more widely accessible, and Sri Lankan entrepreneur Lilan Dayananda said healthy competition could prevent technological monopolies. Both points suggest that the two countries are still weighing rivalry against the gains from working together.

stories.Headline: AI offers answers, curiosity drives discovery
stories.Summary:
Nobel Prize-winning chemist Michael Levitt, who shared the 2013 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, spoke at the 2026 World Laureates Forum in Shanghai about the role of curiosity and artificial intelligence in scientific work. He urged young researchers around the world to take up both. Levitt, a professor of structural biology at Stanford University, said that asking good questions matters most when working with AI. He described AI as something like a conversation partner that offers many answers, which is why a researcher needs curiosity to choose among them.

Levitt said that scientists must be open-minded yet skeptical, since AI does not always give correct information. In his own practice, he said, he checks an AI answer by asking someone else, and he tends to trust a result only when two sources agree. He praised the rapid spread of AI in China, across education and research, and called China's use of the technology very strong. He also said he was pleased to see AI so widely adopted there. Levitt added that a Nobel Prize brings a wider responsibility, which he compared to acting as a diplomat of science.

Levitt said he wants as many young people as possible to enter science, because he believes the field benefits the world and can produce discoveries with large effects. He pointed to the forum as a rare setting where established laureates and emerging researchers exchange ideas. He recalled hearing five lectures on very different subjects that he said would be almost impossible to hear anywhere else. He stressed that young people are the focus of the forum and that new ideas usually come from them. He said the future belongs to young people in every field.

Levitt noted that his own career has crossed several countries and continents, and his Stanford research group included people from India, China, Europe and South America. He said science is international and that his work, kept on a computer, lets him work from anywhere, and he said he feels very at home in China. Looking ahead, he named stability and engagement with young people as priorities for the forum's future success in building international scientific collaboration. The article does not give details of any specific future events or plans beyond these priorities.

stories.Headline: Ocient Raises $100M Series C Funding to Advance AI Solutions for Petabyte-Scale Environments
stories.Summary:
Ocient, a Chicago-based data and analytics company, announced on November 5, 2026 that it had closed a $100 million Series C funding round. The round was co-led by BOKA Capital and OCA Ventures, with all existing investors participating, and it brings Ocient's total capital raised to $260 million. Several earlier backers joined the round, including Greycroft, In-Q-Tel, Blue Bear Capital, and Buoyant Ventures, while Dallas Venture Capital came in as a new investor. The company said the money will speed up delivery of its OcientAIQ Solutions for organizations running AI agents against large, constantly changing datasets.

The funding comes as Ocient expects to more than triple its revenue this year, driven by customers in industries that depend on high-volume, continuously growing data. The company describes its OcientAIQ Solutions as tailored to specific industries and built on its OcientAIQ Unified Data Platform, which handles governance and fast analysis. Ocient also said it has widened its partner network this year and formally set up its India operations and Ocient National Security Solutions as dedicated subsidiaries. The press release frames the platform's value around governance, since it enforces access, policy, and lineage controls on agent activity. It adds that analysis runs inside the engine rather than through a language model, so results can be reproduced and audited.

John Morris, Ocient's chief executive, said customers operate at a scale where the speed and reliability of an answer can carry serious consequences, and that the investment will help extend the reach of OcientAIQ to more customers. John James, chief executive of BOKA Capital, said turning advanced technology into dependable operational capability is now the key test in defense and national security, and that he expects to join the board. Jim Dugan, founding managing partner of OCA Ventures, said his firm first invested because it believed in the team's ability to tackle problems others had largely left unsolved. The release also cites Gartner's projection that worldwide IT spending will reach $7.35 trillion in 2027, up 15% from 2026, as organizations push to industrialize AI.

stories.Headline: Together AI Compiler Cuts AI Engine Setup Time to 9 Seconds
stories.Summary:
Together AI introduced a compiler for AI inference workloads on November 4, 2026, saying it cut engine setup time from 467 seconds to nine seconds. The system can reload candidate GPU-code changes without restarting, according to the company. The compiler uses agents to rewrite GPU code and tests candidate changes through a two-tier system. Fast engines support quick iterations, while slower engines give more accurate measurements. The company says the approach raised experimentation throughput to 252 times the level of baseline agentic systems and that the compiler is now operational.

In tests completed in under 24 hours, throughput rose between 1.3 and 3 times across Kimi K3, GLM 5.3, MiniMax M3.1-Flash and DeepSeek v4.1-Flash. On the InferenceX low-latency benchmark, the compiler reached 1,111 tokens per second on MiniMax M3.1-Flash and 1,205 tokens per second on DeepSeek v4.1-Flash. It also beat open-source megakernels by 1.7 times in a Llama 1B test with a batch size of one. Together AI is the party behind the announcement, and its figures come from its own testing. The company says its optimization system selects parallelism strategies using hardware specifications, microbenchmarks and real-world traffic data.

Its results are reported by TokenPost, which noted that inference performance can vary with the model, hardware and traffic patterns. The article also cites an overnight optimization that cut Phonic-1's median time to first speech by nearly 50 percent. Together AI says the compiler can also be applied to weather modeling, partial differential equations, time-series analysis and biology. The articles do not describe any further rollout plans or independent verification of the benchmark results. For now, the claims rest on the company's own tests and the figures it has published.
