The piece draws on a report from the startup Vals AI, which tested the most popular AI models on immigration scenarios and checked their answers against rubrics written by immigration law experts. The article's author, Dara, is a journalist and senior fellow at the American Immigration Council who has covered immigration policy for years. The story points to the growing reach of AI in everyday searches, where a 2026 Pew Research study found that 42% of Americans use AI chatbots to look for information.

According to the Vals AI report, even the best-performing model, a costly version of Anthropic's Claude, gave incomplete answers in most situations, and other models did worse. The report concluded that AI tools should not be relied on to independently advise clients on their specific situation. The article gives two main reasons: AI models are limited by their training data, which may predate recent policy changes, and they cannot tell which details matter, so they may miss facts that change a case. When asked about 2025 and 2026 policy changes, even models that could search the web provided less than a third of the information experts sought. The weakest category was temporary or fragile status, including Temporary Protected Status and Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, which are the cases where people face the highest risk of losing status.

The article notes that the report's findings are the author's reading of the Vals AI study and of surveys, not the statements of a government agency or company spokesperson on the matter. A 2025 survey by Rev found that 43% of Americans were comfortable asking AI for help clarifying legal terms, but only 6% would rely on it for an immigration case. The author also cites a 2021 University of Denver study showing that few immigrants with immigration-related problems used the internet as a resource, and many of those who did went straight to agency websites. The article says that only a quarter of closed immigration court cases as of August 2026 had legal representation, which leaves many people with few options beyond online sources. The author's advice is to seek out real immigration lawyers when possible and to rely on trusted expert sources such as free legal clinics and reliable news outlets.

Articles.Title: Immigration Seekers Face Risks Using AI for Legal Advice

stories.Headline: Tesla to axe Cybertruck as Musk shifts focus to robotics and AI
stories.Summary:
The Financial Times reported on November 6, 2026, that Tesla plans to end production of its Cybertruck, as chief executive Elon Musk shifts the company's focus toward robotics and artificial intelligence. The report appeared under the headline "Tesla to axe Cybertruck as Musk shifts focus to robotics and AI." The article itself is largely a subscription page, and the body text visible in the extract does not give further details on timing, production volumes, or the reasoning behind the decision. Nothing in the material indicates how many vehicles have been built or sold, or what will happen to existing owners.

The available text does not specify any figures, dates, or formal requirements beyond the report's publication date. It also does not say whether the decision has been confirmed by Tesla through an official statement, whether it affects other models, or how it will affect the company's finances. The surrounding material is almost entirely promotional content about subscription plans, which means the reporting that would normally explain the decision is not visible in the extract. Readers would need the full article to learn more.

Because the extract contains so little reporting, the most accurate account of the story is limited to the headline claim and its publication details. The report links the planned end of the Cybertruck to a broader change in Musk's priorities, but the text does not explain that link in any detail. Any further context about the company's plans for robotics or AI, or about how those plans relate to the vehicle, is absent from the material provided. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Tesla to axe Cybertruck as Musk shifts focus to robotics and AI

stories.Headline: Genspark: How AI Agent Workspace Hit a US$2.6bn Valuation
stories.Summary:
Genspark, a Palo Alto start-up, reached a US$2.6bn valuation in June 2026, according to Reuters, after a further US$100m raise lifted its Series B to US$485m. The company began in 2023 as an AI search engine, but it pivoted in April 2025 to a Super Agent that plans and carries out tasks such as building slides, spreadsheets, documents and code. It announced a US$200m annual run-rate in March 2026, eleven months after relaunching as an agent company, when it had first reached US$10m. Its newest product, Genspark Claw, is an always-on AI agent with its own cloud computer for each user, reachable through WhatsApp, Slack or Teams.

The workspace draws on a mixture of agents built on more than 30 models, 150 tools and 20 premium datasets, and the company has added products including AI Slides, AI Sheets, AI Docs and AI Developer. Growth has been fast, with Genspark for Business passing 1,000 organisations by early 2026 and more than 6,000 within six months. The company became a launch partner for Microsoft Agent 365 in November 2025, bringing its agents into Teams and Microsoft 365, and added plugins for PowerPoint, Excel and Word in April 2026. Claw connects to about 20 apps, from Google Workspace to Salesforce, and was launched in March 2026.

The company is led by co-founder and CEO Eric Jing, a former Baidu executive, who founded Genspark with Kay Zhu in 2023. Eric Jing has said that Genspark has built an all-in-one AI Workspace where agents autonomously plan and execute to deliver finished outcomes. Co-founder and COO Wen Sang has said that the company sees a fundamental shift in how everyone will interact with work. Investors include Emergence Capital, which led a US$275m Series B at a US$1.25bn valuation in November 2025, along with LG Technology Ventures, SBI Investment, UpHonest Capital and Pavilion Capital. Genspark names OpenAI, Anthropic and Microsoft among its technology partners, and its models from those partners sit within its orchestration system.

Articles.Title: Genspark: How AI Agent Workspace Hit a US$2.6bn Valuation

stories.Headline: Which movie most accurately depicts our AI-disrupted future? A new nationwide poll may surprise you
stories.Summary:
A Deseret News and University of Utah Hinckley Institute of Politics poll asked respondents which movie would most accurately depict life with AI, and "I, Robot" came out on top in both the Utah and national samples. "The Terminator" took second place in both, while the third-place film differed, with Utahns choosing "2001: A Space Odyssey" and the rest of the country choosing "War Games." The Utah survey was conducted Oct. 13-20 among 875 registered voters with a margin of error of plus or minus 3%, and the national survey was conducted Oct. 13-19 among 2,050 registered voters with a margin of error of plus or minus 2%. Morning Consult conducted the polling. A plurality of respondents, 24% of Utahns and 34% nationally, selected "none of the above."

The poll offered films such as "Big Hero 6," "Her," "Avengers: Age of Ultron," "M3GAN," and "Ex Machina" as alternatives. University of Utah film and media arts professor Kenneth Collins reviewed the results and said the choices reflect a broader pattern in popular culture, which has mostly imagined dystopian or apocalyptic outcomes from AI. He argued that the high share choosing "none of the above" suggests many people have not seen their future in these films and that stories offering a hopeful picture of AI remain largely untold. He pointed to the XPRIZE Foundation's Future Vision contest, which awarded $2.6 million to the winner for an optimistic, abundant future for humanity.

Separately, the article reports that ChatGPT, Grok and Claude each named "Her," the 2013 film about a lonely letter writer who falls in love with an AI operating system, as the most accurate depiction. The chatbots said the film better captures the everyday feel of living with AI than the catastrophic plots of the other options, though ChatGPT also noted that some films predict the technology well while others predict human behavior better. Claude said the film was accurate about the texture of daily life rather than its plot. The article does not describe any formal policy changes or regulatory actions tied to the poll.

Articles.Title: Which movie most accurately depicts our AI-disrupted future? A new nationwide poll may surprise you

stories.Headline: China’s AI chipmakers report first profits, but will the trend continue?
stories.Summary:
China's pure-play artificial intelligence chipmakers reached a milestone in the third quarter, when several firms swung into profit for the first time. Domestic GPU developers including Moore Threads, MetaX and Iluvatar CoreX are racing to fill the gap left by Nvidia, whose high-end processors face strict US export controls. The firms are competing hard to win over domestic enterprise clients and to gain a foothold with major cloud service providers. Their reports were published in early November 2026, and the coverage notes that the gains came despite a difficult operating environment.

Severe supply chain hurdles and soaring memory costs, however, cloud the long-term growth prospects of these companies. The article reports that major investment banks have pared back their margin forecasts for the sector in response. Memory prices in particular have climbed sharply, squeezing the cost structure of chip designers that depend on outside suppliers. Because the profits are recent and the pressures are ongoing, analysts are unsure whether the early earnings will hold.

The reporting centers on the firms themselves and on the analysts who cover them, with the article describing their outlook in general terms. It presents the banks' revised forecasts as a sign of caution rather than a verdict on any single company. The piece does not offer detailed quotations from company executives in the portion available here. Responsibility for the financial results rests with the individual firms, while the margin forecasts come from the investment banks that publish them.

The broader context is the effort to build a domestic alternative to Nvidia's chips under export restrictions imposed by the United States. The article does not give specific figures for the profits or the forecast cuts beyond the fact of the revisions. It also does not describe what the firms plan to do next to address memory costs or supply shortages. Whether the profitability trend continues will depend on how those supply pressures develop in the coming quarters.

Articles.Title: China’s AI chipmakers report first profits, but will the trend continue?

stories.Headline: Windward Acquires Azimut.ai to Add Optical Sensing to Maritime Intelligence
stories.Summary:
Windward, a maritime AI company, has acquired Azimut.ai, a maritime visual intelligence company, to add an optical sensing layer to its maritime intelligence offering. The company announced the purchase on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, according to its statement reported on November 6, 2026. The deal is Windward's first venture into sensors mounted on ships and on the ground. Windward said the move is meant to expand its capabilities for public and private sector customers. The optical sensing technology is designed to recognize ships and capture their distinguishing features in real time at ports and chokepoints.

It can detect vessels that have gone dark to avoid detection. Windward plans to station cameras along key sea routes and chokepoints. Customers will receive vessel analytics rather than raw camera footage, and the system is designed to analyze vessel activity rather than identify or verify people. Windward said it built the system with privacy and security in mind.

Windward said existing tracking methods, such as Automatic Identification System transmissions, radio frequency data and satellite imagery, have limits. Some ships do not transmit signals, and cooperative systems can be disabled, jammed or disrupted by weather. Each visual sighting will be matched against Windward's behavioral intelligence and risk layers, along with cargo, sanctions and ownership records. CEO and Co-Founder Ami Daniel called the purchase the company's first step in building a proprietary visual intelligence layer.

He said owning the sensors would give customers unmatched awareness, and he invited maritime stakeholders to sign on as site partners. Windward has built on earlier partnerships to strengthen its maritime domain awareness. In April, it began integrating Vantor's Sentry persistent monitoring system with its Maritime AI, which allows continuous tracking when tracking systems are disabled. It also previously worked with HawkEye 360 to add space-based radio frequency data to its platform.

In June, the company appointed retired U.S. Navy Vice Adm. Robert Sharp as chief maritime intelligence officer. Sharp previously led the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency from 2019 to 2022 and works directly with Daniel on intelligence strategy. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Windward Acquires Azimut.ai to Add Optical Sensing to Maritime Intelligence

stories.Headline: Chaos brings AI design exploration into Enscape
stories.Summary:
Chaos has upgraded the link between its Enscape real-time visualisation software and its AI visualisation tool Veras 2.0, bringing AI-powered design exploration into the Enscape interface. The update was launched on 6 November 2026 as part of Enscape 4.22. It is meant to help architects bring AI into their existing workflows, generate design variations and test different materials and moods. The integration removes the need to open a separate Veras window, so architects can reach AI rendering tools directly within Enscape.

New AI video models offer further ways to show and communicate design ideas. Enscape 4.22 also adds Chaos AI Assistant in beta, which gives in-product guidance and recommends relevant assets while designers work. Changes to the Chaos Cosmos 3D content library are intended to turn visual inspiration into usable 3D assets. Its Image-Based Search lets architects find visually similar assets using reference images instead of keywords.

When no suitable asset exists, AI 3D Model Generation in beta can create a textured 3D asset from an image, and the feature is free during beta, subject to usage limits, and does not consume Chaos Credits. Petr Mitev, VP Product, Solutions for Designers at Chaos, said that AI has large potential to support architects' creativity, not just efficiency. He said the closer link to Veras makes it easier for designers to explore possibilities and make informed creative decisions without disrupting how they already work. To encourage adoption, Chaos is offering 500 additional Chaos Credits with eligible new Enscape trials and annual licence purchases until 15 November 2026, and the credits can be used to experiment with Veras and test design variations.

Articles.Title: Chaos brings AI design exploration into Enscape

stories.Headline: Boeing uses AI-powered drones to speed up C-17 aircraft inspections
stories.Summary:
Boeing is testing AI-powered drones to inspect C-17 Globemaster III transport aircraft at its San Antonio maintenance facility in Texas. Under its Advanced Aircraft Inspection programme, camera-equipped drones fly around the aircraft and photograph its exterior. Boeing's Automated Damage Detection Software then checks those photographs for possible damage, and technicians review the findings. The approach is meant to shorten inspections and reduce work on elevated platforms, which the company says could also improve worker safety. The article dates the report to November 6, 2026.

The drones photograph areas that would otherwise need close-range inspection, and the software flags anything that needs a closer look. Boeing is training the software to spot problems such as corrosion and lightning strikes, but it does not make the final call. Maintenance staff must examine suspected defects and decide what work is needed. Boeing says it has tested the main inspection procedures and written guidance for staff training and quality checks. A shorter inspection could return a C-17 to service sooner, which matters because the US Air Force and other operators use the aircraft to carry troops, vehicles and equipment.

Boeing's Travis Williams, vice president of Mobility and Surveillance Aircraft Services, described the programme as turning innovation into operational value. He said the company is delivering measurable improvements and building a capability that can be scaled once outcomes are validated. The San Antonio team is still refining the process before wider use. The work follows several years of development with autonomous flight specialist Near Earth Autonomy, in which Boeing invested through its HorizonX Ventures arm in 2017.

The companies tested autonomous inspections at Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam in Hawaii, and the National Centre for Manufacturing Sciences reports that the system cut inspection time by at least 40 percent during C-17 heavy maintenance visits. Its detection model identified more than 95 percent of anomalies in each scan. The technology has also been tested on other military aircraft. Boeing wants to extend the drone inspections to other maintenance sites and aircraft, and its teams are sharing what they learn from the trials.

Articles.Title: Boeing uses AI-powered drones to speed up C-17 aircraft inspections

stories.Headline: Anthropic’s AI is improving itself and could suddenly become ‘extreme’ and ‘risky’, major report warns
stories.Summary:
An independent AI safety monitoring group, Model Evaluation and Threat Research (METR), has published a report finding that Anthropic's AI models are accelerating their own development. According to the report, released on a Thursday and reported on November 6, 2026, Anthropic's AI progress is now about twice as fast as it was a year earlier. The researchers said Anthropic had effectively achieved two years of benchmark progress over the past year. Anthropic had invited METR to review its internal data and evaluate its models' capabilities.

The researchers attributed the speed-up to recursive self-improvement, meaning the AI models are helping build later generations, rather than to growth in the computing power used for training. They warned that if AI systems significantly accelerated further AI development, this could lead to a sudden emergence of extreme and risky capabilities. The report also said that humans still oversee the most critical parts of model training, but that AI is not yet able to make fully autonomous contributions there. It added that researchers saw significant signs that such contributions could arrive soon, with the level of maturity varying by area.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has been calling for a slowdown. In a September essay titled "We Must Pace the Frontier," he proposed a three-point plan for developing AI safely and argued that recursive self-improvement, left unchecked, could outrun humanity's ability to understand and control these systems. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said at the time that he agreed the industry needs to pace itself and called Amodei's proposal for independent evaluators a great idea. The article also links to related coverage of wider calls to slow AI development and of Anthropic's own warnings about catastrophic risks.

Articles.Title: Anthropic’s AI is improving itself and could suddenly become ‘extreme’ and ‘risky’, major report warns

stories.Headline: Teaching AI to Build Better Enzymes
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the University of California, Santa Barbara, led by HHMI Freeman Hrabowski Scholar Yang Yang, have developed SynFit, an open-source machine learning tool that predicts enzyme variants likely to perform well on several traits at once. The work was co-developed with Yunan Luo at the Georgia Institute of Technology and was reported by the Howard Hughes Medical Institute on November 5, 2026. The tool is designed to work even when experimental data are limited. Its code and data are freely available so that other labs can try it.

Enzymes help scientists make valuable chemicals, but nature's versions do not cover every reaction a researcher might want, so engineers modify them and test the results. The difficulty is that a useful enzyme usually has to be fast, stable, productive, and correctly shaped all at once, and improving one feature can undermine another. Traditional directed evolution handles this by making and screening many variants over repeated rounds, which takes considerable time. Many computational models predict only one trait at a time, so they do little to narrow that search. SynFit instead learns several measurements together and ranks candidates by how well they balance the traits that matter.

The team tested the approach on a cytochrome c enzyme engineered to build carbon-boron bonds, which can serve as building blocks for complex molecules used in medicines and materials. After training on a small batch of lab data, the researchers used SynFit to choose new variants, and many of them achieved the high yield and high selectivity the team wanted. The group also tested the tool on public protein datasets where the same protein was measured in more than one way, and it outperformed models that handled each measurement separately. Yang said the method is not limited to a specific protein and that his team is already applying SynFit and related tools to other enzymes.

Articles.Title: Teaching AI to Build Better Enzymes

stories.Headline: Kickstarter’s CEO is championing human creativity in a flood of AI
stories.Summary:
Kickstarter CEO Everette Taylor used a Fortune CEO Daily column, published on November 6, 2026, to argue that human creativity still matters even as artificial intelligence floods the creative economy. The column, written by Diane Brady, reports that AI is both a catalyst and a challenge for creators on the crowdfunding platform. Taylor said the technology encourages more people to become creators and entrepreneurs, which in turn brings more people to Kickstarter. He also expressed concern about how much AI can produce on its own. Taylor described a test in which he asked ChatGPT for a script about a "Mosquito Man" from the Bronx, and the tool returned a complete film script.

The column notes that AI can write such a script but cannot supply the network of people willing to back a project. Kickstarter reinforced that message at a Times Square event held with the projector maker XGIMI, which showcased a laser TV that raised a record $10 million in two hours. The event was tied to a brand campaign Kickstarter launched in the summer under the tagline "belief is human." The column adds that the company's own data points the same way, since one 2026 study of 63,000 campaigns found projects labeled as using AI raised about 40% less money and drew almost a quarter fewer backers.

Taylor said Kickstarter believes in the importance of human creativity regardless of how far AI advances, and he pointed to a $1 million Kickstarter Culture Fund that helps independent creators earn a living. He argued that a large social media following matters less than the smaller group of committed supporters a creator has on the platform. The column also cites Kickstarter's scale, with more than 24 million backers having spent close to $9 billion on 277,302 projects as of April 2025, creating more than 1 million jobs. Kickstarter launched in 2009 and became a public benefit corporation in 2015.

Brady frames Taylor's comments within a broader trend in which a "friendship economy" and a growing creator economy gain appeal as AI and a weak job market unsettle traditional careers. The same newsletter reports that Goldman Sachs projects the number of creators will grow from 67 million to 107 million by 2030, and the creator economy will generate half a trillion dollars by next year. The column does not describe any further regulatory action or company response beyond Taylor's comments and Kickstarter's campaign. Its coverage of the wider market, including the Nasdaq's drop of more than 5% on a single Thursday, is separate from the Kickstarter story.

Articles.Title: Kickstarter’s CEO is championing human creativity in a flood of AI

stories.Headline: Kalepa raises $75m to scale AI across insurance
stories.Summary:
Kalepa, a New York-based InsurTech that develops artificial intelligence for insurance professionals, has raised $75m in a Series B round at a $470m valuation, following a year in which its revenue and client base each tripled. The round was led by Updata Partners, with existing investors IA Ventures and Inspired Capital also taking part. The investment brings the company's total funding to $91m, following a $14m Series A in 2021 led by Inspired Capital. Kalepa plans to use the proceeds to expand its AI product portfolio, enter additional markets and double its workforce during 2027.

The company says it has kept positive cash flow for more than two years while achieving its recent growth. Its customers include major insurance carriers and managing general agents such as W. R. Berkley, Bowhead Specialty and AmRisc. The funding comes as insurers face pressure to improve underwriting efficiency, manage rising claims costs and replace experienced staff who are leaving the industry. Softer insurance pricing leaves less room for underwriting errors, and newer AI-focused rivals are raising expectations for speed. Kalepa's platform coordinates work across operations, underwriting, pricing and portfolio management, with human professionals involved where specialist judgement or approval is required.

Kalepa reports that customers have achieved between 30% and 60% more premium per underwriter, a 58% cut in quoting times, a 960-basis-point improvement in combined ratios and a doubling of quote-to-bind rates. The volume of work processed through the platform rose fourfold over the past 12 months. The company also appointed Garrett Schlesinger as chief technology officer, a role he takes up after 12 years at Affirm, where he joined as its 12th employee. Schlesinger joins chief revenue officer David Meister, head of product Audrey Howell and head of talent Tim Khoo-Jones.

Founded in 2018, Kalepa provides technology to insurance carriers, MGAs, reinsurers and programme administrators worldwide. Co-founder and CEO Paul Monasterio said the company's AI is held to the same standard as experienced professionals, so insurers can decide whether a given task is better handled by AI or by a person. He argued that this division of labour lets staff focus on complex risks, close calls and broker relationships. According to the article, the funding will allow Kalepa to bring its AI capabilities to more parts of the insurance value chain.

Articles.Title: Kalepa raises $75m to scale AI across insurance

stories.Headline: GreenboardGo2.0 brings AI harness era to compliance teams
stories.Summary:
Greenboard, a company that makes AI-native software for SEC and FINRA compliance, has launched GreenboardGo2.0, which it calls the first AI harness built specifically for compliance teams. The firm presents the release as the start of a new product category. The launch extends GreenboardGo, the conversational AI layer Greenboard rolled out in May, and now runs across the whole Greenboard platform. The article is dated November 6, 2026.

The new version lets compliance staff query, configure and automate any part of their programme from one place, with each action captured in a WORM-based, 17a-4 compliant record. It also connects with Slack, Teams, Claude and ChatGPT, giving users access to more than 240 Greenboard tools through MCP. All activity stays within permissions set by the compliance team, and a person must approve any output before it is finalised. Rather than offering a fixed feature set, the product lets teams build their own agents by choosing the trigger, context, sequence of actions and the stage where human approval is needed. Greenboard has also released a fiduciary commitment built on six principles: loyalty, care, candour, supervision, agency and continuity.

Greenboard argues that foundation models cannot manage compliance work alone, because the work depends on reaching the right policy, record, tool and person at the right moment. In its view, a harness fills that gap by adding firm-specific context, guardrails and an audit trail that examiners can follow. Under the fiduciary pledge, GreenboardGo serves only the firm that deploys it, Greenboard will not sell firm data, and clients can take their data with them on request. Founder and CEO Dave Feldman said GreenboardGo is a new category and predicted that AI harnesses will replace all other compliance software by 2030. Co-founder and CTO Ed Schembor said harnesses turn AI models into large productivity gains in real work, and that compliance professionals will come to see this as lawyers and software engineers already do.

The underlying platform supported 750 regulated firms and 35,000 users in the most recent quarter, according to the company. Its modules cover archiving and AI-native supervision across email, social media and text messaging, employee compliance including attestations, pre-clearance and trade monitoring, marketing review, firm compliance and filings, and third-party due diligence. Because every module shares one record, the harness can adjust workflows, forms, rules and settings, produce programme-wide reports and automate any process a team builds within the platform. The articles provide no independent assessment of these claims, and no details on pricing or availability.

Articles.Title: GreenboardGo2.0 brings AI harness era to compliance teams

stories.Headline: Jim Cramer says the AI sell-off isn't over, but it isn't another dot-com crash
stories.Summary:
CNBC host Jim Cramer said on Thursday that the steep sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks likely has further to run, but he urged investors not to panic. The downturn followed growing opposition to new data centers after the midterm elections, which raised doubts about future spending on AI infrastructure. Shares of companies tied to that buildout fell sharply, with Micron down 17%, GE Vernova down 7% and Sandisk down 22% on Thursday. All three stocks had also been hit hard in Wednesday's session.

Cramer said he wished today's drop marked the bottom, but he cautioned that more downside could come. He did not believe the decline was a repeat of the internet bubble that burst in 2000. He argued that many of today's AI companies are profitable, unlike the speculative businesses that collapsed during the dot-com bust. He said the decline is orderly because these companies are mostly lucrative, though their stocks rose too high.

Cramer said investors had pushed AI stocks too high by assuming the rapid pace of data center construction would continue indefinitely. He said smaller developers such as CoreWeave, Iren and Nebius face particular risk because they borrowed money to finance projects that could now face regulatory delays. He said that debt concern is what he is chiefly worried about, but he also noted that no one of significance is currently defaulting on its debt. He added that this exposure is not enough to sink the market.

Cramer suggested that a swift sell-off could work off the excesses of the AI boom more effectively than a prolonged one. For investors, he recommended keeping sufficient cash, and he pointed to falling interest rates, signs of easing inflation and a possible end to the Iran war as reasons for optimism. He said semiconductor stocks could still decline further. He concluded that investors with cash will not panic and can lose less money while clear-headed until conditions improve.

Articles.Title: Jim Cramer says the AI sell-off isn't over, but it isn't another dot-com crash

stories.Headline: Apple Capped AI Spending. PYMNTS Data Shows Where CFOs Should Spend More.
stories.Summary:
Apple has reportedly tightened the AI usage of its employees, cutting the AI budget for certain internal teams by as much as a third. The move was reported in the week before this PYMNTS article, which was published on November 5, 2026. Other tech companies have also set limits, with Tesla reportedly capping employee AI spending at $200 a week, Uber at $1,500 a month, and Meta encouraging staff to use its own tools. These restrictions reflect the growing cost of enterprise AI as models scale and usage-based charges rise with each prompt and automated task. The article frames the question for chief financial officers as how to cut AI costs without sacrificing growth.

The article argues that flat spending caps can be a poor tool because they may penalize heavy use that produces real value. It cites PYMNTS Intelligence research finding that 62% of U.S. enterprises with at least $1 billion in annual revenue spend more than $10 million on new forms of AI, with the median between $10 million and $25 million. A separate PYMNTS Intelligence study found that 71% of executives see organizational readiness, not technology, as the chief limit on AI performance. Another found that 90% to 100% of surveyed firms rated their recent AI returns positively, yet only 5% to 10% reported full payback, with many expecting returns to take five or six years. The article also notes that AI-generated cash-flow insights are gaining use in finance teams, rising from 44% to 64% in a year.

The article's central point is that controlling consumption addresses only part of the problem, since a company that caps spending but keeps inefficient workflows may save on computing while preserving the underlying expense. It suggests that deeper integration, rather than deployment across more functions, is associated with stronger financial returns. It also says that some AI value, such as better financial decisions, appears outside the technology budget. The author presents a PYMNTS Intelligence report finding that 84% of large U.S. companies expect growth without a matching rise in staff over the next three years, and 75% expect changes in employee roles and skills. The article is written by PYMNTS and does not attribute new statements to Apple or other companies beyond the reported policies.

Articles.Title: Apple Capped AI Spending. PYMNTS Data Shows Where CFOs Should Spend More.

stories.Headline: Agentic AI boom expected to reshape CPU market
stories.Summary:
Growing use of autonomous AI agents is expected to raise demand for central processing units in data centers, according to a November 5, 2026 report from Network World reporter Andy Patrizio. The reporting cites semiconductor research firm TrendForce, which says these agents could push operators to deploy substantially more CPUs and to reconsider how many CPUs they install alongside GPUs. TrendForce's analysis draws on the point that AI agents place a heavier load on processors than conventional large language model inference does. Although GPUs remain essential for training AI models, CPUs handle the coordination of multistep tasks that agents perform on their own.

TrendForce says these CPU-bound activities include planning, scheduling subtasks, calling outside tools, managing interactions among several agents, and evaluating results. Agents also depend on general computing resources to run code, search databases, crawl websites, and process information. Traditional AI data centers have typically used roughly one CPU for every four to eight GPUs, but TrendForce expects agentic AI infrastructure to move toward one CPU for every one to two GPUs. Citing estimates from Arm, the firm says CPU core requirements could rise from about 30 million cores per gigawatt of data center capacity to 120 million cores per gigawatt, a potential fourfold increase.

The shift also bears on performance, energy use, and cost. Research cited by TrendForce indicates that CPU-based tool processing can account for as much as 90.6 percent of total latency in some agentic workloads, and CPU dynamic energy can make up a large share of system energy use under certain conditions. The analysis suggests that adding GPU capacity alone may not improve overall performance if the CPUs coordinating agents become bottlenecks. The article points to Nvidia as a sign of this change, noting that the company once downplayed CPUs but later introduced its Grace processor, now in the Vera generation.

Vera has 88 CPU cores and 176 threads, and Nvidia is also developing dedicated Vera CPU racks for customers who want CPU systems apart from GPU systems. The article frames the trend as part of a broader change in AI computing, in which systems move from generating single responses toward carrying out multistep tasks autonomously. TrendForce's analysis holds that the processors coordinating those tasks will become increasingly important. The reporting does not give a timeline for when these infrastructure changes will arrive at scale, and it does not describe further steps beyond the TrendForce analysis itself.

Articles.Title: Agentic AI boom expected to reshape CPU market

stories.Headline: Language-guided inverse design of multiclass metamaterials using generative artificial intelligence
stories.Summary:
MetaGen-LLM is a research framework, published in npj Metamaterials on November 5, 2026, that generates metamaterial designs from free-form language requests. The framework was developed by researchers who describe it as a way to map natural-language design requests to geometries across eight metamaterial classes. The article reports that the system converts user prompts into structured morphological and property conditions using a fine-tuned large language model. It then uses a condition encoder, a generator classifier, and a diffusion model to choose a geometry generator and predict modeling parameters.

The framework is designed to refine candidates toward target relative density, directional Young's moduli, and thermal conductivities using a surrogate model. Its geometry generators render smooth mesh representations that can be exported directly for additive manufacturing, avoiding an extra voxel-to-mesh step. The article says the generated designs closely matched the requested properties in both in-distribution and controlled out-of-distribution tests. The trained models are also integrated into an agentic interface that supports iterative language-based design and three-dimensional visualization.

The eight classes span four procedural generators: ordered and disordered truss and plate lattices, ordered bicontinuous and shell triply periodic minimal-surface structures, and disordered bicontinuous and shell spinodoid structures. The authors describe the work as addressing gaps in unifying these classes under one conditional design framework and in translating natural-language requests into structured conditions. They say the framework builds on earlier work such as Txt2Microstruct-Net and TrussGPT, which handled voxel-based and truss-only language-guided design. The article reports fabricated examples with a length of 40 millimeters, and it says the authors plan to continue developing the framework, though specific next steps are not detailed in the excerpt available.

Articles.Title: Language-guided inverse design of multiclass metamaterials using generative artificial intelligence

stories.Headline: Oil-rich UAE makes massive AI bet as Sam Altman unveils ambitious plan to transform energy industry
stories.Summary:
The UAE and OpenAI have announced a partnership to bring advanced artificial intelligence into the energy industry, unveiled at the opening of the ADIPEC 2026 energy conference in Abu Dhabi. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman joined senior UAE officials for the announcement, which involves state-owned energy company ADNOC, OpenAI and Abu Dhabi-based technology firm G42. The opening ceremony took place on November 2, 2026, while global energy supplies were under strain from the war involving Iran and disruptions to the Strait of Hormuz. Dr. Sultan Al Jaber, the UAE's minister of industry and advanced technology and ADNOC's chief executive, framed the deal as a two-way exchange, saying the world had asked what energy could do for AI and would now learn what AI could do for energy.

According to ADNOC, the first application will combine decades of information from thousands of oil wells, multiple reservoirs and hundreds of facilities. The aim is to finish complex development plans in hours rather than months. The company says the technology could improve operational efficiency, lower costs and help producers respond faster to changing market conditions. Those projected gains have not yet been independently demonstrated.

The system is meant to reach across oilfield development, reservoir management, refining, logistics and commercial trading. Dr. Angela Wilkinson, secretary general and CEO of the World Energy Council, told Fox News Digital that she was encouraged by the emphasis on people, saying AI should enable people to make better decisions rather than take decisions for humanity. Amos Hochstein, a managing partner at TWG Global and a former senior adviser to President Joe Biden, welcomed the potential benefits but warned that the expansion of AI must be weighed against its financial and societal costs. He said the United States must stay a leader in advanced AI while making sure Americans do not bear the cost of that expansion, and he urged the Trump administration to work more closely with industry and other sectors of society.

The UAE is already a partner in the planned Stargate UAE project, a large computing infrastructure initiative involving American technology companies, which forms part of Abu Dhabi's effort to become an international AI hub. Mohammed Baharoon, director general of the research center B'huth, described this as a shift from exporting barrels of oil to exporting digital computing capacity. He said AI could drive an economic transformation comparable to earlier industrial revolutions, creating new industries even as existing jobs are disrupted. He also warned that governments are struggling to keep pace, and argued that regulation must be built in during development rather than after it.

Articles.Title: Oil-rich UAE makes massive AI bet as Sam Altman unveils ambitious plan to transform energy industry

stories.Headline: CPI | Japan Steps Up Pressure on US Tech Giants Over Security and AI
stories.Summary:
Japan is seeking earlier access to information about software security vulnerabilities from major US technology and artificial intelligence companies, as its government responds to a rise in cyberattacks. The initiative, reported by MLex, is aimed at strengthening cybersecurity cooperation with foreign technology providers whose products are widely used across Japan's economy. Officials are reportedly preparing an emergency cybersecurity package that could be discussed at a ministerial meeting as soon as Friday, November 6, according to Reuters citing Nikkei. The proposed measures would focus on receiving advance notice of significant software weaknesses, giving public agencies and operators of essential services more time to protect their systems before technical details become public.

Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi directed officials in late October to develop stronger cybersecurity protections after attacks increased, according to Nikkei as reported by MLex. The urgency follows a series of October disruptions involving government and corporate websites across several countries. Reuters reported that the disclosure of serious security flaws affecting the PHP programming language led to millions of attempted intrusions, and some website administrators restricted access or took systems offline temporarily. Japan has also announced plans to set up a team that will use artificial intelligence to simulate cyberattacks and find weaknesses in computer systems, Reuters reported. The effort would add automated testing to the country's work on identifying security threats.

The government has also approached major US AI developers, including OpenAI and Anthropic, about obtaining broader access to their advanced AI models, according to Nikkei as cited by Reuters. Those talks followed cyberattacks suspected of involving AI-assisted techniques. Early disclosure of vulnerabilities would let Japanese authorities coordinate protections before attackers exploit newly found flaws, though the articles note this raises questions about how companies handle sensitive security information and decide which governments or organizations get access before public release. The cybersecurity push comes as Japan also examines the influence of major technology companies over digital markets, including their business practices and their use of data in artificial intelligence, according to MLex's separate reporting on that scrutiny.

Articles.Title: CPI | Japan Steps Up Pressure on US Tech Giants Over Security and AI

stories.Headline: From Ticketing To Vocals, The ‘Mind-Blowing’ Ways Concerts Are Using AI
stories.Summary:
Billboard reported on November 5, 2026 that artificial intelligence is being used across the live concert business, from ticket sales to sound mixing. The article, written by Ariel King, centers on Nine Inch Nails, whose front of house engineer, Jamie Pollock, used L-Acoustics' Source Intelligence on the band's Peel It Back Tour for the first time this year. That technology applies nongenerative machine learning to pick out an artist's voice in real time and send it to the crowd without the background noise a microphone might pick up onstage. Pollock kept the experiment quiet during the whole run, yet fans noticed the clearer vocals. The article also notes that the technology has since been used by Bruno Mars, Rüfüs Du Sol and Harry Styles on the road.

The article says the tools cover several areas of the industry. In marketing, companies such as Laylo and HIVE send text and email campaigns for artists and venues, and Laylo's user-generated-content agent finds fan videos and asks fans for permission to use them in ads. Ticketmaster has added AI chatbots, including ChatGPT and Claude, so fans can ask about tour plans and view seats before buying through its own site. SeatGeek launched a product in October called TourIQ, which uses data the company already collects to recommend a price for every seat in a venue. At the Hollywood Bowl, the team installed 26 L-Acoustics speakers, and the Los Angeles Philharmonic used the new system for the first time on June 20.

Several executives describe these tools in their own words. Saumil Mehta, global president of Ticketmaster, says the company applies AI and machine learning at every layer of its ticketing platform to identify bots and help fans get tickets. Patrick Hannigan, HIVE's co-founder and chief technology officer, says some of the company's clients now have AI draft all of their emails, text messages and Meta ad campaigns. L-Acoustics CEO Laurent Vaissié says the company's technology helps engineers get a cleaner signal from noisy stages and calls the results "pretty mind-blowing." Fred Vogler, the Hollywood Bowl's principal sound designer, says the new system gives audiences clarity and low distortion that they had not heard outdoors before.

The article also points to a downside. Scalpers are using more bots than ever, and singer RAYE wrote on Instagram in October that her London Royal Albert Hall show had received 1.8 million presale sign-ups, including "hundreds of thousands of fake registrations." The article notes that ticketing platforms expect situations like this to become more common and are preparing for them. Suno, an AI company, hired former Ticketmaster executive Michael Chua in October to lead its new Suno Live Experiences division. The article does not say what further changes are planned beyond these tools.

Articles.Title: From Ticketing To Vocals, The ‘Mind-Blowing’ Ways Concerts Are Using AI

stories.Headline: New AI tool speeds up food science research and development
stories.Summary:
A food scientist at Penn State University has been using artificial intelligence to make food engineering research easier to access and apply, according to a Brownfield Ag News report published November 5, 2026. The report, written by Nicole Heslip, centers on a tool called AgentXtract, which mines scientific research data. Xu Zhou, who works in the Department of Food Science, is the researcher behind the work. The tool is described as an AI system that can answer questions in plain language, so users do not need to read large numbers of papers or work through complex equations.

Zhou told Brownfield that people can simply ask questions in natural language and receive explanations grounded in scientific research. The system is compared to Penn State Extension's Tilva app, which gives science-based answers to agricultural questions. Zhou also said the tool can help keep institutional knowledge from being lost when experienced workers retire. He noted that much hands-on expertise sits with human experts, and that losing them would mean losing that expertise. The article does not describe any specific rules, mandates or funding requirements tied to the tool.

Zhou is the person quoted as responsible for the project, and he said the work could speed up early-stage research and development in the food industry. He added that it could also support gains in food safety, quality and waste reduction. The report does not say whether AgentXtract is commercially available, how widely it is in use, or what its accuracy has been tested against. It also does not describe any next steps or timeline for the research. The coverage is a short feature rather than a breaking news story.

Articles.Title: New AI tool speeds up food science research and development

stories.Headline: Democrats Train Sights on AI and Crypto
stories.Summary:
When Democrats take full control of Congress in January, they are preparing to turn their oversight attention toward the artificial intelligence and cryptocurrency industries, which spent heavily on the losing side of the midterm elections. The party will hold 54 Senate seats and could gain two more, and it is expected to begin with subpoenas and investigations. According to the article, crypto groups spent $180 million and AI-affiliated groups spent over $72 million in the 2026 cycle, mostly supporting Republicans. The reporting also notes that a purely partisan push would likely fail with a Republican president who strongly backs both industries, so early actions are expected to be bipartisan.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts is expected to lead the Senate Banking Committee, a role that would let her schedule hearings, direct investigations and set staff priorities. With a majority vote, the committee can issue subpoenas for documents and witnesses, something Warren could not do while in the minority. Her focus includes Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, whom she has criticized over alleged ties to a Chinese "intelligence asset," and several House Republican committee chairs have asked Huang to appear for a closed-door briefing on those allegations. Warren also introduced an April bill with Sen. Jim Banks, a Republican from Indiana, that would bar exports of the most advanced AI chips to countries of concern, and it has several Republican co-sponsors. Most Senate legislation needs 60 votes, which is why the bipartisan approach matters.

Warren has said Congress "can no longer be a bystander" as AI risks grow and American chips reach China, and she made that point at a June 11 hearing. Other Democrats have pushed broader ideas, including Sen. Maria Cantwell's proposed safety standards, temporary pauses on AI development backed by Warren, Sen. Michael Bennet and Sen. Peter Welch, and a ban proposed by Sen. Bernie Sanders. Shaunna Thomas of Guardrails Alliance, a super PAC that backs AI safety rules, said she sees a broad opportunity for oversight covering both human safety and economic harms. On crypto, Solana Policy Institute president Kristin Smith said the CLARITY Act is all but dead and that new legislation is unlikely before 2029 or 2030, while Sen. Ruben Gallego of Arizona pointed to bad blood after crypto groups spent $63 million against Sherrod Brown's Ohio Senate bid, which Brown won. Many Democrats also want to probe Trump's ties to the crypto industry, and industry groups say they are still deciding how to respond.

Articles.Title: Democrats Train Sights on AI and Crypto

stories.Headline: Setting a new standard for responsible AI infrastructure
stories.Summary:
On November 5, 2026, OpenAI published two documents setting out how it plans to build and run its future compute campuses in the United States: a National Community Compact and a Compute Campus Policy Blueprint. The announcement, posted on the company's website under the headline "Setting a new standard for responsible AI infrastructure," said the compact covers campuses that OpenAI itself owns and operates. It described the move as the next step in work the company began in January under its Stargate Community commitments, which had already included specific pledges in Georgia and Ohio. Under the compact, each future campus would have its own local agreement reflecting local priorities, with early resident engagement, a local point of contact and annual public reporting.

Common commitments include paying the full cost of the electricity and infrastructure the campus uses, and providing financial assurances before major spending so other customers are protected if a project is delayed or canceled. OpenAI also says it will develop a water plan for each site, favor closed-loop or low-water cooling, publish water and electricity use, and release construction plans and noise studies. The company says it will not use non-disclosure agreements with public officials, except for narrow protections covering legitimate security information, trade secrets or competitively sensitive data. Examples cited include a $4.8 million grant for free school meals for all 14,000 students in Effingham County, Georgia, and a joint $6 million childcare commitment with SB Energy in Pike County, Ohio.

The accompanying blueprint asks federal, state and local policymakers to set clear rules for the industry rather than relying only on voluntary pledges. It proposes that state utility commissions require large electricity customers to cover the grid costs they add and protect other customers if a project falls through, and that Congress speed up transmission upgrades and restore and expand tax incentives for clean electricity. The document also calls for public reporting on water, energy, noise and hiring, narrow limits on NDAs with officials, and public terms for tax incentives with a way to recover benefits if a developer falls short. OpenAI points to its planned Effingham County campus, where an agreement with Georgia Power would let the utility reduce power delivered by up to 1,000 megawatts during periods of high demand.

The company also suggests early sharing of purchasing plans with local suppliers and hiring forecasts that community colleges and unions can use to train residents. OpenAI is the party making these commitments, and the company frames the effort as a way to ensure that the benefits of AI infrastructure are broadly shared. The published text does not describe any regulator's response or any enacted policy, and it does not say when the blueprint's proposals might be taken up by lawmakers. The articles provided do not indicate what happens next beyond the company's stated plan to engage residents, publish annual reports and continue its ongoing work with communities.

Articles.Title: Setting a new standard for responsible AI infrastructure

stories.Headline: Visa Finds AI Models Fail 43% of Shopping Test Runs
stories.Summary:
Visa reported on Thursday, November 5, 2026, that 22 artificial intelligence models from 12 labs failed a large share of realistic shopping tests. Across the test runs, 57.2% passed and 42.8% failed, according to a press release from the company. The results came from Visa's new industry benchmark for AI shopping, called the Visa Agentic Commerce Benchmark. The article describes the findings as the first round of testing.

The benchmark checks whether an AI model can identify a consumer's needs from a conversation, gather enough information to justify a purchase, and decline to buy when nothing meets the customer's requirements. For the first round, Visa had the models attempt challenges that included buying a television, a laptop or a personal care appliance. Among the best-performing models, 82.2% of runs passed, while among the worst-performing models, 28.9% passed. The five models with the highest average cost per run passed 67.1% of runs, compared with 50.2% for the five least expensive models.

Visa stated that 54% of the failed runs still ended with the AI making a purchase. In those cases, the purchase either did not meet the customer's stated requirements or the AI had not uncovered all of those requirements. Rubail Birwadker, global head of growth at Visa, said in the release that AI agents could power the next era of commerce but that trust is key to making it work. He described the benchmark as another way Visa is working to raise standards across the industry.

The release also said the test can be used by consumers. The article places the findings alongside a PYMNTS Intelligence report that found nearly 132 million U.S. adults have bought a product with AI's help. That report indicates AI has gained a role in product discovery, while consumers still control the purchase decision. The article does not say what further rounds of testing or changes to the benchmark are planned.

Articles.Title: Visa Finds AI Models Fail 43% of Shopping Test Runs

stories.Headline: West Virginia sues Snap over children's safety, AI chatbot
stories.Summary:
West Virginia Attorney General JB McCuskey has filed a consumer protection lawsuit against Snap, the maker of Snapchat, according to a November 6, 2026 report from MLex. The suit alleges that Snap deceived West Virginia parents and children about how safe its platform was, even though the company knew it exposed young users to sexual exploitation, harmful content and compulsive-use design. It also claims Snap rushed the launch of its "My AI" chatbot to children without adequate safety testing. The complaint further says the company misled families about what the chatbot does with private conversations and location data.

The articles provided do not describe specific penalties, damages sought, or a court schedule, so those details are not available from this material. The reporting indicates the case rests on claims that Snap made misleading statements to families about its safety practices and its chatbot. A complaint document is referenced in the report, but its contents beyond the summary are not reproduced in the text provided. Snap's response to the allegations is not included in the articles.

The lawsuit is brought by the state attorney general, who is the official named as the party pursuing the claims against the company. The report frames the action as a consumer protection case centered on children's safety and the handling of their data. Beyond the filing itself, the articles do not say what further steps are planned or when any ruling might come. More to follow.

Articles.Title: West Virginia sues Snap over children's safety, AI chatbot

stories.Headline: Australia’s 2026 risk review identifies AI as a growing threat multiplier for critical infrastructure security
stories.Summary:
Australia's Critical Infrastructure Security Centre released its 2026 Critical Infrastructure Annual Risk Review during Critical Infrastructure Security Month. The fourth annual edition names trusted insiders, cyber incidents, physical threats, supply chain vulnerabilities and natural hazards as the main risks to essential services over the past twelve months. It covers energy, food, water, transport, communications, health, banking and finance. The review's central finding is that artificial intelligence has become a growing threat multiplier across every category of hazard.

The review is meant to help owners and operators understand their risk exposure, assess potential consequences and identify suitable mitigations. It describes AI as rapidly uncovering cyber vulnerabilities, so defences will need AI-enabled mitigation as well. It also flags mounting digital supply chain risk tied to reliance on AI software tools and to demand for the hardware behind AI, and it treats physical security for AI infrastructure as a frontline resilience issue. Governance guardrails for AI use in operations are now presented as a key personnel security requirement.

Minister for Home Affairs and Cyber Security Tony Burke wrote in the review that rapid advances in AI, automation and connectivity improve service delivery but can also create or extend vulnerabilities. He said the government is working with technical experts and international partners to strengthen protection of energy, water, healthcare, transport and communications. Burke added that the government and the Department of Home Affairs will keep providing practical guidance on risk management and regulatory responsibilities. The CISC said its work will continue to promote a proportionate, risk-based security culture.

The review places these threats within a wider global polycrisis, in which Australia's risk environment has shifted from complicated to complex. Geopolitical tensions and trade disputes are disrupting supply chains while technology reshapes the economy, and overlapping crises such as climate change and regional conflict can worsen one another. Over four years of the review, reporting has moved from traditional operational and cyber risks toward interconnected systemic risks. More broadly, the review notes that the Strait of Hormuz closure exposed diversification gaps across supply chains, and that the Enhanced CIRMP Rules require entities to understand third-party providers and address legacy system risk. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Australia’s 2026 risk review identifies AI as a growing threat multiplier for critical infrastructure security

stories.Headline: BuzzFeed Stock in Free Fall as Pivot to AI Blows Up in Its Face
stories.Summary:
BuzzFeed's stock fell sharply on November 5, 2026, dropping from a high of $2.09 earlier that year to $0.57 in a single morning, a 38 percent decline. The fall followed the company's third-quarter earnings report, which showed earnings per share of negative $0.22, 13 cents worse than analysts had expected. Back in March, the company had warned there was "substantial doubt" about its ability to continue operating, after reporting a net loss of $57.3 million for 2025. The stock had already drawn some enthusiasm in May, when a family affiliate of TV personality Byron Allen bought a majority stake in the company.

Allen's affiliate pushed the company toward free-streaming video, audio and user-generated content, and Jonah Peretti received the title of "president of BuzzFeed AI." Allen said the company was chasing YouTube and aimed to become a free video streaming service powered by AI. BuzzFeed has since laid off 33 percent of its remaining staff, roughly two months after Allen took over. The article notes that the company's AI push began in 2023 after the launch of ChatGPT, when it published quizzes and AI-generated travel guides that drew criticism.

The article places much of the blame on Peretti, who has long championed AI and launched several apps built on the technology. It describes his decision to double down on AI content as the source of the company's troubles. In a May interview with The Verge, Peretti said AI was the thing he was most passionate about and claimed it would create a new medium for content. The article says no evidence of that new medium has yet appeared, and it frames the broader picture as one of continued losses and a shrinking business.

Articles.Title: BuzzFeed Stock in Free Fall as Pivot to AI Blows Up in Its Face

stories.Headline: OpenAI Forms JPMorgan Partnership Ahead of 2027 IPO
stories.Summary:
OpenAI co-founder and president Greg Brockman said on Wednesday, November 4, 2026, that the company could be ready for an initial public offering in 2027. He made the remarks at the WSJ Tech conference, and the same day the company said it had formed a strategic partnership with JPMorganChase to supply the bank with artificial intelligence services. The details come from a Wall Street Journal report that PYMNTS cited. Brockman's comments were made as the company faces questions about its financing.

Under the partnership, OpenAI will give the bank access to cybersecurity-focused models through its Daybreak program. According to OpenAI's website, Daybreak gives approved individuals and organizations access to its advanced cybersecurity capabilities, along with security solutions, partners and support for protecting systems. After the event, Brockman posted on X that the two companies will explore how advanced AI can help the bank's engineers, security teams, employees and customers. He wrote that he was especially excited about working together on cybersecurity to protect the financial system. Brockman also said the company wants to go public when the timing is right for it.

Brockman's remarks followed a Wall Street Journal report that OpenAI had secured about $11 billion in commitments for its current funding round, less than half of its initial $30 billion target. The report said the company plans to raise more money from family offices and high-net-worth individuals over the coming weeks to reach $20 billion. OpenAI had described this round as an "opportunistic" bridge before a potential IPO, according to a report from October 22. In June, the company said it had submitted a confidential S-1 registration statement to the Securities and Exchange Commission. At that time it said it had not decided on timing and that it may be a while, because some plans are likely easier as a private company.

Articles.Title: OpenAI Forms JPMorgan Partnership Ahead of 2027 IPO

stories.Headline: Dr. Mackensie Alston Explores Artificial Intelligence as a Bias-Detection Tool
stories.Summary:
Economist Mackensie Alston, Ph.D., visited Swarthmore College last week to deliver the annual Frank C. Pierson lecture, titled "Constructing the Criminal: Race and the Perception of AI-Generated Suspects." Alston is an assistant professor in the Department of Finance at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign and a faculty affiliate for the Wilson Sheehan Lab for Economic Opportunities at the University of Notre Dame. The lecture was hosted by the college's economics department and honors Frank Pierson '34, a former department chair whose work on anti-discrimination in labor economics aligns with Alston's field. Her latest research uses AI-generated images, differing only by race, to examine bias among police candidates and to improve hiring practices.

Alston said her interest in economics began with Dan Ariely's 2008 book "Predictably Irrational," which challenges the idea that people always act rationally. She described wanting to document behavior that existing theory could not explain, and she designs experiments to test such phenomena. The articles note that economists use lab, online, and field experiments, as well as observational data, and Alston said she prefers defining economics as the study of decision-making. Conclusive research, she argued, lets policymakers test ideas before wide adoption and compare predictions with real-world outcomes. Her work applies this approach to the factors behind police decisions to use potentially lethal force.

Alston drew on Gary Becker's 1968 rational criminal model, which weighs the probability and severity of punishment against the payoff from crime. She and her partner, Dr. Emily Owens, were motivated by research showing Black people face mistreatment by police in many ways. The articles report that improved anti-bias training has shown positive effects, but its impact can fade and depends on ongoing supervisor support. Alston's approach instead targets bias in new officers before they are hired. She has so far conducted two studies using AI images created with Midjourney and Gemini Proshop, and her results have not yet been published because further studies are planned.

During the question period, Alston said she is weighing ways to address social desirability bias, including asking participants how others might describe the images. When asked whether the AI origin of the images affected responses, she said about 70 percent of participants thought the images resembled AI, with 30 percent disagreeing. In an interview with The Phoenix, she stressed interdisciplinary work, noting that economists, sociologists, and psychologists each contribute distinct insight. She suggested that such cooperation can help the academic community move toward solutions.

Articles.Title: Dr. Mackensie Alston Explores Artificial Intelligence as a Bias-Detection Tool

stories.Headline: Artificial intelligence exposes antiquities trafficking: Türkiye recovers 100 historical treasures from America
stories.Summary:
Turkey has recovered 100 looted historical artifacts from the United States, a milestone the Voice of Emirates reported on November 6, 2026. The operation was carried out by Turkish authorities, who used artificial intelligence and digital analysis to locate the pieces and check their historical origins. The article describes the recovery as the latest step in an ongoing effort to bring back objects that were illegally taken out of the country. Officials were said to have used image analysis and data comparison to match the artifacts' technical features and trace how they moved between owners.

The article says the artifacts had ended up in private collections or foreign institutions after being smuggled abroad. Returning them is presented as part of a wider effort to protect historical heritage and preserve cultural identity. The technology helped with both finding the objects and gathering evidence of where they came from, which the article says strengthens the case for their return. It also notes that the work depended on documenting each piece in enough detail to prove its origin.

The article credits Turkish authorities with leading the recovery but does not name specific officials or quote any statements from them. It does not identify the American holders of the artifacts, the institutions involved, or the individuals suspected of smuggling them. The piece frames the success as an example of how modern technology is becoming a valuable tool against the illicit trade in cultural property. It stresses that the recovery reflects the importance of international cooperation in protecting human heritage.

The article calls for continued legal and technical efforts to pursue those responsible for smuggling historical objects. It also says that returning such artifacts to their countries of origin is essential. The report does not describe any further steps, charges, or timelines for the remaining cases. Readers should look to later coverage for details on the legal process and the artifacts' eventual return.

Articles.Title: Artificial intelligence exposes antiquities trafficking: Türkiye recovers 100 historical treasures from America

stories.Headline: HK cheer as Trump thumping may spell woe for AI boom
stories.Summary:
Stock markets in Asia were shaken on Thursday, with tech shares falling sharply as investors weighed the future of the AI boom after Democrats won control of Congress in the US midterm elections. In Hong Kong, the Hang Seng Index nonetheless rose 877 points, or 3.7 percent, to close at 24,796, on turnover of HK$356.67 billion. The Hang Seng Tech Index climbed 218 points, or 5.5 percent, to 4,154, while the China Enterprises Index gained 311 points, or 3.9 percent, to 8,369. Tokyo and Seoul told a different story, since losses in AI and chip stocks dragged the Nikkei down 1,110 points, or 1.79 percent, to 61,077, and the Kospi fell 300 points, or 5.28 percent, to 5,383. The election result was a historic defeat for President Donald Trump's Republicans, and the articles say voters were angry about high prices, tariffs and the Iran war.

Some investors hoped the result would push Trump to wind down the Middle East conflict, which could ease inflation and soften his trade stance. However, AI-linked firms came under pressure over fears for planned data centre construction projects and renewed scrutiny from the newly installed Democrats on Capitol Hill. Investors had already been questioning the huge sums going into new facilities, research and chip development, and when those companies would turn a profit. Charu Chanana of Saxo Markets said the vote was speeding up a reassessment of AI that was already under way. She named three main risks: more oversight, restrictions on data centres, and uncertainty about capital spending.

She said congressional scrutiny could accelerate demands for AI safety standards, independent model evaluations and greater accountability for data centre developers. Chanana also cautioned that this does not amount to an outright anti-AI policy agenda, because AI remains strategically important for US competitiveness, particularly against China, and there is considerable bipartisan interest in keeping American leadership. The sell-off came after the Nikkei and Kospi had already been hit by overnight losses in US tech stocks. Overall, the articles describe a market torn between hopes of a calmer policy path and worries about tighter scrutiny of the AI sector.

Articles.Title: HK cheer as Trump thumping may spell woe for AI boom - RTHK News

stories.Headline: UM establishes Montana’s first artificial intelligence career certificate
stories.Summary:
The University of Montana has established the Human-Centered AI Career Certificate, the first of its kind in the state, and it is being offered this year. Lee Banville, director of the School of Journalism, and Michael Cassens, an associate professor of game design and interactive media, created the nine-credit certificate together and teach its three courses, all of which are taught online. Banville said the goal is to help students understand that artificial intelligence will affect people's lives and careers, not to promote or discourage its use. He stressed that the program is not a sales pitch for the technology.

Cassens said the certificate would strengthen students' resumes and give them foundational knowledge for a changing technological landscape. He said students would be required to use AI tools for assignments, including ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, Gemini, Meta and UM's own model, Chat MT, to see how each works. A typical exercise would be entering the same prompt into several models to compare their responses. Cassens said he accepts AI use as long as students can reasonably defend their choice and explain it openly.

The first course, Creatively Exploring AI, is already taught by Cassens and covers AI's history, hallucinations, biases, terminology, ethics and effects on various disciplines. The second course, Calling Bullshit in the Age of AI, is a journalism class taught by Banville that focuses on critical thinking and recognizing when AI is wrong, and it will be renamed next semester. The third, Human-Centered Leadership in AI, is a new class that Cassens will offer in the spring, adapted from a leadership course he previously taught. Cassens said the curriculum is meant to be adaptable as the technology changes and that the program is grounded in human concerns.

Student reactions are mixed: Grace Smith, a 23-year-old graduate student in game design, said the courses promote discussion rather than either side of the debate, while Kylie Heit, a 23-year-old senior cello performance major from Helena, said the program normalizes AI and that its "Human-Centered" title is misleading. Banville acknowledged that many people fear AI and that real questions about it deserve attention, but he noted that a free one-day, one-credit AI course the School of Journalism offered last spring drew only about 15 students, far fewer than he expected. He hopes the certificate will attract more interest and that students will engage with the topic regardless of local debates over data centers. He told students that the tools are already here and will change their lives, and that his aim is for them to be prepared to decide how, when and whether to use them.

Articles.Title: UM establishes Montana’s first artificial intelligence career certificate

stories.Headline: Doctors take minutes to measure heart function. AI takes seconds
stories.Summary:
An AI tool that measures how well the heart pumps from MRI scans predicted patient death slightly better than expert clinicians, according to a retrospective study published in The Lancet Digital Health on November 6, 2026. The researchers analyzed cardiac MRI scans from 27,382 patients at two centers, one in the UK and one in the USA, and 13% of them died during a median follow-up of 5.6 years. The AI processed each scan in about three to four seconds, compared with a median of 13 minutes per patient for clinician segmentation in an earlier study. Before adjusting for age and sex, the AI model reached a C-index of 0.669, against 0.637 for clinician measurements.

After adjustment, the gap narrowed to 0.781 for the AI and 0.777 for clinicians, a difference the authors describe as statistically significant but small. The AI made segmentation errors in six of 600 randomly selected patients, about a 1% error rate, and these errors were more common in scans with extreme ejection fraction values, especially very low ones. The AI also produced a lower median ejection fraction, 57.8% compared with 62.1% from clinicians, and the study did not establish which figures were more anatomically accurate. Subgroup results varied: the AI did better in patients with obstructive coronary artery disease, while clinicians performed slightly better in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. The authors concluded that the tool could serve as a first-line measure with clinician oversight, but said prospective studies are needed to establish clinical utility and cost-effectiveness.

The authors acknowledged several limits. The analysis was retrospective, lacked cause-specific mortality data, and did not assess risk calibration or whether AI-guided measurements improve decisions or outcomes. Most participants came from one UK center, and performance across ethnic groups was not evaluated. Several authors disclosed financial relationships with MycardiumAI, the company associated with the segmentation technology used in the study. The article reports that the findings are consistent with earlier research on AI-derived ejection fraction from echocardiography in patients hospitalized with acute COVID-19.

Articles.Title: Doctors take minutes to measure heart function. AI takes seconds

stories.Headline: Top 100 AI Venture Capitalists 2026: K2 Global and Ozi Amanat
stories.Summary:
