Those concerns frame his case that the state should set rules now. Schweyer described a package of bills in the Pennsylvania House that would regulate AI in schools. Rep. Brandon Dukes, D-Butler, has a bill requiring every school district to adopt an AI policy that protects the privacy of teachers and students and prevents cheating. Rep. Melissa Shusterman, D-Chester, has legislation barring schools from using AI chatbots for mental and behavioral health services, and Rep. Chris Pielli, D-Chester, wants a grant program to fund teacher training on using AI in classrooms.

Schweyer said his own bill would make it easier for districts and public charter schools to buy only the safest and most ethical AI education programs. Schweyer concluded that AI could prove either transformative or highly destructive, and that the truth probably lies somewhere in between. In his view, Pennsylvania must ensure that all students have access to age- and curriculum-appropriate AI instruction led by well-trained human teachers, while protecting students from bad actors who would misuse their privacy or information. The column is a contributed opinion piece, and the article notes that its views belong to Schweyer and do not reflect those of The Morning Call.

Articles.Title: Opinion: Pennsylvania needs a clear AI education policy - The Morning Call

stories.Headline: Teddy Schleifer: Democrats' Sweep Turns AI's Data Center Boom Into a Local Land War
stories.Summary:
Voters in at least 38 US jurisdictions passed bans or restrictions on data centers on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, and the result has begun to reshape how the AI industry views its political future. Democrats won both chambers of Congress in the midterms, and Texas elected Democrat Gina Hinojosa as governor after she campaigned on a construction moratorium. Local voters across the country also rejected nearly every measure that would have supported new data center construction. Reporting from the Big Technology Podcast and other outlets points to rising costs, water use, noise, and land use as the main concerns behind these votes.

The results do not mean sweeping federal AI law is imminent. Any bill would need both chambers of Congress and the signature of President Trump, a Republican, which makes major federal legislation unlikely. The immediate effects are more practical: committee chairs and subpoena power shift to Democrats, and local land-use votes can block individual projects. Senators elected this cycle serve six-year terms, so their oversight role will extend through 2032. Teddy Schleifer of The New York Times described the period ahead as a major change from the largely unrestricted environment the industry has enjoyed.

Teddy Schleifer, speaking on the Big Technology Podcast with host Alex Kantrowitz, argued that the local votes amounted to something close to a national referendum on data centers. He noted that the margins were lopsided, with 38 jurisdictions passing restrictions and few or none rejecting them. Kantrowitz said that AI growth depends on public support for building the facilities that supply computing power, and that the industry faces a real compute shortage. The data center industry formed its first super PAC this cycle, which spent heavily in South Carolina to back a candidate who lost. Schleifer expects political spending on data centers to rise sharply before the 2028 presidential race.

Financial markets reacted in a way that surprised many observers. Shares of the largest technology companies rose after the election, on the view that a Democratic Congress might restrain the heavy capital spending on AI that has weighed on free cash flow. Schleifer said he did not have a clear explanation for this reaction. Elon Musk, who spent roughly $500 million on the midterms, saw most of his preferred candidates lose, and California's proposed billionaire tax appeared headed for defeat after opponents raised more than $330 million. Schleifer said Congress may now probe matters such as Musk's work on federal agencies through DOGE, and he expects oversight hearings to become a central feature of the next two years.

Articles.Title: Teddy Schleifer: Democrats' Sweep Turns AI's Data Center Boom Into a Local Land War - BigGo Finance

stories.Headline: Flipsnack grows product signups with conversion optimization
stories.Summary:
Flipsnack, a company that helps teams turn static documents into interactive digital experiences, reported on OpenAI's site that it grew product signups by shifting its ChatGPT Ads campaigns to a conversion focus. The company had previously run click-focused campaigns with fixed bids, and in November 2026 it described the change and the results it saw. Its tests ran across five US campaign pairs, comparing late August with early September 2026. The company said it had relied heavily on search advertising before trying ChatGPT Ads.

The change required Flipsnack to rebuild existing campaigns with a conversions objective and bidding set to maximize conversions. It created conversion-focused versions of five US campaigns that had used a clicks objective with fixed bids. Its landing pages sent people into a signup flow, so completed registration became the main measure the team optimized for. The company also split its broad Flipbook campaign into narrower campaigns for Magazine, Catalog, and Brochure, plus campaigns for Sales Enablement, Employee Benefits, Real Estate, and Hospitality.

Flipsnack said the results were encouraging. Across the five campaigns, registrations rose about 310 percent while cost per registration fell about 75 percent, with daily budget limits unchanged and spend up roughly 1.3 percent. The article attributes the figures to Flipsnack's ChatGPT Ads Manager data, measured with 30-day clicks and excluding views, and notes that objectives and bidding changed together. The company's marketing team said the lower cost per signup gave it confidence to make conversion optimization the focus of its campaigns. The article presents these numbers as company-reported results rather than independently verified outcomes.

The article describes the results as a foundation for continued growth with ChatGPT Ads rather than a finished outcome. Flipsnack's team said it aims to bring more prospective customers into the product and help them see how it can support their business. The article does not say how long the campaigns will run or whether the same gains will hold at larger budgets. It also does not report any figures beyond the five campaign pairs.

Articles.Title: Flipsnack grows product signups with conversion optimization

stories.Headline: Super Micro Pops Above 7% in After-Hours: Executive Says a Single AI Order Now Big Enough to ‘Exceed’ an Entire Quarter From a Year Ago
stories.Summary:
Super Micro Computer shares rose about 7.2% in after-hours trading on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, after the server maker beat first-quarter estimates and raised its full-year outlook. The stock had closed 3.12% higher at $31.39 before climbing to $33.65 in extended trading. CFO Mark Long made the central point on the company's earnings call, saying a single AI deployment can now exceed the company's total quarterly revenue from a year earlier. The stock's rise followed the release of results that investors had been watching closely. The company posted earnings of $1.81 per share against a Street estimate of $1.20, with revenue of $19.95 billion compared with a consensus of $16.16 billion.

That revenue was up 297.49% from $5.02 billion a year earlier. For the second quarter, Super Micro expects adjusted earnings of $1.66 to $1.90 per share and revenue of $19.5 billion to $21.5 billion. It also raised its fiscal 2027 revenue outlook to between $72 billion and $82 billion, above a $69.17 billion estimate. Long said one large data center customer accounted for 44% of revenue in the quarter, up from 28% for all of fiscal 2026, which he described as a consequence of the scale of today's AI buildouts. He also said deferred revenue rose about $3.1 billion in the quarter, mostly from advance payments by customers.

On the limits to the outlook, Long said they reflect neither demand nor the company's ability to build systems, but how quickly customer facilities are ready and the availability of key components. He named land, power and data center shells as the binding constraints on AI buildouts across the industry. Investors have been wary of how much AI spending is being done, and JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon said in September that AI-related spending across the hyperscaler ecosystem could reach $1 trillion in 2027, up from about $300 billion last year and $700 billion this year. The articles do not say what happens to the stock or the company's outlook after the extended-trading session. The reports also show a sharp market selloff on the same day, with the Nasdaq Composite and S&P 500 both falling.

Articles.Title: Super Micro Pops Above 7% in After-Hours: Executive Says a Single AI Order Now Big Enough to ‘Exceed’ an Entire Quarter From a Year Ago - Yahoo Finance

stories.Headline: GPT‑6 Cyber: Advancing the frontier of aligned cybersecurity agents
stories.Summary:
OpenAI announced GPT-6 Cyber on November 5, 2026, a cybersecurity model designed to find and validate exploitable vulnerabilities while staying within the scope that researchers set. The company says the model delivers major gains over its predecessor, GPT-5.6 Cyber, scoring 48.5% on the ExploitGym benchmark against 32.1% for the earlier model, a relative improvement of about 51%. On an alignment test measuring whether the model avoids attacking out-of-scope services, GPT-6 Cyber stayed within bounds in 99.93% of cases without its deployment prompt and 100% with it, up from 94.49% for GPT-5.6 Cyber without the prompt. The model is already in use on real software, and OpenAI's researchers used it to develop 948 privilege escalation exploits in Linux and identify 81 previously unknown high-severity vulnerabilities in Firefox, for which Mozilla has released fixes for many issues.

OpenAI says the model is classified as Critical in cybersecurity under its Preparedness Framework, up from High for GPT-5.6 Cyber. The company also describes a tiered access program called Daybreak, which includes Daybreak Blue for verified defenders who need validation of vulnerabilities and fixes with fewer refusals, and Daybreak Red for deeper exploit development and authorized security testing with GPT-6 Cyber. On a new benchmark called RemoteExploitBench, the company reports that GPT-6 Astra running with Daybreak Blue refused all tasks, while GPT-6 Cyber completed 95%. The company also says it plans to expand Daybreak to organizations of every size, independent researchers, and open-source maintainers, and that it sees a limited window to use frontier models to secure software.

OpenAI is responsible for the announcement and is the source of all the performance figures, which come from its own evaluations and system card. Several security firms, including Cisco, CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Networks, SentinelOne, and CodeRabbit, along with Mozilla and the developer Calif, provided testimonials praising the model's usefulness for vulnerability research and code review. The announcement also notes that OpenAI used the model to harden its own infrastructure, where agents chaining vulnerabilities in controlled red-team campaigns were found to escape microVMs, prompting patches and network restrictions. The articles provided do not describe independent verification of these results or any regulatory response.

Articles.Title: GPT‑6 Cyber: Advancing the frontier of aligned cybersecurity agents

stories.Headline: AI can help — or engulf — the legal process
stories.Summary:
Cedar Rapids lawyer Tim Semelroth has been warning colleagues and the public that artificial intelligence is creating real problems in the legal system, and he has been doing so through more than 30 presentations around the country since he first wrote about lawyers' practical uses of AI three years ago. He describes AI as "Average Intelligence" because of widely reported "hallucinations," fabricated material that has appeared in legal briefs and other papers. Some 2,000 such filings have been reported, and judges have sanctioned lawyers who submitted them. Because AI draws on internet material that includes misinformation and poor legal opinions, it cannot reliably tell that content apart from legitimate cases.

The costs fall on the courts and on the people who must respond. Lawyers must review AI-generated filings, judges must rule on them, and both spend time and money doing so. Semelroth warns that if judges face very long, AI-written briefs, the system could slow badly. He says lawyers have an ethical duty to understand the technology and check its output, since clients, witnesses and staff are already using it, sometimes to prepare for legal matters.

He advises that nothing AI produces should leave an office without a human reviewing it, and he distinguishes free AI tools from the subscription versions lawyers use, which carry safety protocols that are still not fail-safe. For the public, he says AI is a poor source of legal advice because chats carry no privacy guarantee, citing a New York case in which a judge allowed prosecutors to see a defendant's chat history. The Iowa Supreme Court has also acted. Its first AI-related ruling upheld the 2023 conviction of Max Amyda, 37, of Woodbury County, for third-degree sexual abuse, after he argued that video evidence was a "deepfake."

The court found his claim rested on conjecture and that the video's distinctive characteristics, including the victim's identification of her body, items in her room and Amyda's hand, supported its admission. In July, Chief Justice Susan Christensen signed an order adopting a new chapter of the Iowa Court Rules on judicial use of AI tools. Those rules take effect Jan. 1 and create a Judicial Branch Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Governance Committee, on which Semelroth served as part of the earlier working group and University of Iowa professor Megan Graham now sits, to approve tools and set their permitted uses. Semelroth also says AI can be a useful thinking partner when used with proper human oversight.

Articles.Title: AI can help — or engulf — the legal process - The Gazette

stories.Headline: Cult.fit builds operational muscle with Codex
stories.Summary:
Cult.fit, an Indian fitness company, has standardized its software engineering on OpenAI's Codex and extended it across the organization, according to a customer story published by OpenAI on November 5, 2026. The company operates 708 fitness centers in 77 cities and serves nearly one million paid members. Its business mixes subscription gym and trainer-led class access with a growing line of consumer fitness products. The article describes this as a way to solve operational and product problems without adding layers of process.

Engineering was the first area to change. Before standardizing, developers used a mix of coding agents and assistants that followed different conventions for repositories, agent instructions, skills, and workflows, which made sharing knowledge harder. Cult.fit chose Codex as a shared platform so repository structures, testing, code review, and feedback loops could follow common rules across teams. The company then built specialized agents on top of it, including a Site Reliability Engineering agent that investigates incidents and often proposes a fix as a pull request, along with security and on-call agents. A recent social feed project, which the CTO estimates would previously have taken more than a year, was built and shipped in two months using this workflow.

The change has since reached non-engineering staff. Cult.fit made its company data easier for Codex to use, so teams can run routine analysis themselves instead of routing every request through a central analyst team. HR, for example, built a Codex workflow for performance reviews, scheduling, and feedback collection, and more than 20 internal applications have been built by non-engineering teams in recent months. When the cost of its internal dashboard software rose sharply, one engineer rebuilt that capability with Codex over a weekend, which the company says avoids more than $100,000 in annual software costs. Support for this shift included an employee hackathon, a one-day session in which management built relevant tools, and twice-weekly engineering office hours.

Santhosh Kumar, the company's CTO, said the company wanted to become more AI-native in how it runs operations and what customer experiences it offers. He said Codex has been the company's biggest step toward data democratization and that software has been democratized so employees can build what their teams need. Cult.fit is also using the OpenAI API for its AI Trainer, which about 20 percent of its gym users currently use and which over 45 percent of members, who are first-time gym goers, rely on for guidance. The newest version is voice-first and uses GPT Realtime to give coaching cues and support workout logging. The company also uses AI agents in customer support to decide whether to waive penalties for missed classes, and the article says it plans to move toward an "autopilot operations org" and a "trainer in your pocket."

Articles.Title: Cult.fit builds operational muscle with Codex

stories.Headline: Australian universities are creating AI-native graduates
stories.Summary:
Australian universities are partnering with OpenAI to give students and staff access to advanced AI tools, and the work is already taking shape on campuses. According to the article, UNSW Sydney, the University of Sydney, La Trobe University and Adelaide University are all forging these collaborations, which the piece dates to 5 November 2026. The institutions are using AI in clinical simulations, robot-assisted teacher training and student projects meant to lead into industry. Students, educators and IT teams are involved in this work. UNSW is bringing ChatGPT Edu to more than 80,000 students and staff, with access expanding in stages.

The university plans to build generative AI foundations and Codex into courses, with hackathons, industry projects, internships and startup connections. The University of Sydney will give students and staff supported access to ChatGPT Edu, with training, and access for all students is scheduled for Semester 1, 2027 after a trial. It is also setting up a $1 million AI Sustainability Research and Innovation Fund. La Trobe has given all 3,500 staff access to ChatGPT Edu, with universal access planned for its 45,000 students and staff in the first quarter of 2027, and it will launch Australia's first Bachelor of AI Engineering (Honours) in 2027. Adelaide University is using OpenAI's API and has adopted OpenAI Daybreak Blue for authorised defensive security work.

The universities themselves lead these programs, and their leaders have described their goals. Phil Laufenberg, La Trobe's Pro Vice-Chancellor AI and Chief AI Officer, said students in every discipline should be able to help shape how AI is used in their profession. Abhishek Singh, Adelaide University's Chief Technology and Security Officer, said the tools would strengthen the university's cyber security posture. The article also quotes UNSW Master of IT student Nalin Iyer, who said it matters to understand what industry wants and how AI fits into that. The article notes that the survey was commissioned by OpenAI, so its findings reflect the company's research.

The surrounding research shows that students already use AI heavily. In a Pureprofile survey of 1,018 Australian university students, conducted for OpenAI from 3 to 7 August 2026, 81% said they use AI several times a week and 28% had built an AI agent or assistant. Four in five students want more chances to use advanced AI on real projects. Universities are also setting rules for use, with UNSW's Can, Can't, Must framework for assessment and La Trobe's free Responsible and Safe AI modules. The article does not say what the outcomes of these programs will be, and it describes them only as the start of a longer rollout.

Articles.Title: Australian universities are creating AI-native graduates

stories.Headline: Educators face pushback over classroom AI use as grades drop
stories.Summary:
Educators in Central Florida are facing growing pushback over the use of artificial intelligence in classrooms as grades drop. The pushback comes as tech companies adjust their tools for educational settings. Google is allowing schools to disable its AI features while keeping standard search working. The option was introduced amid concerns about how artificial intelligence affects student performance. A study by researchers at the University of California, Irvine, found that students who used AI for writing and research scored 20% lower in science than students who did not.

School districts across the region are setting different rules for AI in instruction. Orange County Public Schools requires students to get a teacher's approval before using AI on any assignment. Seminole County has taken the opposite approach by authorizing specific AI platforms for student use. Its approved tools include Google's Gemini and Microsoft Copilot Chat. The varying rules show how local districts are still working out where AI fits in the classroom.

The article does not say whether either district plans to change its policy. The article is based on reporting by James Tutten of WFTV.com, published November 6, 2026. It does not identify a single official or company that is directly responsible for the classroom changes, and it does not give direct statements from district leaders about their reasons. The story describes the policy choices but leaves open how schools will weigh the test results against the tools' benefits. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Educators face pushback over classroom AI use as grades drop - WFTV

stories.Headline: IBM, AMD, ORNL Debut Quantum-AI Error Correction Platform - News and Statistics
stories.Summary:
IBM, AMD and the Quantum Science Center at Oak Ridge National Laboratory unveiled a joint quantum and AI platform on November 5, 2026, aimed at advancing quantum error correction. The Oak Ridge, Tennessee, project links IBM quantum machines, including the 120-qubit IBM Quantum Nighthawk processor, with ORNL's Umbra high-performance computing system. Umbra uses AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs and 5th Gen AMD EPYC CPUs. The partners say the platform will let researchers judge how classical and quantum computing can work together on error correction. It supports the Department of Energy Quantum Genesis Mission, which targets 100 logical qubits running 100,000 hard operations by late 2028.

IBM reported experiments with up to 70 logical qubits and 438 hard operations, which means the target would require roughly a 230-fold increase in hard-operation count. Jay Gambetta, director of IBM Research, said the central question is how to speed and optimize error correction so systems can tackle meaningful problems. He said the co-design platform lets the partners test approaches and identify which architectures, software and workflows will scale. Seetharami Seelam, IBM's chief architect for classical system co-design, told EE Times that non-Clifford operations are especially costly in fault-tolerant computing. He added that which operations are hard depends on the error-correcting code chosen for a given platform.

AMD executive vice president Mark Papermaster described the platform as a step toward combining quantum processors, high-performance computing and AI into scalable, efficient infrastructure. Travis Humble, director of the Quantum Science Center at ORNL, said solving error-correction problems is essential to making quantum computing a practical scientific tool. Seelam said IBM has led in quantum-centric supercomputing for several years and that the Oak Ridge work is an important next step in applying that approach in the United States. Researchers will compare the qubits, time, samples and classical resources each technique needs to see where GPU accelerators can help most.

The platform builds on earlier work between IBM, ORNL and AMD, including simulations of magnetic materials and fusion fuel candidates on ORNL's Frontier supercomputer. IBM said the work may support its path to Quantum Starling, its first fault-tolerant quantum computer. Quantinuum, which expects its Nexus system to automate error correction and related tasks through 2029, reported that Nexus supports more than 200 organizations and that job submissions rose tenfold in the 12 months through August 2026. IBM and Quantinuum are among nine U.S. companies that received $2 billion from the administration of President Donald Trump to secure the nation's quantum leadership. Jose Ignacio Latorre, director of Singapore's Centre for Quantum Technologies, said quantum computers are nearing fault tolerance at scale, and the remaining challenge is adapting high-level algorithms to run on error-corrected hardware.

Articles.Title: IBM, AMD, ORNL Debut Quantum-AI Error Correction Platform - News and Statistics - IndexBox

stories.Headline: AI accelerates cyber threats, increases defensive spending
stories.Summary:
AI is accelerating and making cyber threats more sophisticated, according to executives, and this is straining IT departments around the world. In response, companies are increasing their investment in AI-powered security tools to help manage the growing workload. Nearly 37,000 security flaws were reported in the third quarter of 2026, according to the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures list, a figure that tripled from a year earlier. The reporting ties the surge to the growing pressure on defenders as well as the attackers.

Booking.com's chief security officer, Marnie Wilking, said hundreds of engineers at the company are now building AI-powered defence systems. Markus Noga, chief technology officer of the German web hosting company Ionos, told Reuters that the company is seeing events of a magnitude every week that used to come months apart. After a spike in vulnerabilities in July, Ionos changed its security practices by deploying AI-based monitoring systems and AI-assisted tools for round-the-clock patching. Binance, which suffered a $6.3 billion cryptocurrency theft, plans to increase its investment in AI-enhanced detection systems.

Other organizations are following a similar path. The Port of Rotterdam is developing an AI-powered "cyber shield," and Siemens is testing advanced AI models for defensive security. Researchers at Claroty used widely available AI tools to reproduce refrigeration controller flaws for $6 in 28 minutes after attacks began. Two AI-discovered flaws in the PHP programming language, disclosed in October, led governments and companies worldwide to take websites offline as a precaution. Cloudflare reported that attempts to exploit the PHP flaws rose from thousands to millions within hours of their disclosure.

Business leaders are also weighing in on the shift. Kraft Heinz chief executive Steve Cahillane said cybersecurity is becoming increasingly important to the company. Holcim chief financial officer Steffen Kindler said that both sides in the cyber battle are heavily equipped with AI. Their comments suggest that the arms race between attackers and defenders is now being fought largely with the same kind of technology.

Articles.Title: AI accelerates cyber threats, increases defensive spending

stories.Headline: Asian shares sink out of fear of a sudden slowdown in investment in artificial intelligence - Demócrata
stories.Summary:
Asian stock markets fell sharply on Friday, led by South Korea, Taiwan and Japan, after technology shares slumped on Wall Street and investors grew uneasy about future spending on artificial intelligence. The Seoul Kospi index dropped 8.52% in the first moments of trading, its lowest level since February, which triggered a 20-minute trading suspension under South Korea's automatic halt mechanism. Taiwan's Taiex fell 8.85% at the opening, and Japan's Nikkei 225 lost more than 6% and briefly fell below 60,000 points. The selloff followed a 5.52% drop in the Nasdaq on Thursday, its worst session since April 2025.

Investors reacted to the possibility that Democratic victories in the U.S. midterm elections could bring tighter limits on building data centers and expanding the infrastructure needed for AI. Semiconductor makers were hit hardest, with Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix falling more than 10% and 13% respectively before recovering part of their losses. South Korea's finance minister, Lee Hyoung-il, called an emergency meeting of top economic officials, and the authorities agreed to temporarily loosen rules on leveraged investing by small investors to contain forced sales. In Wall Street, the Nasdaq closed at 24,315 points, the S&P 500 fell 4.4% to 7,353.73 points, and the Dow Jones dropped 3.44%. Nvidia slid 9.3% and AMD plunged 17.3%.

Taiwanese companies central to the AI supply chain, including TSMC, Foxconn, MediaTek and Delta Electronics, were among the most affected, given the island's role in advanced chip manufacturing and data center equipment. In Japan, chip equipment makers, data center-linked firms and SoftBank, a major international AI investor, led the losses. Indian markets bucked the trend, with the Nifty 50 and Sensex rising during the session, which Reuters links to foreign capital inflows, a recent fall in oil prices and limited exposure to AI-related investment. Analysts consulted by Reuters warned that the Asian reaction may overstate the consequences, since slower projects do not necessarily mean canceled data center investment or disappearing demand for AI components.

Articles.Title: Asian shares sink out of fear of a sudden slowdown in investment in artificial intelligence - Demócrata

stories.Headline: Ahrefs adds prompt theme analysis to Brand Radar, comparing your own and competitors' visibility in AI search
stories.Summary:
Ahrefs Pte. Ltd. announced on November 6, 2026, that it has added a prompt category analysis feature to Brand Radar, its tool for tracking how brands are mentioned and cited in AI search. The feature sorts the questions users put to AI tools such as ChatGPT and Google's AI Overviews into topic categories. The company says the change lets users compare their own brand's visibility with that of competitors in each subject area, rather than only looking at overall mentions.

Each prompt can carry up to three topic categories, and the first one is treated as the main category. The categorization uses the same taxonomy as Ahrefs' Keyword Explorer, so users can start theme-level analysis without classifying prompts by hand. In the "By category" view of the Prompts report, users can see the share of prompts falling into each category next to brand mention rates, expand categories into subcategories, and search by category name. By default, counts use only the main category, but turning off the "Main category only" setting includes all assigned categories.

The release describes the feature as a way for marketers to see where their brand is strong and where competitors lead, and to decide which content or information areas to prioritize. The category column and filters are also available in the Topics, Cited pages, and Cited domains reports, which show which pages and domains AI tools cite for a given theme. Ahrefs describes itself as an all-in-one marketing toolkit built on its own large-scale web crawler, and says it serves users in more than 180 countries. The release does not say whether the feature is available to all plans or give any pricing or rollout timeline, so the details of next steps remain unclear.

Articles.Title: Ahrefs adds prompt theme analysis to Brand Radar, comparing your own and competitors' visibility in AI search

stories.Headline: Oscillatory Phase Coding Emerges in Adaptive RNNS for Flexible Working Memory
stories.Summary:
Kehan Lu, Tianhao Chu, AIERSI TUERHONG, Yiwen Sun, Huan Luo, Fang Fang and SI WU posted a preprint on bioRxiv on 5 November 2026. They trained recurrent neural networks with adaptation to perform sequence working memory tasks with variable delays. After training, oscillatory phase coding emerged in the networks on its own. In this pattern, memorized items recur at distinct phases of a shared rhythm.

The amplitude of the oscillation encodes item identity, and its phase encodes serial order. Ablation studies found three elements required for the coding: adaptation in neural dynamics, variable delay in memory retention, and flexibility in reading out information. Neuron-type analysis showed content cells and time cells emerging in the trained network, handling item identity and sequence order separately. Connectivity analysis showed phase-organized connections among time cells and structured connections within digit-selective content-cell groups.

The authors say the coding arises from network structures and task demands. They propose a neural circuit model that reproduces it through interactions between content units and an adaptive time ring. They state that the work offers insights into how the coding is implemented and computed in biological systems. They also say it can inspire computational models for human-like cognitive functions.

The authors declared no competing interests. The preprint is published under a CC-BY-NC-ND 4.0 International license. The copyright holder has granted bioRxiv a license to display it in perpetuity. The articles do not say what happens next.

Articles.Title: Oscillatory Phase Coding Emerges in Adaptive RNNS for Flexible Working Memory

stories.Headline: Employees at Microsoft, long known for its stability, are grappling with its decision to offer buyouts to 60,000 people as its spending priorities shift to AI (Emmy Martin/New York Times)
stories.Summary:
Microsoft has offered buyouts to about 60,000 employees, more than a quarter of its work force, in the largest such offer in the company's history. The announcement came last week, and employees rushed to an internal site within an hour to see whether they had been included, so many that colleagues joked the site had buckled under the traffic. It was the company's second buyout this year. The offer landed on a staff already on edge about artificial intelligence.

The buyouts follow a clear shift in where the company is putting its money. Two days after the announcement, Microsoft reported a 32 percent jump in quarterly profit, to $36.6 billion, on revenue of $92.3 billion. Its capital spending, largely on data centers, rose 30 percent to $45.2 billion, and the company said it expected to spend roughly $170 billion this year. Microsoft is doing better financially than most of its peers, yet it is plainly directing its resources toward AI.

Employees describe a workplace that has changed sharply. For years, Microsoft was known for strong benefits and stability, even though its pay often trailed rivals such as Google and Meta. As recently as September, Forbes ranked it the world's best employer for the third straight year. Six Microsoft employees who spoke anonymously said the buyout offer hit workers already strained by pressure to use AI, stagnant pay, and a growing sense that their jobs were no longer secure.

Some workers have started to organize in response. Before the buyout offer, current and former employees circulated an open letter accusing the company of pursuing AI with a speed-at-all-costs approach. The letter asked Microsoft to involve employees in decisions about how AI is built and used, and to stop tying AI use to rewards or reprimands. The article does not say how the company has responded to the letter, and it leaves open what the coming months will bring for those who remain.

Articles.Title: Employees at Microsoft, long known for its stability, are grappling with its decision to offer buyouts to 60,000 people as its spending priorities shift to AI (Emmy Martin/New York Times)

stories.Headline: CodeCap-Bench: Can Code Serve as a Good Video Caption?
stories.Summary:
A group of researchers led by Jiafu Tang has released a paper exploring whether computer code can work as a video caption. The work, posted on arXiv on November 5, 2026, has 13 authors in total, including Yifan Xu, Eric Tang and Junjie Zhao. The team compared code captions with ordinary natural language descriptions on two tasks, answering questions about videos and rebuilding videos from their captions. They found that code captions gave better reasoning accuracy and higher reconstruction fidelity.

The paper argues that natural language often struggles to express fine-grained spatial structures and temporal dynamics precisely, which can make descriptions long and ambiguous. Code captions instead use graphical primitives, layout rules and functions of time as an executable program that represents the visual content. To test how well current models can produce such captions, the authors built CodeCap-Bench, which contains 323 videos across five categories of structured 2D content. The benchmark also includes fine-grained annotations and a multi-level evaluation framework.

The authors report that leading proprietary multimodal large language models show promising code captioning abilities but still struggle to capture complex temporal dynamics faithfully. Open-source models, they say, lag substantially behind. The paper states that realizing the potential of code captioning depends on whether these models can generate faithful code captions. The authors present these findings as their own assessment based on extensive experiments.

The articles do not say what happens next, beyond the paper's conclusion that current models fall short on faithful code captioning. The work is published on arXiv, where the full PDF, HTML and TeX source are available. The abstract frames code as a complementary representation of visual content rather than a replacement for natural language. No further steps, follow-up studies or deadlines are mentioned.

Articles.Title: CodeCap-Bench: Can Code Serve as a Good Video Caption?

stories.Headline: Leveraging Dale's Principle as an Inductive Bias in Recurrent Neural Networks
stories.Summary:
Jiyi Wang, Chenxiao Yang, Yujia Zhao, Jingzhao Zhang and Lu Mi posted a paper to arXiv on 5 November 2026 describing a recurrent neural network called EISep RNN. The paper says biological neurons obey Dale's principle, meaning each neuron sends out only excitatory or only inhibitory signals. It says earlier attempts to impose this rule on artificial networks often caused unstable training or worse performance. The authors present their architecture as a way to implement the principle through a learnable excitatory-inhibitory separation.

The paper reports results across several learning settings, including multi-task learning, continual learning and reinforcement learning. It says EISep gives more stable training dynamics and performance that is competitive with or better than vanilla RNNs and earlier Dale-constrained models. It also reports sparser, more modular connectivity and stable, informative latent dynamics. The authors conclude that Dale's principle works as a biologically grounded and computationally effective inductive bias for recurrent networks.

The work is credited to the five named authors, and the abstract presents the claims as their findings. The paper says the separation of excitatory and inhibitory outputs is learnable in EISep. It frames the results as establishing Dale's principle as a useful inductive bias, in the authors' words. The abstract does not name any other institution or individual as responsible.

The posting is listed with a DOI and a date of 5 November 2026, and the page offers a PDF, experimental HTML and TeX source. The page also describes arXivLabs, a framework where collaborators develop and share features on the site. It says partners in arXivLabs accept values of openness, community, excellence and user data privacy. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the paper's availability.

Articles.Title: Leveraging Dale's Principle as an Inductive Bias in Recurrent Neural Networks

stories.Headline: EvaOmni: An Evidence-Grounded Benchmark for Audio-Visual Reasoning
stories.Summary:
Xiaoxing Hu and 19 other authors posted a paper titled EvaOmni: An Evidence-Grounded Benchmark for Audio-Visual Reasoning on arXiv on November 5, 2026. The paper introduces a benchmark for testing whether Omni large language models can find key audio and visual evidence and combine information across modalities. The authors say existing audio-visual benchmarks mostly use multiple-choice questions and score models only on whether the answer is correct. That makes it hard to tell whether a model really builds a reasoning chain from evidence to the right answer.

The benchmark contains 392 videos and 1,027 question-answer pairs, all annotated purely by humans. It covers 15 capabilities across three levels: retrieval and localization, basic understanding, and complex reasoning. The authors designed annotation procedures in which experts mark audio and visual evidence and build video-based distractors, humans review whether questions meet strict criteria, and models filter out textual and unimodal shortcuts. Models must return both the answer and the supporting evidence intervals, and the authors propose the Coverage Grounded Score (C.G.) to measure how much annotated evidence a model identifies and the Bottleneck Grounded Score (B.G.) to penalize poor temporal localization in either modality, with both folded into answer correctness.

The authors tested 7 open-weight and 17 proprietary Omni LLMs. Gemini3.7-Flash had the highest overall accuracy at 79.4%, the highest C.G. at 70.8%, and the highest B.G. at 35.1%. At Level 3 it reached 79.1% accuracy, but its B.G. was only 12.3%. The authors say these results show that even the most advanced models still have room to develop in grounded audio-visual reasoning.

The paper appears on arXiv, which also describes arXivLabs as a framework that lets collaborators develop and share features on the site. The authors state that individuals and organizations working with arXivLabs have accepted values of openness, community, excellence, and user data privacy. arXiv says it is committed to these values and works only with partners that adhere to them. The page also invites ideas for projects that would add value for the arXiv community.

Articles.Title: EvaOmni: An Evidence-Grounded Benchmark for Audio-Visual Reasoning

stories.Headline: CasePlay: Self-Play Reinforcement Learning from Case Reports for Medical Reasoning
stories.Summary:
Hao Wang, Zihan Wang, Kai Wu, Jian Yao, Yiwen Ye, Yongcan Luo, Dapeng Wu, Jiale Chen and Haihua Yang posted a paper on arXiv on 5 November 2026 describing CasePlay, a self-play reinforcement learning framework for medical reasoning. The work asks whether self-play grounded in documents can turn clinical case reports into effective training signals for large language models. Case reports trace the full clinical course from first presentation to final treatment decisions, and the authors note that the medical literature holds many such high-quality unlabeled documents. Current pipelines for improving clinical reasoning often depend on expert-labeled questions or costly synthetic data generation. The paper identifies two problems with existing self-play methods in this setting.

The first is knowledge-point fixation, where the proposer keeps asking about a narrow set of salient clues in a source report. The second is difficulty-quality mismatch, where questions of suitable difficulty may still be poorly formed or shallow and so are of limited value for training a reasoner. CasePlay addresses these with a Knowledge-Conditioned Proposer, which anchors question generation to case-specific knowledge points so questions draw on a broader range of evidence, and a Rubric-Judge Reasoner, which adds rubric-based quality feedback on clue integration, reasoning depth and option quality to answer-accuracy feedback. The authors say this guides the proposer toward reasoning-intensive questions that better support reasoner training. The authors report experiments across seven medically related benchmarks.

They say CasePlay outperforms existing self-play baselines and improves the SFT warm-start model by 3.1 points on average. They highlight a 6.3-point gain on LiveClin. The paper is listed under Machine Learning, with Artificial Intelligence and Computation and Language also given as categories. The authors present the approach as an effective path toward continually improving medical reasoning ability through self-play reinforcement learning. The abstract does not say what happens next beyond that claim.

Articles.Title: CasePlay: Self-Play Reinforcement Learning from Case Reports for Medical Reasoning

stories.Headline: GeoReason: Bridging Logical Reasoning and Spatial Fidelity in Remote Sensing Segmentation
stories.Summary:
Cheng Fan, Han Wu, Tingzhang Luo, Minjing Dong, Yehui Tang and Jianyuan Guo posted a paper on arXiv on November 5, 2026 describing a framework called GeoReason for remote sensing segmentation. The work addresses instruction-driven perception in Multimodal Large Language Models under the “Embedding-as-Mask” paradigm. The authors say extending this capability to remote sensing reasoning segmentation is exceptionally challenging in cluttered geographical contexts with extreme scale variations. These conditions often lead to what the paper calls Spatial Fidelity Degradation and Target Misidentification.

The paper identifies a bottleneck it describes as the sequential alienation of the segmentation token [SEG] from its initial visual grounding within autoregressive generation. Because [SEG] is produced only at the end of long reasoning chains, it relies on visual evidence progressively diluted by linguistic abstraction and autoregressive noise. The authors call this information decay particularly catastrophic for remote sensing targets with minuscule pixel footprints, where even marginal fidelity loss leads to localization failure. GeoReason introduces an Anticipatory Prior mechanism that injects the [SEG] token directly into the initial user query, shifting it from a terminal output to a primary condition. This transforms the token into a persistent spatial anchor intended to prevent information decay during long-form linguistic inference.

The framework also adds a Location-aware Chain-of-Thought that enforces coarse-to-fine localization using bounding boxes. A Latent Patch-to-Token Alignment Loss explicitly aligns the latent segmentation token with physical remote sensing textures. The authors report that GeoReason consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods on the Earthreason and RRSIS-D benchmarks. They say code is available at a URL given in the paper.

The paper was posted on arXiv under identifier 2610.23416. The abstract page offers a PDF, experimental HTML and TeX source, and lists Cheng Fan and five other authors. The posting appears on arXiv, which describes arXivLabs as a framework allowing collaborators to develop and share features on the site. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the reported benchmark results and the availability of the code.

Articles.Title: GeoReason: Bridging Logical Reasoning and Spatial Fidelity in Remote Sensing Segmentation

stories.Headline: Event-STVG: Spatio-Temporal Video Grounding for Long-Form Event Reasoning
stories.Summary:
Yizhe Zhang and 12 other authors posted a paper titled Event-STVG: Spatio-Temporal Video Grounding for Long-Form Event Reasoning on arXiv on November 5, 2026. The paper introduces Event-STVG, a task that moves spatio-temporal video grounding from locating what is described toward event-level reasoning. The task unifies long-form context, repeated-event reasoning, event localization, role inference, and multi-target grounding. The authors say existing STVG benchmarks are largely centered on localizing targets through instance-specific descriptions and are largely decoupled from long-form reasoning emphasized in multimodal large language models. To support research on the task, the authors built a large-scale benchmark with 4,016 annotated event occurrences across soccer and seven additional domains.

Experiments with state-of-the-art multimodal large language models show substantial difficulty, with the strongest model reaching only 5.4% m-vIoU at the 10-minute horizon. Across domains, the authors consistently observe confusion among repeated same-type events, spatial grounding bottlenecks, and rare success in jointly grounding all required roles. The paper states that Event-STVG sets a new challenge for visual understanding in multimodal large language models. The authors say the task calls for future models that can jointly reason about complex events across space and time.

They state that code and annotations are available at a URL given in the paper. The paper is listed with a PDF, experimental HTML, and TeX source on arXiv. The abstract page also includes standard text about arXivLabs, a framework that lets collaborators develop and share features on the arXiv website. The articles give no further information on what happens next beyond the call for future models and the released code and annotations.

Articles.Title: Event-STVG: Spatio-Temporal Video Grounding for Long-Form Event Reasoning

stories.Headline: PACE: Pareto-Adaptive Compression for Efficient Native MLLMs
stories.Summary:
Lei Tian, Chunzheng Zhu, Kai Wu, Yifan Zhang and Haihua Yang posted a paper titled PACE: Pareto-Adaptive Compression for Efficient Native MLLMs to arXiv on November 5, 2026. The paper describes a compression framework for native multimodal large language models, which encode visual and linguistic sequences together in one autoregressive Transformer. Unlike conventional models that rely on external vision encoders, these native models tokenize pixel patches directly and can suffer from severe visual token redundancy. The authors say a pilot study confirmed that native models tolerate aggressive compression with near-lossless or even improved performance, while ViT-based models degrade under compression.

The paper says existing compression methods target ViT-based settings, leaving native models unexplored. The authors introduce an analysis pipeline centered on token discriminability and cross-dimensional heterogeneous redundancy. They report that redundancy is distributed independently and heterogeneously along height and width axes, and that early-layer visual tokens are indiscriminable and uniformly redundant. PACE is described as the first visual token compression framework tailored for native MLLMs with Multimodal-RoPE, and experiments show it maintains near-lossless performance at only 25% to 50% visual token retention, even improving several benchmarks, while delivering over 2x FLOPs reduction.

The authors are responsible for the work, and the paper is listed under Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition and Artificial Intelligence. The abstract says PACE uses dimensional decoupling of positional encoding to decompose attention into two orthogonal spatial saliency estimates along height and width, gated by a positional attention signal, yielding direction-aware importance with negligible overhead. It further casts token budget allocation as Pareto optimization over performance preservation, inference efficiency and spatial coverage, jointly identifying optimal compression depths and retention ratios. The paper is available as a PDF, HTML and TeX source on arXiv.

The articles do not say what happens next beyond the paper's availability. They describe arXivLabs as a framework that lets collaborators develop and share features on the website, and say both individuals and organizations working with it have embraced values of openness, community, excellence and user data privacy. arXiv says it is committed to working only with partners that adhere to those values. The articles also invite ideas for projects that would add value for the arXiv community through arXivLabs.

Articles.Title: PACE: Pareto-Adaptive Compression for Efficient Native MLLMs

stories.Headline: BlenderWorld: Benchmarking Visual Agents for 3D Creation from Real-World References
stories.Summary:
A team of fifteen researchers led by Xinyu Fang released a benchmark called BlenderWorld on November 5, 2026, according to a paper posted on arXiv. The benchmark is described as the first comprehensive test for evaluating frontier models on realistic 3D creation tasks. It contains 223 tasks covering architecture, products, natural environments, and scientific visualization, and the tasks are driven by text, image, video, and structured specification inputs. The work was posted under the identifier 2610.23986.

The benchmark sets up a unified evaluation protocol, rendering submitted Blender projects from multiple viewpoints and scoring them against 2,651 task-specific binary rubrics along with holistic visual quality scores. The authors tested thirteen frontier models. GPT-6-Astra received the highest overall fused score of 79.9, followed by Opus-5 at 73.0 and GPT-5.6-Sol at 67.7. The paper reports that current models can parse broad instructions but still struggle with fine-grained 3D spatial coherence and accurate structural reproduction in Blender.

Separately, Loova AI launched Loova MCP, a Model Context Protocol integration, on November 3, 2026, according to a company announcement carried by GlobeNewswire. The integration brings AI image generation, AI video generation, and creative workflows directly to compatible AI agents. It runs on two layers, a foundational layer powered by premium models including Seedance, Kling, and Wan AI, and a second layer of creative workflows that orchestrate multiple production steps. The initial release includes nine specialized workflows across four production categories, including Product Photoshoot, Product Listing Images, UGC Ad Creator, Product Video Maker, Character Swap, Mimic Motion, and a Viral Video Clone workflow that accepts a reference video and lets creators review and revise an adaptation script before production begins.

Anbang Xu, founder at Loova, said professional creators need more ways to develop an idea and make it their own, and that with Loova MCP they can bring existing assets to the agent they prefer and choose the workflow that fits the project. The company says a single source asset can become a studio photograph, a listing image set, or a promotional video without rebuilding context or switching tools. Loova plans to expand into animation, short-form drama production, script development, storyboard generation, and video assembly tools. The BlenderWorld authors conclude that substantial headroom remains for future 3D-native agentics.

Articles.Title: BlenderWorld: Benchmarking Visual Agents for 3D Creation from Real-World References

stories.Headline: Deep Mesoscopic Dynamics
stories.Summary:
Yue Zhao, Shiqi Wu, Yihang Ouyang, Sergey Grebenchuk, Magdalena Grzeszczyk, Xiaoxu Zhao, Kostya S. Novoselov, Maciej Koperski and Qianxiao Li posted a paper titled Deep Mesoscopic Dynamics on arXiv on 5 November 2026. The work introduces a method called DeepMesoD, which uses neural networks to learn an effective mesoscopic field equation from microscopic trajectories at a set coarse-graining scale. The authors say microscopic simulations resolve spatial patterns but only over small domains and short timescales, while bulk descriptions average those patterns away. Mesoscopic fields keep the spatial organisation, but their effective equations are known only for selected systems and scaling limits.

For the nonconserved dissipative dynamics studied, DeepMesoD learns a free-energy functional with a spatial interaction kernel and a state-dependent dissipation operator tied to the fluctuation-dissipation relation. The method was first checked in the Ising-Kac model, where the learned equation recovered the known hydrodynamic limit and rollouts stayed stable well past the training horizon. The authors then treated two systems with no closed-form mesoscopic description. For a two-dimensional Heisenberg ferromagnet under atomistic spin dynamics, predictions matched atomistic references up to 1 ns and a rollout with an unseen initial condition stayed bounded up to 25 ns. For layered CrBr3, the learned kernel captured the suppression and sign reversal of interlayer coupling at a stacking fault whose location and strength were not given as inputs.

The authors report that controlled changes to the learned interaction show how fault number and placement shape multistep magnetic responses, complementing their magneto-photoluminescence measurements. Across the two atomistic systems, they say DeepMesoD gives a three-to-four-order-of-magnitude reduction in wall-clock time compared with atomistic spin dynamics. The paper is listed under Machine Learning, Statistical Mechanics and Computational Physics. The posting also describes arXivLabs, a framework for collaborators to develop and share features on the site, and says arXiv works only with partners who accept its values of openness, community, excellence and user data privacy.

Articles.Title: Deep Mesoscopic Dynamics

stories.Headline: From Stages to States: Unified Iterative Reasoning for MLLMs
stories.Summary:
Chuang Yu and 11 other authors posted a paper on arXiv on November 5, 2026, titled From Stages to States: Unified Iterative Reasoning for MLLMs. The paper proposes a framework called ReState for multimodal reasoning in Multimodal Large Language Models. Most learning-based Multimodal Chain-of-Thought methods follow a stage-centric paradigm, where different reasoning behaviors are assigned to predefined stages and optimized separately. The authors say this results in fragmented reasoning and a gap between training and inference reasoning states.

ReState reformulates multimodal reasoning from a stage-driven pipeline into a state-driven dynamic process. It has two components, Unified Reasoning State Modeling (URSM) and Closed-Loop Reasoning-State Learning (CRSL). URSM treats reasoning construction, correct reasoning preservation, and erroneous reasoning correction as transitions within a shared state space, so these behaviors are learned jointly. CRSL uses self-generated historical reasoning states during training and recursively updates the current state during inference, which the authors say mitigates the reasoning-state gap and enables iterative self-refinement without an additional reflection module, critic, or independent correction stage. The authors also built VersaCoT-10K, a CoT dataset spanning eight visual reasoning domains.

The authors report that experiments show ReState adapts across different MLLM backbones and performs strongly on multiple public reasoning benchmarks. They say the results support a shift from stage-centric reasoning toward state-centric reasoning. The paper lists Chuang Yu, Xuefei Ma, Yuanhao Feng, Wuxiong Zeng, Bo Wang, Minghong Cai, Dongming Wu, Fei Zhou, Chen Tang, Wenwen Tong, Lewei Lu, and Xiangyu Yue as authors. The abstract does not give further details on the experiments or the benchmarks used.

The paper's data and code are available at a link given in the abstract. The abstract frames the work as addressing the limitations of stage-centric MCoT methods. The posting also includes standard arXivLabs text about the framework for collaborators and its values of openness, community, excellence, and user data privacy. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the release of the paper and its data and code.

Articles.Title: From Stages to States: Unified Iterative Reasoning for MLLMs

stories.Headline: OWLET: On-Policy Weighted Learning via Evidence Transfer for Video Large Language Model Post-Training
stories.Summary:
Qitan Lv, Ke Fan, Hong Wang, Wen Wu, Yilin Wang, Bowen Zhou, Feng Wu and Chao Zhang posted a paper to arXiv on 5 November 2026 describing a post-training method for Video Large Language Models called OWLET. The method is built on an observation from their experiments: the same model reasons more accurately when its video view combines global temporal context with question-relevant details. Comparing the same student-generated response under that view and under uniform sampling showed changes in token likelihoods and internal representations, which the authors treat as a training signal for evidence use. The paper is listed under the identifier 2610.13272. The authors say existing post-training methods follow two main paradigms, reinforcement learning and on-policy distillation, and that neither fully exploits visual evidence.

Reinforcement learning, in their account, supervises the policy with a single trajectory-level reward, which they call too coarse-grained for video reasoning because the same response-level advantage is applied to every generated token. On-policy distillation gives token-level supervision through output-distribution matching but lacks direct supervision of the spatiotemporal representations that produce those outputs. OWLET is described as an evidence-privileged reinforcement learning method that derives training signals from a richer teacher view, which couples uniform global context with question-conditioned local windows and provides visual evidence without requiring a larger model. To exploit this privileged visual evidence, OWLET introduces two components. The first is evidence-aware credit redistribution, which compares token likelihoods across the two views and redistributes positive response-level advantages according to their relative evidence support.

The second is spatiotemporal state alignment, which aligns the two views' hidden states on responses accepted by a verifier. The paper presents these as its contributions for better using visual evidence during post-training. The abstract frames post-training as a key stage for eliciting reasoning capabilities in Video Large Language Models. It states that the authors observed the reasoning difference across extensive experiments. The article does not say what happens next, such as whether code or models will be released or where the work will be published.

Articles.Title: OWLET: On-Policy Weighted Learning via Evidence Transfer for Video Large Language Model Post-Training

stories.Headline: Cova-PINN: Cross-Domain Conservation Physics-Informed Neural Network for Fluid-Solid Conjugate Heat Transfer in Complex Geometries
stories.Summary:
Weizheng Zhang, Xunjie Xie, Hao Pan and Lin Lu posted a paper to arXiv on November 5, 2026 describing a new framework called Cova-PINN. The work addresses fluid-solid conjugate heat transfer in complex geometries, a problem that multi-domain physics-informed neural networks, or PINNs, are used to model. Standard multi-domain PINNs enforce governing equations and interface conditions on separately sampled domain supports. According to the abstract, this can produce plausible temperature fields but inaccurate end-to-end energy transfer and outlet temperatures.

Cova-PINN aligns conservation support with thermal interaction paths in complex geometries. It jointly optimizes cross-domain composite control-volume balances at the local scale and paired-wall closure at the global exchanger scale. The authors evaluated it on four triply periodic minimal surface, or TPMS, heat exchangers and on a geometrically distinct DualMS design. They compared it against CHT-specific, optimization-oriented and complex-geometry PINN baselines under a common protocol.

Relative to the closest baseline, MUSA-PINN-CHT, Cova-PINN reduces average outlet-temperature errors by 37.7 percent across the four TPMS topologies. It reduces device-level closure errors by 60.2 percent over the same set. The abstract also reports improved full-field and heat-duty accuracy, with consistent gains on DualMS. The authors present these results as evidence that the framework improves on the baselines under the shared protocol.

The paper is listed on arXiv with the identifier 2610.11108, and the full PDF and experimental HTML versions are available. The abstract frames the motivation as the gap between plausible temperature fields and accurate end-to-end energy transfer in standard multi-domain PINNs. It does not state any deployment, publication in a journal, or follow-up work. The articles give no further details on what happens next.

Articles.Title: Cova-PINN: Cross-Domain Conservation Physics-Informed Neural Network for Fluid-Solid Conjugate Heat Transfer in Complex Geometries

stories.Headline: Origins of Universal Machine Learning Force-Field Errors in Multicomponent Materials
stories.Summary:
A study posted on arXiv on November 5, 2026 examines why universal machine learning force fields make errors when applied to multicomponent materials. Hongwei Du and 13 other authors built a benchmark of 7,599 multicomponent configurations, inspired by high-entropy design, elemental substitution and anion mixing. They evaluated eleven pretrained models against density functional theory for energies, forces and stresses, and extended the assessment to elastic, vibrational and adsorption-related properties. The work is listed under materials science, machine learning and computational physics.

The study analyzes force errors through training-reference coverage, local geometric heterogeneity, distance directionality and elemental response. Distances to training-reference environments show a qualitative link between coverage differences and growing errors, though substantial variation remains at similar distances. Higher-error groups show greater local geometric heterogeneity, even though OMat24 covers these environments broadly. Relative to training-reference pair medians, errors stay low near the median, rise steeply on the compression side and increase more weakly on the extension side. After matching element pairs and absolute distance deviations, compression-side force errors are 1.81 to 1.95 times extension-side errors, and model-predicted pairwise interaction curves show greater curvature under compression.

The authors report that fitting difficulty in independent elemental systems correlates with electronic band-energy responses to atomic displacements and Fermi-level shifts, with a similar pattern in multicomponent systems. In parameter-matched comparisons, spherical-harmonic representations with maximum degrees of 2 and 4 lower test force errors for 38 and 40 of 43 elements respectively, while differences in elemental difficulty remain. The authors say the findings can inform force-field selection for experimental compositional design and identify targets for training-data sampling and model representations. The abstract does not state further planned work.

Articles.Title: Origins of Universal Machine Learning Force-Field Errors in Multicomponent Materials

stories.Headline: VisionWeave: Weaving Elastic Visual Representations as a Native Capability of MLLMs
stories.Summary:
A team of researchers led by Yuan Feng and Qize Yang, with co-authors Qize Yang, Ruizhe Chen, Sibo Song, Haolin He, Muzhi Zhu, Zihan Liu, Yunfei Chu, Xize Cheng, Yuxuan Wang, Jin Xu and Xike Xie, posted a paper on arXiv on November 5, 2026 describing a method called VisionWeave. The work addresses a cost problem in multimodal large language models, which encode visual inputs into dense, fixed-size patch tokens even though visual information is unevenly distributed across an image. The authors say downsampling loses detail, while existing token pruning and adaptive approaches are limited in content-adaptive granularity, task generalization, and integration with modern models and serving infrastructure. They propose teaching models to learn end to end where, and at what granularity, to allocate visual representations, a capability they call elastic visual representation weaving.

VisionWeave has two parts. A gated spatial pooler builds coarse-grained representations alongside native fine-grained ones within a shared MRoPE coordinate, and a granularity router learns how to allocate them based on content. The authors validated the capability through self-distillation alone on Qwen3.5-4B and scaled to Qwen3.8-27B using over 30K A100 GPU-hours. Based on Qwen3.8-27B, the method saved 43.0% of tokens on average while retaining 98.9% of native performance across eight benchmarks, compared with only 88% performance preserved by token pruning baselines with a fixed 50% savings target. On the SGLang serving engine it achieved a 2.3x throughput gain while reducing mean TTFT by 54.4% and mean TPOT by 60.6%.

The authors state that extensive evaluations confirm robust efficiency-quality trade-offs across diverse tasks, resolutions and video frames. They write that they believe these results position elastic visual weaving as a promising capability for next-generation multimodal models. The paper is listed under Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition, Artificial Intelligence, and Computation and Language. The abstract does not say what happens next beyond presenting the results and the authors' stated belief about the capability's promise.

Articles.Title: VisionWeave: Weaving Elastic Visual Representations as a Native Capability of MLLMs

stories.Headline: AI chatbot answers on data centers vary sharply
stories.Summary:
Research from Five Blocks, a digital reputation management company, found major differences in how eight AI engines described 25 major U.S. data center projects, TechGig reported on November 5, 2026. General descriptions were not negative, but 55 per cent of answers about project challenges were classified as negative. Google AI Mode gave negative responses to challenge questions 88 per cent of the time, while ChatGPT gave negative answers only 6 per cent of the time. A second Five Blocks study found that 83 per cent of answers discussing data centers and their neighbours offered one-sided criticism.

That second study compared the results with other industries, finding the share was similar to oil and gas pipelines but much higher than solar farms, which saw 35 per cent. ChatGPT was an outlier in the second study, consistently giving balanced responses about community concerns, while the other seven AI engines were rated as one-sided in nearly every evaluated answer. The research suggests AI-generated descriptions may not be reliable snapshots of a project's current status. It cited Microsoft's Fairwater Wisconsin project, where Copilot incorrectly claimed it did not exist until September 24.

The findings point to a problem for users trying to understand complicated issues, because two systems can give very different impressions without necessarily inventing any facts. The research underscores the need for critical evaluation, according to the report. The articles do not say who else is responsible or what happens next. More to follow.

Articles.Title: AI chatbot answers on data centers vary sharply

stories.Headline: Bengaluru leads India in FDE talent with 34 per cent share
stories.Summary:
Bengaluru accounts for 34 per cent of India's Forward Deployed Engineer talent, making it the country's largest hub, according to a report by FDE Academy. Hyderabad follows with 14 per cent of the talent pool, and Delhi NCR contributes 13 per cent. Together these three centres hold 61 per cent of India's FDE talent. Pune and Mumbai add 12 per cent and 11 per cent respectively, while Chennai and other cities each account for 8 per cent.

About 38 per cent of FDE professionals work in Big Tech companies, while product companies and IT services and consulting firms each employ 24 per cent. AI-first startups make up the remaining 14 per cent. Around 70 per cent of FDE professionals have eight years of experience or less, which the report says points to a need for deeper pools of experienced talent as enterprise AI adoption grows. Customer and consulting capabilities appear in 98 per cent of FDE job postings analysed, core engineering skills in 94 per cent, and cloud and AI operations in 84 per cent. Employers are moving beyond conventional coding tests, using deployment case studies, system design interviews, client simulations, and portfolio reviews.

The report gives indicative median annual salaries for field-deployed AI builders of ₹32 lakh for those with zero to three years of experience, rising to ₹1.55 crore for those with more than 15 years. Transformation, governance, and risk roles are the top hiring priority for 28 per cent of employer respondents, though only 18 per cent of professionals said they preferred that career path. Raghav Gupta, Founder and CEO of FDE Academy, said AI deployment requires a mix of engineering depth, business understanding, and the ability to take ownership of outcomes in a customer's environment. He added that access to this combination of skills will become increasingly important as organisations move beyond pilots.

Articles.Title: Bengaluru leads India in FDE talent with 34 per cent share

stories.Headline: Sam Altman praises Indian AI optimism, calls US pessimistic
stories.Summary:
Sam Altman, the CEO of OpenAI, said on the “Figuring Out” podcast with entrepreneur Raj Shamani that Indians show considerable optimism about artificial intelligence while Americans are generally more pessimistic. He confirmed that India has overtaken the US to become OpenAI’s largest market by user count. The remarks were published in a TechGig report on November 5, 2026. Altman linked the differing attitudes to economic conditions, saying developing economies with rapid growth and high demand for products are more receptive to new technology.

Altman pointed to India’s strong community for AI experimentation and cited Indians using AI tools for practical tasks, including a student who organised a school fundraiser without prior experience. He also said his decision to hold no equity in OpenAI was a mistake. He explained that the choice has caused confusion despite his initial good intentions for the company. The report gave no further figures beyond India passing the US as OpenAI’s largest user market.

Altman is responsible for the comments, which he made in the podcast conversation with Shamani. He described India’s optimism and the US pessimism as a notable contrast in how the two countries see AI. He attributed the gap to economic conditions rather than to anything specific about the technology itself. He also acknowledged the equity decision as an error on his part.

The context is OpenAI’s user base, where India now leads by user count ahead of the US. The report ties the more receptive attitude in developing economies to rapid growth and high demand for products. It does not say what OpenAI plans to do next or whether any policy or product changes follow from the remarks. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Sam Altman praises Indian AI optimism, calls US pessimistic

stories.Headline: AI-linked breaches target access tokens, accelerate attacks
stories.Summary:
AI-related cyberattacks are rising, with hackers stealing AI access tokens and using AI tools to speed up intrusions. Over the past month, at least a dozen AI developer platforms were hit, including CommandCode, Northflank, Trigger.dev, Chainstack and WorkOS. The attackers mainly sought stored customer secrets. The Cloud Security Alliance said intruders reach AI provider credentials through intermediary layers such as hosting platforms, evaluation services and developer consoles, and a single intrusion at that layer can expose keys for many inference accounts at once.

Chainstack was hit on October 26, when attackers reached a development environment and parts of its production environment through a third-party component. This exposed customer account information including organization names, account holder names, email addresses and password hashes, and node credentials may also have been exposed, prompting customers to rotate them. On October 30, hackers compromised an internal application used by WorkOS's sales team, accessing business contact details, customer account histories, sales details, customer-relationship information and customer communications. Chainstack and WorkOS disclosed attacks that used the open-source Artex AI penetration testing framework for automation, and multiple companies have linked attacks attributed to the Chinese APT Storm-0940 to Artex.

Wiz's analysis says the surge is driven by the rise of LLM-jacking and LLM broker infrastructure, which makes stolen AI access tokens easily monetizable and attracts more threat actors to credential theft. Wiz also observed hackers abusing enterprise credentials compromised in these attacks, including two cases with identical unauthorized activity within 30 minutes of reported access. Multiple threat actors using the same compromised keys suggest a robust market for this type of credential. The articles do not say what happens next.

Articles.Title: AI-linked breaches target access tokens, accelerate attacks

stories.Headline: NIST Tests AI Tool to Map Building Interiors for First Responders
stories.Summary:
NIST's Communications Technology Laboratory, through its PSCR Innovation Lab, is testing an automated tool called INSIGHT that turns building scans into structured data to help first responders plan for indoor emergencies. The article, published November 6, 2026 by HPCwire, explains that outdoor disasters give responders satellite imagery, GIS, GPS, and drone data, but indoor incidents do not offer those tools. Existing building records are usually flat two-dimensional blueprints that may be outdated and often leave out standpipes, shutoffs, alarm panels, and AEDs. The pipeline is designed to produce that missing information more quickly and at lower cost than manual documentation. The article says the stakes are high because responders currently must make risky decisions with incomplete information.

NFPA 1660 and NFPA 950, safety standards published by the National Fire Protection Association, call for detailed, interoperable pre-incident data, but departments have no practical way to produce it at scale. INSIGHT addresses this by generating scene graphs from scans, with a human reviewer correcting the automated output rather than labeling everything from scratch. The article states that the results can be delivered to responders within seconds over existing broadband infrastructure. It also describes a query-time role filter that lets dispatch, incident command, and discipline-specific teams each see the view most relevant to them.

PSCR describes the tool as following the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, which calls for explainable and accountable automation in high-risk settings. Independent detection paths within the pipeline check one another, and any disagreement between them is flagged for a person to review. Building codes are used to identify implausible results. The article attributes a key finding to a 2025 cross-dataset analysis that used PSCR-funded Point Cloud City data, which showed that existing 3D methods performed at near zero on small safety fixtures such as exit signs, AEDs, and alarm panels.

INSIGHT is built to address that measured gap. The article says the current work covers only the pre-incident planning phase, and PSCR plans later phases that add live tracking and command applications.
