The pipeline is built on a public dataset and open-source tools, and its outputs follow ISO 19164, IndoorGML, and IFC naming conventions, with source code and dataset documentation to be published. More to follow.

Articles.Title: NIST Tests AI Tool to Map Building Interiors for First Responders

stories.Headline: Indian IT firms face FDE talent gap for AI projects
stories.Summary:
Indian IT services companies are building workforces of forward-deployed engineers, known as FDEs, for AI projects, TechGig reported on November 5, 2026. These engineers work directly with customers to identify business problems, develop AI-powered solutions, and take them into production. The push has exposed a talent gap, because the role needs hands-on experience that conventional training does not provide. HCLTech, LTM, Wipro, and Coforge are combining external recruitment with internal upskilling to fill it. A report by Scaler and CyberMedia Research found that 88 per cent of surveyed enterprises expect demand for FDE capabilities to rise by 2030, while only 1 per cent of engineers currently hold explicit FDE roles.

During the September quarter of FY27, about 15 per cent of HCLTech's 6,136 freshers were recruited under its elite engineer category for further FDE training. HCLTech is also launching an enterprise-wide FDE Academy, with training tracks aligned to technologies from OpenAI, Anthropic, Amazon Web Services, Google, and Nvidia, plus a programme being developed with Microsoft. Wipro's AI-native business unit has over 2,000 engineers, including FDEs, and Coforge is moving towards hybrid human-agent delivery teams supported by FDEs. HCLTech acknowledged that freshly recruited engineers cannot immediately perform FDE responsibilities. LTM chief executive officer Venu Lambu said the company was accelerating hiring in data and AI areas while upgrading the capabilities of its existing workforce.

Amar Srivastava, CEO of Online Business and Group CPO at Scaler, said companies struggle to find employees with the full range of FDE skills, and suggested that a long-term strategy for 60 to 70 per cent of talent is internal upskilling. Wipro chief executive officer Srinivas Pallia said the company was developing FDE capabilities within its AI-native unit and through technology partnerships, and Coforge chief executive officer Sudhir Singh sees hybrid teams of engineers and AI agents as an important part of its future delivery model. The gap is significant as Indian IT companies reorganise delivery teams around AI agents and smaller groups of engineers responsible for business outcomes. Demand for engineers with a mix of technical expertise, business understanding, and client-facing skills continues to outstrip availability. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the companies' current recruitment, training, and partnership efforts.

Articles.Title: Indian IT firms face FDE talent gap for AI projects

stories.Headline: OpenAI’s AI models assist Mazda, Chip Ganassi in vehicle design
stories.Summary:
OpenAI has begun working with Mazda and Chip Ganassi Racing to apply its AI models to vehicle engineering, according to a report published on November 5, 2026. OpenAI's forward-deployed engineers are working alongside Mazda's aerodynamics and crash-safety engineers to explore how the company's models can help develop and evaluate vehicle designs. The research collaboration uses airflow and structural simulations to assess performance while also accounting for styling and manufacturing costs. Within this work, GPT-6 Astra, used through Codex, helps Mazda engineers explore different vehicle nose shapes, simulate airflow, and find designs that could reduce aerodynamic drag.

Akihiro Nakata, Principal Engineer at Mazda, said the models let engineers test dozens of design variations and see how individual features affect airflow. OpenAI is also widening its work with Chip Ganassi Racing, known as CGR, to apply its models to engineering and prototyping. Working with CGR's research and development team, OpenAI is testing workflows that turn 3D scans of existing components into editable CAD models and two-dimensional manufacturing drawings. Matthew Ortman, an R&D engineer at Chip Ganassi Racing, said Codex lets engineers work directly in CAD software, apply feedback to generated models, and make manual adjustments.

OpenAI itself acknowledged that its models still struggle to account consistently for manufacturing constraints, tolerances, and assembly requirements. That shortcoming means human engineering review remains necessary before designs move into production. The collaboration is at an early research stage, and the articles do not say how long it will run or when any resulting designs might reach vehicles on the road. The reports also do not provide details on the results achieved so far.

Articles.Title: OpenAI’s AI models assist Mazda, Chip Ganassi in vehicle design

stories.Headline: WorkOS sales app breached by ARTEX AI, customer data accessed
stories.Summary:
WorkOS reported a data breach affecting an internal sales application, identified on October 30, 2026. An attacker used an AI offensive security framework called ARTEX AI to access business contact records and customer communication summaries. The company said its app data and production services were not affected. WorkOS provides APIs and tools for enterprise authentication and identity management.

The accessed data included names, email addresses, job titles, and company affiliations from CRM systems. Customer account histories and summaries of sales calls, support discussions, and Slack conversations were also compromised. Company founder Michael Grinich said the investigating team found user agents such as "artex-enrich/1.0" in web requests from the threat actor. WorkOS disabled external access to the compromised application and engaged an independent forensics firm.

Grinich said the incident is now contained and promised further information once the investigation is complete. WorkOS will directly notify affected customers and advised users to be vigilant for phishing attempts. ARTEX AI was released by Chinese developers as an open-source project and became private after being linked to attacks on South Korean banks. CrowdStrike reported that the cyber-espionage group Vapor Panda used the framework in a global campaign targeting 200 organisations, and the non-profit DIVD said the framework powered its attacks in September.

Articles.Title: WorkOS sales app breached by ARTEX AI, customer data accessed

stories.Headline: Agentic AI Foundation aims for rapid AI agent standards
stories.Summary:
The Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation is working to set standards for AI agents, including the Model Context Protocol. Its executive director, Mazin Gilbert, said the foundation must move faster than its member companies to stay relevant. He said protocols like MCP act as plumbing that keeps the ecosystem from becoming a mess that is expensive and prohibitive for companies to deploy at scale. OpenAI, Anthropic and Google contribute to the standards even though they compete on products, and they build products both with and without them.

The MCP specification, which made the protocol stateless, was released in July, and companies updated their entire stacks to it. MCP downloads grew tenfold in its first 10 months at the foundation after Anthropic donated it in December. Fewer than 15 per cent of MCP maintainers now work at Anthropic, while over 1,000 organisations contribute 75 per cent of pull requests, including US retailers and global companies. The AAIF has 305 members, with roughly one new company joining daily, making it the fastest-growing foundation in the Linux Foundation's history.

The foundation launched its Model Context Protocol Associate certification in September to help companies and developers learn about agents. The Gates Foundation, which joined in September, is helping developers in parts of Africa and South Asia access training and certification. The AAIF hosts 10 projects, including Agent Skills from Anthropic, Open Responses from OpenAI, OpenEnv from Hugging Face and OpenSandbox from Alibaba. Gilbert wants to expand the foundation's work to identity, security, trust, observability and agent commerce, including protocols for transactional agents, with physical AI also a future focus.

Articles.Title: Agentic AI Foundation aims for rapid AI agent standards

stories.Headline: Razorpay gets SEBI nod for ₹6,000 Cr IPO
stories.Summary:
Razorpay has received approval from the Securities and Exchange Board of India for its proposed initial public offering worth ₹5,000 to ₹6,000 crore. The fintech firm, founded in 2014 by Shashank Kumar and Harshil Mathur, secured the regulator's nod for the listing. Sources cited by Inc42 said the listing is expected between January and March 2027. The company is targeting a valuation of around $5 billion for the offering. The IPO is projected to include both a fresh issue and an offer-for-sale, though the split between the two remains undisclosed.

The $5 billion target is below the $7.5 billion valuation Razorpay commanded in its last funding round during 2021. Ahead of the listing, the company shifted its domicile from the US to India. Razorpay reported a net loss in FY25, mainly due to ₹1,209 crore in ESOP expenses and one-time restructuring and tax costs, while operating revenue rose 65 per cent to ₹3,783 crore in the same year. Razorpay has also been expanding its artificial intelligence offerings alongside its IPO preparations. Last month it announced an expanded partnership with OpenAI to help Indian brands advertise on ChatGPT through its growth marketing platform, Razorpay Engage.

The company also introduced Vulcan, a transformer-based AI model for digital payments built with NVIDIA and AWS technology, which it says can score payment routes in real time and identify fraud patterns. It is additionally developing Agent Studio, a platform for deploying task-specific AI agents, which about 200 businesses were using in beta as of August. Razorpay has raised over $800 million to date, with investors including Y Combinator, Tiger Global Management, Ribbit Capital, and Lightspeed. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the expected listing window and the planned IPO structure.

Articles.Title: Razorpay gets SEBI nod for ₹6,000 Cr IPO

stories.Headline: Thinking Machines’ new model takes the lead in western open-weight AI
stories.Summary:
Thinking Machines, a small AI startup founded by former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati, has released a new model called Inkling 2 Small. According to third-party tester Artificial Analysis, the model is set to challenge Chinese models, which have led the open-weight field for several years. The company said it will make the model's weights available next week, after the model was initially offered as proprietary. The model has 594 billion parameters, accepts image inputs and produces only text. Thinking Machines said it is stronger at coding and easier to use inside real agent loops.

Artificial Analysis gave it a score of 31 on its Intelligence Index, tying it with Gemini 3.8 Flash, while Gemini 4 Carbon and Claude Opus 5.5 score 60 and 59. Reviewers said it improved 41% in automation capabilities and 20% in coding over its predecessor. Artificial Analysis said the model's planned weight release would make it the highest-scoring open-weight model developed outside China based on current rankings. The firm also described Inkling 2 Small as notably slow per task and very verbose, and called its pricing somewhat expensive at $0.30 per million input tokens against a class median of $0.24.

It also reported that the hallucination rate on its AA-Omniscience test fell from 61% to 27%. The staggered release follows a pattern in which AI companies test models with cybersecurity teams and safety reviewers for a few weeks before publishing weights, given heightened security concerns. French lab Mistral recently released its Le Chonk model the same way, and it matches OpenAI's GPT-6.1 Terra in coding, which is rare for Western open models. The article notes that Chinese models from DeepSeek and Moonshot have rivaled far more expensive closed models since DeepSeek's R1 appeared in January 2025.

Articles.Title: Thinking Machines’ new model takes the lead in western open-weight AI

stories.Headline: AI coding agents shift bottleneck to debugging, comprehension
stories.Summary:
AI coding agents now generate code quickly, but engineers struggle to understand and debug what the agents produce. Dr. Greg Law, co-founder and CTO of Undo, described this shift in the development bottleneck. Engineers have trouble grasping what AI-generated code does and how it interacts with existing systems. That makes tracking down bugs and investigating incidents harder.

As AI produces more code, duplicated logic and layers of change create what the article calls a spaghettification of the codebase. Nine in ten engineering leaders say code comprehension and debugging take longer in complex environments such as C/C++ codebases. Despite faster code generation, 79 per cent of engineering leaders report their release cycles are no quicker. AI agents also work from static context like source code and logs, which does not show what the code actually did at runtime. That lack of context can lead to incorrect diagnoses, with 93 per cent of engineering organisations reporting problems from AI hallucinations.

The article says the focus should be on giving agents better evidence rather than more powerful models. Providing a record of what happened when code ran helps an agent understand how an issue occurred. This lets AI trace problems to their root causes and support engineers with debugging. The article adds that AI's effectiveness ultimately depends on the quality of the information it receives.

Articles.Title: AI coding agents shift bottleneck to debugging, comprehension

stories.Headline: India's IT ministry proposes AI model vetting framework
stories.Summary:
India's IT ministry released a draft framework for training AI models on October 29, 2026. The proposal sets out end-to-end safeguards, including verification before deployment. Under the draft, models must be verified as "fit for use" before they are deployed. The framework recommends that a competent government authority carry out the diligence process.

The verification would check compliance with standards for fairness, bias mitigation, and data security, according to the draft Data Empowerment and Protection Architecture for AI Training. Institutions holding valuable AI training data, such as hospitals and banks, are classified as Training Data Providers. Entities seeking to use that data, including startups and researchers, are designated Training Data Consumers. Both would register on a Data Exchange Platform, and actual training would occur within a Secure Data Environment. Models trained under this DEPA network would undergo validation and bias detection, and only those that pass would receive approval for pilot deployment and scaling.

Salman Waris, founder and managing partner at law firm TechLegis, told Moneycontrol that the industry should treat the framework as a proto-licence that could harden into one through future rules or sectoral guidelines. He clarified that participation is voluntary and that the verification obligation would attach only to models trained through the DEPA network, not to all AI models in India. He noted that the trajectory suggests a de facto sector-specific pre-deployment approval if the framework is formalised, especially with planned pilots in regulated sectors like finance and healthcare. Sharad Sharma, co-founder of iSPIRT Foundation and a member of the steering committee that drafted the framework, dismissed the licensing categorisation. He said the proposal aims to establish a self-regulatory, multi-stakeholder governance collective.

That collective would bring together data providers, AI developers, technology providers, domain experts, civil society, and government representatives. Sharma told Moneycontrol that this body would undertake due diligence, oversee, and enforce compliance in alignment with applicable laws, which he distinguished from government licensing. A similar advisory in 2024 was withdrawn after widespread criticism, which cited fears of throttling innovation and creating bureaucratic bottlenecks. Industry stakeholders have expressed concerns that the framework could function as a licensing mechanism.

Articles.Title: India's IT ministry proposes AI model vetting framework

stories.Headline: SUSE to cut 10 per cent of global workforce, cites AI and automation
stories.Summary:
SUSE plans to cut about 10 per cent of its global workforce, which could affect around 190 employees from a reported 1,900-strong workforce. CEO Dirk-Peter van Leeuwen cited artificial intelligence and automation in an internal memo sent on Monday. Affected employees are expected to be informed by November 4. Employee representatives are scheduled to be nominated the following day, and individual meetings are expected to begin early next week.

The memo said automation and AI are fundamentally shifting how software companies operate. It said modern tooling is already changing daily workflows, letting teams move faster with less operational overhead and flatter reporting lines. The requirement for some existing roles has greatly diminished, and other roles will evolve over the next few years. The company has not disclosed which roles or geographical regions will be affected, and the impact on its Indian workforce remains unclear.

Van Leeuwen described the decision as painful for employees, the company's culture and its open-source community, but necessary to adapt and build a sustainable SUSE for the long term. He said the existing organizational design and cost base would not carry the company forward successfully. He said the cuts reflect shifting organizational needs, not the talent or commitment of the staff. He added that any organization would be fortunate to have their expertise.

SUSE had previously offered voluntary exits to long-serving employees in September, but the offer reportedly did not attract enough volunteers. The company increased investment in AI in 2025 and announced agentic AI capabilities for its Linux management tools on October 27. The memo did not quantify the productivity improvements attributed to AI. SUSE is expected to brief remaining employees on its fiscal year 2027 strategy on November 16.

More than 137,000 technology workers across 340 companies have lost their jobs in 2026, according to Layoffs.fyi. Microsoft, Amazon, Innodata and Dropbox have also undertaken workforce reductions or voluntary exit programmes in recent weeks. EQT bought SUSE from Micro Focus for $2.5 billion in 2018 and floated it on the Frankfurt Stock Exchange in 2021. EQT took the company private again in 2023, and in March EQT was reportedly considering selling it off again.

Articles.Title: SUSE to cut 10 per cent of global workforce, cites AI and automation

stories.Headline: AI Tutors in Corporate Training: Design Determines Results
stories.Summary:
Randomized trials published in 2026 suggest that AI tutors help corporate and technical training only when they are built to teach rather than to finish tasks for the learner. A study in Nature Human Behaviour, published on October 26, 2026, found that management consultants at Boston Consulting Group who had access to ChatGPT, along with training on its use, scored 18 to 49 percentage points higher than untreated peers on data science tasks outside their skill sets. That advantage disappeared once the tool was removed, and the study's authors wrote that demonstrated technical capability did not show that knowledge had been acquired. Researchers at Boston University describe such general-purpose assistants as exoskeletons that extend what a worker can do without teaching the worker to do it.

The findings point to a different standard for learning tools. Evaluations should measure unassisted skill retention rather than course completion or task output, and designers should require attempts before explanations. In a preregistered Boston University field experiment with 86 Online MBA students, a structured tutor grounded in course materials produced 6.6 more points out of 55 than ability-matched peers and 2.6 more points on the instructor's final exam out of 100. Voice and text delivery produced the same learning, although voice cost 2.8 times as much to deliver. A Chinese cluster-randomized trial of 2,574 power utility employees found that an adaptive platform produced small knowledge gains that held at a follow-up about six weeks later, though the authors noted that the delivery medium and instructor contact changed too, so adaptivity alone cannot be credited.

The reports tie these lessons to Mexico, where surveyed firm adoption of AI rose from 24.3% in September 2025 to 48.5% in June 2026, reaching 69.9% among firms with more than 1,000 workers, according to MBN. The same report cites Mexico's National Human Resources Survey 2026, which found that 82% of employees have received no training in general-purpose AI tools. The MBN reporting also says that 65% of Mexican workers report difficulty obtaining certifications, against 48% globally, and that lack of time is the main barrier to skill development. Training providers such as UVM for Business, part of Laureate Mexico, have responded with short-format platforms like Menthera that aim to tie training to business outcomes rather than hours logged.

The articles also warn that adding a tutor does not guarantee gains. An October 2026 randomized trial of 2,379 undergraduates at a large US public university found that access to a course-integrated AI tutor lowered final grades by 0.37 standard deviations and reduced learning management system participation by 0.90 standard deviations, with greater losses among first-generation students. The authors suggested the tutor displaced existing engagement without improving performance. The articles frame this as a warning for companies that add tutors to existing programs without redesigning how employees learn.

Articles.Title: AI Tutors in Corporate Training: Design Determines Results

stories.Headline: Chip Stocks Cheaper Than S&P 500 as AI Premium Vanishes - Invesco PHLX Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SOXQ)
stories.Summary:
Chip stocks have fallen to a valuation below the broader market, a shift that analysts say marks the end of the premium investors paid for artificial intelligence exposure during the recent boom. According to a note shared on Friday by Bank of America analyst Vivek Arya, the PHLX Semiconductor Index, tracked by the Invesco PHLX Semiconductor ETF (SOXQ), trades at 13.7 times expected earnings over the next 12 months, while the S&P 500 trades at 17.7 times. That leaves chipmakers at a 22% discount to the market, compared with a 15% premium during the AI cycle. The article was published on November 6, 2026.

The index peaked at 14,634.72 on June 22 and closed Thursday at 9,011.14, a decline of 38% over 136 days, while the S&P 500 lost 2% over the same period. Bank of America tracked four earlier semiconductor downturns, in 2011, 2015 to 2016, 2018 and 2022, in which chip stocks fell between 23% and 46% and the S&P 500 fell between 12% and 25%, so the current gap is unusual. Chips rebounded on Friday, with the index rising 4.9% and the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) gaining 4.3%, but the index remained 35% below its peak. The article also reports that 28 of the 30 stocks in the iShares Semiconductor ETF now trade at least 20% below record highs.

The analysis ties the selloff to spending by cloud providers, which Bank of America says run about $300 billion a quarter, or $1.2 trillion annualized. Consensus expects $1.55 trillion in 2027, but if spending holds at the current pace, 2027 would come in about $355 billion, or 23%, below expectations. Arya said a 20% cut in 2027 capital spending would reduce sales for AI chipmakers by more than 20% and earnings by 35% to 40% or more. He added that today's discount already reflects considerable skepticism about the cycle. The article notes that in past cycles the index bottomed near 12 times forward earnings, which would imply at most another 12% of downside, but Arya expects earnings cuts to begin in the first quarter of 2027 and says investors will likely need to see them before confidence returns.

Arya's note is the source of the valuation and spending figures, and the article does not name anyone else responsible for the sector's decline. In his baseline case, with a bottom in the first quarter of 2027, he favors Lam Research, Nvidia, Broadcom, Micron and Texas Instruments. If the downturn extends into mid-2027, he expects Cadence Design Systems and Synopsys to hold up better, while in a sharp recovery high-beta names such as Micron and Advanced Micro Devices would lead. Over the past month Lam Research and Micron each fell more than 30%, while Texas Instruments slipped less than 5%. The article concludes that whether the market has fallen far enough depends on how much hyperscalers actually spend in 2027.

Articles.Title: Chip Stocks Cheaper Than S&P 500 as AI Premium Vanishes - Invesco PHLX Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SOXQ)

stories.Headline: Semiconductor Costs, AI Governance Reshape Tech Investment
stories.Summary:
Intel's shares fell more than 20 percent after its third-quarter 2026 earnings showed projected cash burn and weaker forward guidance, which it linked to cyclical softness in the PC market and heavy foundry spending. The sell-off signals liquidity and capital spending strain across the chip supply chain. The articles say this affects corporate IT planning, data center investment and hardware purchasing in Mexico. Some of the coverage points to the Guadalajara Design Center, which focuses on cost-effective enterprise AI architectures and hardware validation, as a sign of closer North American integration.

Marvell Technology has agreed to acquire optical components maker Lumentum in an all-stock deal valued at US$115 billion. The combination would join semiconductor, networking and photonics capabilities as demand for high-speed connectivity reshapes AI data center infrastructure. The articles say the deal would let Marvell compete more directly with Broadcom while widening its technologies for linking increasingly complex AI systems. Separately, Anthropic reported US$17 billion in third-quarter 2026 revenue as it prepares for a potential initial public offering. Its amended registration statement also disclosed US$895.4 billion in future purchase commitments and lease agreements.

Mexico's road modernization faces the challenge of keeping existing bridges and highways safe and operating, not only building new ones. Growing freight traffic, aging assets and greater exposure to climate events have led some managers to consider digital twins, which monitor critical bridges, flag anomalies and anticipate maintenance. The article raises the open question of how managers can confirm these systems catch real problems without producing false alarms or delays that compromise safety. Mexico's AI investment, meanwhile, is reaching a stage where adoption costs cannot be separated from governance costs. Companies are expanding AI into customer service, financial decisions, recruitment, software development and operations, yet many still lack structures to determine who is accountable when these systems fail.

Articles.Title: Semiconductor Costs, AI Governance Reshape Tech Investment

stories.Headline: DSCI proposes framework for AI liability, accountability across value chain
stories.Summary:
The Data Security Council of India proposed an industry framework to decide who is liable when autonomous AI agents cause harm. The framework is titled AI Liability: Industry Guidance for Agentic AI, and TechGig published its report on November 5, 2026. It recommends assigning responsibility across the AI value chain based on the decisions each participant makes and how much control they have. DSCI wants existing laws, contractual obligations, and sectoral regulations applied rather than a new regulatory framework.

The framework identifies five groups in enterprise AI deployment: end-user organisations, service providers and integrators, product companies and startups, tool and framework providers, and cloud and infrastructure providers. AI model providers are examined separately. It lists 12 areas of potential harm, including privacy breaches, security threats, discrimination, safety risks, inaccurate outputs, intellectual property violations, deepfakes, loss of control, and AI-enabled cybercrime. It draws on existing legal principles such as duty of care, product liability, causation, and comparative negligence, and proposes an authority map to establish who controlled a decision and whether they could have prevented or limited the harm. It also proposes six safeguards, including removing unnecessary capabilities, restricting permissions, requiring human approval for significant or irreversible actions, monitoring AI behaviour, enabling systems to scale back safely, and deploying kill switches with clearly defined ownership.

Under the proposal, companies deploying AI agents would be responsible for choosing use cases, setting permissions, assessing operational risks, and deciding when human approval is required. Product companies could be held accountable for product claims, default settings, and model versions, while system integrators would answer for system design, approval mechanisms, and handling failures. Tool and framework providers would be accountable for the orchestration, memory, and safety features they supply, and cloud and infrastructure providers for system isolation, identity management, data retention, and platform logs. DSCI said model providers should remain responsible for the capabilities they develop, safety measures, disclosures about known limitations, and notifications of significant changes in model behaviour, with their liability possibly reduced when others take control of deployment and use.

DSCI has invited AI developers, industry members, policy think tanks, and other stakeholders to submit feedback, and plans further guidance on authority mapping, AI deployment in physical and biological systems, and agents operated by customers and business partners. The proposal comes amid growing scrutiny of autonomous AI systems. Last month, MeitY proposed a consent-based framework called the Data Empowerment and Protection Architecture for AI Training, aimed at helping startups, businesses, and academic institutions access large-scale, India-specific datasets while protecting privacy and complying with the Digital Personal Data Protection Act. Separately, the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India released draft guidelines on responsible AI use in telecom networks and service delivery, with stakeholder comments invited by November 27.

Articles.Title: DSCI proposes framework for AI liability, accountability across value chain
